headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
ASSURING NEWS FROM CANTON.

From the tone of a letter received yesterday by Mr. Wong Tong, it appears that some of the "points" raised at Tuesday night's conference in Canton will be modified. Mr. Wong of the On Lok Yuen Co., was mainly responsible for sending the Chinese delegates from Hongkong to negotiate, with Canton, an end to the strike. The letter to Mr. Wong stated that the military, civil and labour authorities of Canton were very friendly to the Hongkong representatives. Certain demands at first raised would be changed for submission to a second conference which was to have sat last night. Mr. Wong, attributed the delay in news getting through to the temporary dislocation of the cable services. He was confident that excellent results would be forthcoming. His opinion was based on the warm welcome extended to the delegates, and the elaborate precautions regarding a private train with poured cars for prevention conveying troops. Mr. Wong felt that a much better tone would have prevailed at last night.

headline: SAI YINGPUN SCHOOL
text: In reply to the question asked by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak at the Legislative Council meeting to-day, the Colonial Secretary stated that if no unforeseen circumstances arise, it is hoped to complete and open Saiyingpun School by the 30th June, 1926. The work was delayed for about two months mainly owing to the Strike.

headline: SWATOW IMPROVES.
text:
CARGO LANDED BY S.S. "HYDRANGEA."

BOX COTT BELIEVED OVER.

This morning the s.s. "Hydrangea" returned to Hongkong from Swatow.

There was no incident in the voyage. All the cargo shipped from Hongkong was landed and fresh cargo was brought back. About a hundred passengers also travelled from Swatow on the ship.

The agritators are now believed to have put a good distance between themselves and the port of Swatow and the anti-foreign boycott has been described as all over.

headline: DOLLAR INTERESTS.
text:
MORE SHIPPING BOARD BUDS?

MONOPOL a ESTION.

So steamship company was interested at the time in these eve boats, negotiations centring entirely around the Pacific Mail boats, but there have been rumours for some time of negotiations proceeding. Between the Dollar interests and the Shipping Board for the forecast of these vessels also, Reports from Seattle that such negotiations are proceeding were confirmed by Rear Admiral Palmer, president of the Emergency Ship Corporation, in charge of ship entes.

Enquiries at the Hongkong office elicited no information of a definite nature, the only thing that was known being that the Board were seeking for purchasers of the vessels. There would be little change even if the Admiral Oriental Line purchased the ships, the "China Mail" was informed. They were already operated by this line on commission and the difference would be entirely a domestic one.

The bouts concerned are the President. "Madison," "Jackson," "McKinley," "Jefferson," and "Grant" and there are also freighters but whether they form the subject of negotiations is not known. If the five boats mentioned are taken over by the Dollar interests they will be the operators of practically ex-American vessel in the Oriental trade; only two other lines operating Shipping Board ships being in the Pacific. The question of advisability of such a monopoly has been raised in America but Shipping Board officials belittle its significance and refer to the competition with Japanese and Canadian ships on the Orient run which would make impossible any freight or passenger rate inflation.

In this connection it is interesting to recall that when interviewed on the subject of possible monopoly whilst on a visit to Hongkong, Capt. Robert Dollar said that the prosperity of his Company was so mextricably bound up with that of the various countries about the Pacific Ocean that fears regarding a monopoly had no possible foundation in fact.

headline: "UNIVERSITY" MEN / CANTON STUDENTS FINED
text:
SEDITIONS LITERATURE CHAPGE.

Possession of a seditious pamphlet and two Chinese newspapers containing pernicious references to the boycott position led to two Chinese students being brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday. The students came from Swatow by the s.s. "Haining" and the documents were found in their luggage when searched on the wharf.

One of the accused was fined $25, and the other was remanded until this morning as he wished to call a witness.

A shopkeeper from Shamshuipo informed His Worship that he was acquainted with the accused, who was a student from the Kwangtung University, and he had never heard of the man getting into trouble during the time he was in Hongkong.

His Worship was satisfied that the accused had no intention of passing the documents round and imposed a fine of $25.

headline: ENTERPRISE
text:
The reply of the Government to the question asked by the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird was given by the Colonial Secretary as follows at to-day's meeting of the Legislative Council:—

. A bureau for the voluntary registration of Chinese workers of all classes was experimentally established with the assistance of the Government in July last, but the response has hitherto been small.

In the same month a private individual put forward a proposal for the establishment of a Domestic Servants' Employment and Registration Bureau, and, in reply to an enquiry whether the Government would supervise it, he was asked to define the nature of the supervision required. No answer has been received.

The Government does not propose to establish a labour bureau, but it is prepared to consider the giving of assistance to private enterprise in this connection if concrete proposals are put before

headline: GAP IN THE LAW.
text:
HOW TO GET ROUND THE ORDINANCE.

HAPPY VALLEY PESTS:

Leighton Hill Road residents who have complained about the hawker nuisance in their part of Happy Valley will be interested to hear that a licensed seller cannot cry his wares but a man who illegally hawks with permission can shout as much as he likes!

As Mr. S. B. B. McElderry (Magistrate) remarked in the Police Court this morning, there is evidently a gap in the law.

Divisional Inspector Ogg added that the gap had been widened by the strike when unlicensed hawkers were immune from prosecution. The anomalous position then was that a licensed man had to keep silent while those who did not have to pay for licences could make all the noise they wanted.

A man was up charged with hawking Chinese newspapers without a licence. The offence he had actually committed was “crying his wares” in a prohibited area. But as he was unlicensed he could not commit a breach of the licence and he therefore had to be prosecuted for a misdemeanour. However, he satisfied His Worship that he was only a distributor and was, accordingly, discharged.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBT.
text:
SETTLEMENT DISPOINT. MENT RESULTS.

FRANC'S MARKED DROP.

Disappointment at the result of the absence of a permanent settlement of the French Debt is reflected to-day in an initial break of eight points in the France, to 4.61 cents. There is a decline in all French Bonds listed here in Wall Street which was expecting that the debt negotiations would pave the way for a French loan here shortly of probably $100,000,000.

headline: “DELIGHED.”
text:
HOME LABOUR CONGRESS WORK

London, October 2. The Labour Conference has concluded. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, in an interview, said he had been delighted with the Conference. It had been a great consolidating conference. They had removed mountains of misunderstanding and the industrial and political sections of the party were now better co-ordinated than ever.

headline: CANAL MISHAP:
text:
SLAVIC PRINCE STRIKES BANK.

SUGAR CARGO DAMAGED.

. The British steamer "Slavic Prince" from Hongkong and Batavia. to New York, struck a bank of the Suez Canal and is leaking in. No. 1 hold, containing sugar, some of which is wet as a result.

A survey has been recommended. The lives holes have been plugged and the vessel will proceed to Alexandria.

[The "Slavic Prince" left Hongkong on August 5. Very little cargo, if any, was placed on board here. When the "China Mail" inquired, the local office had not received any news from London.]

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / SENSATIONAL FREMANTLE INCIDENT.
text:
STEAMER BOARDED

Fremantle; October 3. Hundreds of strikers last night raided the steamer “Demodocus,” drew the fires and dropped the firebars, and threatened the cap tain and officers with violence if they resisted.

It is noteworthy that Mr. Bruce recently telegraphed the Westralian Premier condemning the failure to afford police protection to the "Demodocus" which the strikers boarded and persuaded the crew to join the strike.

The Marine Workers' Union has received a cable from the strikers in South Africa, asking: 'Is it advisable for strikers in South Africa to accept the following terms:—No prosecution of men; no victimisation and no pay until men resume work. Cape and South African Governments to urge Imperial Government to hold an impartial inquiry. Forty-eight hours given us to reply. Men at Durban solid if Marine Workers' Union considers strike should continue. Reply giving us your absolute confidence.'

A special meeting of the Union is to be called to decide whether these terms are satisfactory. A cable has been sent to the strikers in South Africa that the matter is being considered. A further cable will be sent immediately a decision is reached.

headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
EXPORT EMBARGO ON FOOD.

LATEST NEWS FROM PORT.

At present Swatow has an embargo on the export of food-stuffs from that port. It is not known if the embargo is being enforced as a result of the temporary regulations issued by the new authorities, or as part of the anti-foreign movement.

Chinese merchants who returned yesterday on the "Hydrangea" state that business conditions are returning to normal, and the situation is quiet. When the ship sailed, a number of men boarded the ship to search for foodstuffs but the speaker did not know if they were from labour unions or were empowered by the Government.

The "Hydrangea" brought back general cargo and a good many passengers.

headline: CADETS PAY $3,000.
text:
COMPENSATION FOR KILLE JAPANESE.

WHAMPOA RIVER SEQUEL

Compensation is reported to have been paid by the Canton Government in respect of the Japanese sailor who was killed by the Whampoa Cadets firing at a Japanese vessel, from the shore, on July 30.

For the dead man, $3,000 was offered and $500 each for the two men wounded, so it is stated, on a protest being made by the Japanese Consul at Canton, and following representations.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
CHINESE HOSTILITY TO PICKETS.

FARMER USES HIS POLE.

Reports of 'open hostility, and the loss of life in at least one instance, between Chinese strike pickets and the civil population, have reached Hongkong during the week-end.

headline: THREE STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
Mácao, October 4.

It is reported from Chinshan that strike pickets had the worse of a brawl with farmers in Chinese territory, resulting in the death of three strikers.

Early yesterday morning, a farmer was stated to be coming into Macao with vegetables. On nearing the border he was challenged by pickets. He threw down his two baskets and moved away. On three men of the picket coming up, he belaboured them with his bamboo pole until all three were badly bruised and unable to stand. Even with the pickets down, the farmer is alleged to have continued the assault until, so it is stated, life was extinct in each case. None of the pickets was armed.

headline: Shots: Fired.
text:
In the district of Po On (which adjoins the New Territory) trouble is believed to have broken out between armed tickets and the farmers' volunteers. Feeling has been running him for some time owing to the prompt of export of products to trongkong and consequent consscation.

Firing is said to have broken out between the rival factibns.

headline: Canton Incident.
text:
A passenger who returned on Saturday by the "Honam" relates an incident which he witnessed on the West Bund.

He says that among the food-stuffs sent up to Shameen from Hongkong was beef, in quarters, the dripping of which was cut off and often thrown into the river. Some of the very poor Chinese are said to have dived in the river for the dripping. On going ashore the divers were caught by strike pickets who set upon the divers for picking up cast-off food. One man was tied up on the Bund and beaten for half an hour.

headline: SOVIET CITIZENS.
text:
CONDITIONS OF RECENT AMNESITY.

The council of Commissaries has issued a decree that former prisons of war and interned persons of the old Imperial and Red armies, also participants in risings of White armies who come under conditions of the, amnesty shall lose their citizenship if they neglect to apply for restoration of citizenship within the period laid down by the decree.

This did not apply to persons who have not renewed their citizenship owing to lack of Soviet representatives in the country of their residence.

headline: PEACE DELEGATES:
text:
MERCHANTS RETURNING TO HONGKONG.

NO CONCRETE PROPOSAL.

No proposal that can be described as concrete has been put forward as the result of Hongkong delegation of Chinese merchants to Canton.

Some of the delegates returned yesterday and others are due back this week. They are to prepare a document reporting their activities in Canton, such as reporting the District Commercial Associations — the general guild having sponsored the peace delegation—to be held at 7 p.m. tomorrow.

Summed up briefly the position is that the delegates desired to confine themselves to asking for communication to be resumed whereas the Canton Strike Executive wished to include in the discussion a number of points that can hardly be called relevant.

Unless an improvement results from the conference (in Canton) of last night, it is difficult to see where a. settlement is going to start.

The strikers are reported to have put forward terms, in addition to those published last week, such as the free use of Chinese subsidiary coin in Hongkong, the liberty of deported strikers to return. etc.

headline: MALARIA SCOURGE
text:
INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OPENS.

The inaugural meeting of the International Congress on malaria has opened at the Capitol.

The Premier, M. Mussolini, and a large number of international experts, on malaria were present, including representatives from Burma, India and the Malay States.

Signor Mussolini paid a high tribute to Britain and her dominions for their striking example and collaboration in fighting the scourge of malaria.

The Argentine delegate proposed the establishment of an international anti-malaria institute at Rome to collect worldwide information and to undertake research work for the redemption of infected regions and to organise practical teaching for the training of malaria specialists.

The Italian delegate promised that Italy would support the proposal and was ready to provide building and supply funds towards "be organisation of an institute.

The Congress approved the proposal and entrusted its council to draw up a scheme.

The Board of Education is to sit at a p.m. this Wednesday. Shanghai, October 4—The talopsh strike has been settled. Enter. Enjoy the Offers of the Day at the January Board meeting at 15 p.m. to enter a series of interesting items relative to the return for Embargoes and this year.

Simultaneously, his army headquarters in Canton city was surrounded by a detachment of Cadets who immediately disarmed the bodyguards. headline: THAT £3,000,000.
text:
SINGAPORE TO FIND A THIRD.

INTEREST THAT RISES.

At the urgent request of the Secretary of State, the Government has agreed that the Colony should advance the Hongkong Government sums not exceeding one million pounds, these advances to come out of the currency guarantee fund.

Upon enquiry locally the “China Mail” was informed that owing to the delay which would be involved, it had not been anticipated that the loan would be raised on the London market, and some Colonies had signified willingness to co-operate in providing the money. Such Colonies, in common with Hongkong, conducted the negotiations for the employment of their reserves through the Crown agents and such a loan as that to Hongkong would provide suitable employment.

It can be readily understood that a loan for a short period with suitable interest would serve the interests of such Colonies much better than a long term loan and it is understood that the Hongkong Government looks upon the loan to them as a short one, in fact the interest to be charged them will be on a rising scale so it is obvious that local borrowers will be expected to pay back bbrrowed sums comparatively soon.

headline: CANTON'S ADMIRAL
text:
RESIGNATION OF RUSSIAN CHIEF

ALLEGED MONEY DISPUTE:

一

The Russian officer who has been appointed as admiral of the Canton Navy is reported to be contemplating early resignation on account of financial trouble.

It was expected, says the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" that $500,000 would be paid for refitting the Canton Navy when the appointment was made. Keen disappointment is felt at non-payment. The admiral is believed to be asking, shortly, for leave to return to Russia, where he will then hand in his resignation to Canton.

text:
The s.s. "Empress of Asia" brought in to-day a total of 351 bags comprising letter and newspaper mail from the U.S.A., Canada, Japan and Shanghai.

The mail will be ready for delivery this afternoon.

headline: JUDICIAL INQUIRY.
text:
BOYCOTT BY SHANGHAI CHINESE.

CHAMBER OF COMMERCE FIẾT.

The Shanghai Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, in a full page advertisement in the foreign newspapers, declares that all Chinese citizens will under no circumstances be identified or associated with the judicial inquiry.

The Waichiaopu in a Note to the Senior Minister given out this evening and dated October 2, states that the Chinese Government informed the British Charge d'Affaires on September 1, that judicial enquiry into the Shanghai incident would only further complicate the issue and involve a waste of time, and the Chinese Government does not waver from this attitude.

The Note reiterates the view that the lapse of time has changed the circumstances. Most the requisite evidence has become un-obtainable or, has disappeared.

The Note states that after the Shanghai incident and the Chinese Government's protest the Powers sent diplomatic representatives to Shanghai and these representatives i.e. vestigated the case.

headline: BERLIN VIEWS3.
text:
The newspapers do not share the optimism of the foreign Press and consider the Conference has reached a deadlock. They declare that success or failure depends on private conservations... between statesmen.

Mr. Chamberlain, talking with British Pressmen said that, everyone earnestly wanted peace and he was convinced that it was impossible to leave Locarno without making real progress. To do so would be disaster. He did not believe that any difficulty was unsoluble and had never heard of a discussion conducted on so high a level. Nothing had been said that could offend others.

Paris, October 9. “Le Matin’s” Locarno correspondent declares that the Conference has considerably progressed towards the goal. A formula is in sight and it must be assumed that this has been achieved by linking up the admission of Germany into the League and the projected arbitration treaties. “Petit Parisien” correspondent, however, referring to Herr Stressemann's reservations, says clearly that the negotiations are confronted by secret Russo-German engagements. headline: TODAY'S MEETING.
text:
At a meeting this morning of the shareholders and directors of the China Provident Loan and Mortgage Co., Ltd, Mr. R. G. Shewan made reference to a letter appearing in the morning newspapers. It did not give proof that it was signed by shareholders, he said, and he was not sure whether notice should be taken of it. Abraham Lincoln, who in the speaker's opinion was one of the wisest men who lived, used to say one should never "swop" horses when crossing a stream. "We are in full mid-stream now," said Mr. Shewan, "and the sooner we reach the other side the better."

"To attempt to stop these proceedings now and commence new negotiations with the Tug and Lighter Co. continued Mr. Shewan," would be the height of folly and would result disastrously. It was quite true that the Tug and Lighter Co, made a loss last year but they had since been able to get an insight into the business with the result that better days had been experienced. The Tug and Lighter Company were not pressing the sale. The Provident, Loan and Mortgage Company were using the lighters to advantage to-day and could not do without them and it would be nine or twelve months for the Provident, Loan and Mortgage Company to get other steamers. They would also cost a good deal more than the price the Tug and Lighter Company were asking. If those who had signed the letter would think more deeply into the matter they would appreciate the time it would take and the money it would cost to acquire a fleet which was now being got at once.

headline: STRIKE DOOMED.
text:
COLLAPSE EXPECTED SHORTLY.

FREMANTLE TRUCULENCE.

The National Sailors' and Firemen's Union headquarters report that the strike is expected to collapse in the near future. A definite decision is to be taken at a meeting in London on Sunday.

A similar meeting will be held at Bristol and a ballot will be taken at Southampton while it is believed the strike has collapsed at Liverpool.

In consequence of the violent form, assumed by the seamen's strike at Fremantle, the Australian Steamship lines have decided to discontinue the call there until the restoration of normal conditions.

headline: "SUI YTK" OFFICERS
text:
THE LAST OF THEM.

CHOICE OF DESTINATION

A decision has been arrived at by the Police in conjunction with other officials which will finally dispose of the complement of the s.s. "Sui Yick," the ship seized by the strikers at Shannai, transferred to the Canton Government. The ship was not allowed to troops and returned now to the owners owing to the coxswain having brought it into British waters.

Most of the men were put across the border last Monday but a few officers and others were detained for further enquiries. It has now been decided to send these away from the Colony to places of their own choosing and the last will be seen of them in the course of the last few days.

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
It is expected that the International Telegraph Conference which opens in plenary session on the 10th will increase the terminal transit charges on all telegrams. It is understood that the increase will not be a flat rate but will vary from ten to thirty per cent., countries belonging to the telegraph union being divided into a number of categories en-titling them to greater or lesser increase according to their financial necessities.

The British representatives, in committee, steadily opposed the increase and had the moral support of the American observers, but were overruled by the majority of other countries which emphasised the necessity to offset increased working costs. The increase will apply to Press, besides ordinary and urgent messages. —Reuter.

headline: A GRIEVANCE
text:
SANITARY ARRANGEMENTS CRITICISED.

SOME TRONG : VIEWS.

"J.C." writes concerning the loading of nightsoil from the Praya at Wanchai. "Reclamation work," he says, "is going on, starting from the East and working up towards Arsenal Street. It has been apparently the custom from time immemorial, comparatively speaking, to use a certain pier of the Praya for the unpleasant operation of loading up nightsoil. As the reclamation has progressed westward, so the pier has become engulfed, and as a consequence the nightsoil lighter has come to the edge of the Praya to load. That has resulted in the work being done, and the lighter lying all night at a distance of a very few yards, twenty to windward of dwelling houses."

After referring to the distressing consequences for those in the neighbourhood, "J.C." considers the facts with a view to ameliorating conditions. "Here," he writes, "is a nightsoil junk loading up every night within a few yards of dwelling houses. Here also, is the reclamation already extending a matter of about 100 yards from the Praya. Does it not show a perfectly damnable lack of common sense, not to say common decency, on the part of our most Insanitary Board not to order the nightsoil junk to the edge of the reclamation to do their loading, so at least to go as far away as possible from human dwellings?

Let your readers just try to imagine what it must be like in the Hongkong summer night, with its sweltering and breathless damp heat, the mosquitoes, sleeplessness, etc., to have the added horror of this appalling stench cloaking one round like a pall. If their imaginations can rise to such Dantesque heights, they will, I think, forgive me for airing in publics grievances which many people besides those particularly who have inspired this letter, must feel. This grievance is largely due to the slackness of a public board who though chosen primarily to look after the health and well-being of the public, in this case certainly is guilty of a dereliction of DETENTION OF MERCENARY CONFIRMED.

headline: REQUEST REFUSED.
text:
CANTON MERCHANTS WANT STEAMERS.

SHIPS FROM LONGKONG.

Canton's (Chinese) General Chamber of Commerce has requested the Strike Committee for permission for the s.s. "Paul Beon" and "Charles Hardwin" to ply between Hongkong and Canton, says the "Canton Gizzelle."

Five regulations for the operation of these two ships were put forward by the Chamber. The Strike Committee considered the request to be contrary to the strike rules and the request was refused.

[Note: 'The "Paul Beau" and "Charles Hardouin'" belong to the Caution Navigation Co., Ltd. and were flying between the two ports till the strike had lasted several weeks. They were the last boats called off. Most of the capital is Chinese but the vessels fly the British flag.]

headline: CHINA'S TROUBLES.
text:
HONGKONG UNIVERSITY'S GOODWILL.

VICE-CHANCELLOR'S MESSAGE.

A “double-ten” (tenth day of the tenth month) concert at the conclusion of which they were briefly addressed by the Vice-Chancellor, and a dance which the Vice-Chancellor allowed to continue until 2 a.m., was the manner of celebration by the undergraduates of the Hongkong University of the fourteenth anniversary of the institution of the Republic of China.

At the conclusion of the concert, Mr. W. W. Hornell, C.I.E., Vice-Chancellor, speaking on behalf of the many present, said that they were glad to see that in spite of the troubles of the last few months the undergraduates were celebrating the national festival as usual. Speaking twelve months ago he had wished for the Republic of China a happy issue out of all her afflictions and he would repeat that there was no institution in the world which longed more for a peaceful and contented China than the Hongkong University.

The University of Hongkong continued the Vice-Chancellor, had no solution to offer for the present difficulties of China but he did believe that by their life at the University in friendly relations with the members as a whole students were able to leave better equipped to face the grave complications of the world of to-day. That evening's celebration was an example of the friendliness and good will which existed between all members of the University, and in the name of all the guests present, he desired to thank the undergraduates for inviting them and all those who had been responsible for the ar-ranging of, such an excellent entertainment.

headline: THE CONCERT
text:

headline: ON THE STREETS:
text:
NO SERIOUS WELK-END ACCIDENTS.

一

Although the streets were crowded on Saturday with the Chinese festivities and various attractions at Happy Valley, no cases of serious accident were reported as a direct cause of the congestion of traffic.

A Chinese was knocked down by a motor car at Aberdeen and sustained injuries to his head.

On the Kowloon side, a Chinese was severely bruised in attempting to allight from a moving motor bus. Another accident occurred at Tokowan where a coolie sustained injuries to his legs when he was struck down by an earth truck.

headline: FRENCH STRIKE.
text:
ANOTHER COMMUNIST FIASCO..

POLICE ON THE ALERT.

“Humanité,” the Communist organ, published an order for a general strike all over France on October 11 to protest against the wars in Morocco and Syria and the new taxes.

The opinion is generally expressed that the strike will fail like the transport strike in which the Parisian taxi drivers alone decided to participate.

The Government has taken all measures to suppress attempts to prevent freedom of work.

The Communists' long-expected 24-hour strike principally to protest against the war in Morocco is due on October 12, according to an order issued by the headquarters late last night.

A second order calls on Communist members of the Paris transport services to strike today and remain out till their wage demands are granted.

The transport strike called by the Communists proved a fiasco. The number of strikers was in-significant and the public was in-nowise inconvenienced.

In the afternoon the police searched the offices of the Communist organ "Humanité" and seized several thousand letters inciting the workers to participate in the projected general strike.

headline: LOST CHANCE.
text:
INDIA'S COTTON MILL. FNDUSTRY.

In connection with the controversy regarding the remedy for the repression in the cotton mill industry, the Government of India informs the Mill Owners' Association of Bombay that it does not desire to press an enquiry by the Tariff Board since the industry does not ask the Government's protection. It points out that the Board's report would have been of great value not only to the Government and the public but also to the industry itself and would have helped in sifting hitherto unsubstantiated charges regarding Japanese dumping.

headline: China be Jitail / HONGKONG, TUESDAY / BARE ARMS.
text:
CANTON'S AMAZON DETACHMENT.

BORBED HAIR FIGHTERS.

With their hair bobbed and their arms bared, about twenty women bodyguards have arrived at Canton. The complete description of them in the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" is that they are also barefooted, they carry rifles, appear to be ferocious, and roll their eyes about when looking ahead!

This body of Amazons marched into Canton with the commandant of a detachment of Farmers' Volunteers, the last-named having been defeated and disbanded by General Chan Kwing-ming's troops.

The Volunteers once held sway in the Hoi Luk Fung area, reports the special correspondent of the "Wah Tsz Yac Po."

It is presumed that when the Farmers found that the anti-Reds had expelled the Reds from that territory, the leader mustered his awe-inspiring Amazons and made his way to Canton to offer his services to the Reds.

Reds move to Base. Trainloads of Red troops have been leaving Canton by rail for Shektan, the railway station on the Canton side and next to Shekhang (40 miles or so from the southern metropolis).

The 1st division of the Red Army has arrived at Shektan and encropped. General Cheung Kai-shek has made Shektan his army headquarters and his main strength is massed there.

Having gone to Whampoa and there obtained an issue of a large lot of arms. Wong Kam-guen, commander of the Strike Pickets, is reported to be equipping the pickets with a view to their volunteering for active military service against the anti-Rede on the East River.

headline: FACTORY ACCIDENT.
text: A fatal accident occurred at the Leman Hing Kwok Knitting Factory at Cheong Lok Street, Yaumati yesterday afternoon when one of the workers was caught by the belting and drawn into the machinery.

headline: CONFUCIUS DAY.
text:
TO-MORROWS CELEBRATION IN TOWN.

This year has seen a marked tendency towards observing Confucius Day, which falls on the 27th day of the 8th moon (tomorrow) according to the Chinese Calendar) as a general holiday. It seems as if the time is not far distant when the anniversary of the birth of China's most famous sage—although not ranking as one of the four big festivals—will take second place to New Year in the round of Chinese festivities in Hongkong.

It is estimated that more than half the shops in the Colony will be closed to-morrow whereas in previous years only a small percentage observed the day. At the Tai Ping Theatre, the local Confucius Society will hold a mass meeting with speeches from the society's officials, followed by a dramatic show. Nearly all the schools attended by Chinese students will have a day off and some of the schools have arranged their own celebration. The amisture of the Ching Shing Harvest Society are assisting the Confucius Society by presenting old-style Chinese items on the stage.

headline: BOYCOTT OVER?
text:
SWATOW FREE TO TRADING VESSELS.

ALL NATIONS WANTED.

Merchant vessels of all nations can now proceed freely to Swatow, says the Foreign Commissioner of the port. Mr. Wong Keung. In a letter to the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Wong explains that since the troops of his party retook Swatow, steps have been taken to restore commerce. Accordingly all mercantile marine ships may put in there for commercial purposes, he concludes.

text:

It is only the “outside” shipping firms which insert the type-written clause anent the 24 hours' notice. A large number of members of the Guild recognised that such a clause is not desirable in that it is not conducive to good discipline that an officer may be dismissed at such short notice as a result of complaint by members of the crew. Again, so long as the clause remains legal, so long will remain the danger of ship's officers undercutting each other in wages, for although there are fixed rates, there are ways and means of getting round this by an officer who has been out of work for a long time. If the possibility is removed of a man drawing full pay being dismissed within 24 hours in order that he may be replaced by another willing to take less it will go a long way to solve the problem, added the Guild official.

Asked how it was that the Guild does not take action in the matter and make representations direct in favour of abolishing this 24 hours' notice term, the Guild official said that a number of the officers are in favour of the clause as it obviously cuts both ways and if an officer had the chance of getting a better job in the course of his six months' undertaking the 24 hours' notice provision enables him to avail himself of it. The official was of the opinion that the matter rests not with the Guilds but with the Hongkong Government to whom have been made both the reports of the "Sul-an" Commission and of the Senior Naval Officer in Charge of West River Patrol, recommending the rendering illegal of such a clause.

headline: Britain's Lead.
text:
Referring to the Bifference of opinion existing as to whether Great Britain should have acted on her own, to protect her trade in the Far East in preference to the painfully long process of consulting other Powers, the "Telegraph" states:

Three months have passed by since the fatal riot in the international settlement at Shanghai provoked the Chinese boycott of British residents which has done untold harm. It is now announced that the Treaty Powers, some eighteen in all, have agreed upon the text of the Notes in which they will reply to the Chinese Government's demands in respect of the Shanghai affair, and in respect also of the revision of the foreign treaties with China. Delays are doubtless inevitable in diplomacy, especially when so many Powers have to be consulted and brought into line. But for Great Britain, whose commercial interests in China are older and still more important, relatively, than those of any other Power, this long postponement of action of any kind has been peculiarly unfortunate. If the settlement had been under British control, the Shanghai affair could have been promptly investigated and amicably arranged. As it is, though the representatives of the British ratepayers predominate in the Municipal Council administering the settlement, the Council itself is responsible to the whole diplomatic corps at Peking. Whether the Foreign Office could have done more by independent diplomacy without violating the principle that the Powers should deal in concert with Chinese questions is a matter on which our Government and the British firms interested in the trade of the Far East seem to differ. But it remains true that British interests have suffered severely and are still suffering, while the Power have been slowly exchanging Notes. We can only hope that events will now move more rapidly, and that the British Government will take the lead in the important negotiations this autumn at Peking.

The attitude of Japan is less clearly defined but her vast trading interests in China must incline her to take much the same view as Great Britain and America. If the three Powers can act together, energetically and firmly, the Treaty Conference and the Extra-territoriality Commission ought to lead to some tangible results, and at any rate should assunge the bitterness of the anti-foreign feeling among the more responsible leaders of Chinese opinion.

headline: Britain's Concern.
text: Meanwhile Mr. Chamberlain has done well to emphasise a fresh, in a Note to Peking, the deep concern of the British Government at the loss of life and damage to property in the Shanghai riots, and their desire that prompt and impartial justice shall be done. It will be remembered that the Peking Government prevented a judicial inquiry from being held early in July by insisting that larger questions totally distinct from the riots, should be discussed at the same time. The Peking Ministers were known to have acted under duress in making these impossible conditions before they would agree to an inquiry and appoint a Chinese judge to take part in it. It is possible that they may now feel free to take a wiser course, and to participate in the investigation of the Shanghai affair without further delay. headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
The action of the Chinese contractors in conveying food stuffs to H.M.S. "Magnolia," British cruiser which replaced the "Fox-glove," is significant of the general improvement at Swatow.

This is the first time the contractors have done this since the institution of the boycott.

headline: China" the Atail / FEWER TOURISTS.
text:
LOCAL SILK STORE LOSE TRADE

EFFECTS OF THE STRIKE

SHAMEEN STOCKS BROUGHT TO HONGKONG

Looking at their glittering windows and splendid wares, most people think that the local Indian stores are among the Colony's few thriving concerns.

Yet the local Indian merchants were also badly hit by the strike and the position which it created. However a gradual improvement is now taking place.

The silk stores have suffered heavy losses owing to the Canton market—the source of their supplies—being closed, and the coast ports discontinuing purchases of Indian goods.

The branches at Shameen are all closed, and to prevent deterioration stocks of valuable material have been removed to Hongkong.

Orders from foreign places for Chinese silks, shawls and other goods are for the major part held up. In the earlier months of the strike Canton goods were unobtainable, but the position has improved by small supplies coming via Shanghai, which involves delay and higher cost.

The trade with local customers also suffered for economic reasons. In normal times tourists visiting at odd intervals other than the excursion season increased the turnover of the silk shops, but the number visiting the Colony during the strike has been small and business has naturally suffered.

With an improvement taking place gradually, the silk stores are making reduced profits and are on the whole not so badly affected as other trades.

The imports consist largely of shellac, gunny bags and Indian produce. The business is done on an indent basis, and with the tightness of money and the closing of the Canton market, which received a large share of the purchases of the local Chinese customers; trade came to a standstill during July and August. A little business, however, is now being done in gunny bags, the larger part of which is re-shipped to Shanghai.

Cassia, which forms an important article of export to India, comes from Canton, and since June not a single bag has been shipped, although the merchants have large orders on hand. The trade in Chinese produce is also at a standstill.

headline: WORLD SERIES.
text:
PIRATES OVERCOME THE SENATORS:

A MIGHTY STRUGGLE.

Pittsburgh, October 15. Over 40,000 rain-soaked, delirious enthusiasts cheered to victory, the home players who by prodigious labour had overcome an initial lead of four runs scored by Washington in the first innings.

With a. change pitcher, the Pirates drew up to tie the score only to be again left behind by the Senators.

Finally in the eighth inning when the score was again tied and bases full, one of the Pittsburgh out-fielders at the bat, smashed a two-bagger. This mighty fly definitely turned the tide of the battle.

headline: . OFFICIAL STATEMENT
text: A British communiqué states that the Conference, after adopting the text of the draft of the Security Pact took up the question of Arbitration Treaties and invited representatives of Poland and Czechoslovakia to join in a meeting to hear statements in regard to the work of the jurists on the Draft Treaties on arbitration between Germany and France on the one part, and Germany and Belgium on the other, the texts of which have been adopted by the Delegations concerned. The representatives of Poland and Czechoslovakia then gave the Conference an account of their own negotiations with the representatives of the German Government in regard to drafting the Arbitration Treaties between Germany and Poland on the one part, and Germany and Czechoslovakia on the other.

headline: MEFFAN—MUIRHEAD
text:
A pretty wedding also took place to-day at Union Church; Hongkong, the parties being Miss Helen D. Muirhead, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. William Muirhead, of Bannockburn, Scotland, and Mr. Norman D. Meffan, of Tarkham Dock, eldest son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Richard L. Arbroach, Scotland. The bride was given away by Mr. R. Wallace and was prettily attired in a simple tunic dress of ivory silk georgette with pearl and diamante trimming, veil of white, embroidered net with wreath of orange blossoms and white heather. Her bouquet was of white roses and Honolulu creeper.

Miss Nancy McNeillie, the bridesmaid, wore a dress of coral pink embroidered georgette with soft blue French crinoline hat and carried a bouquet of pink roses and Honolulu creeper.

The matron of honour, Mrs. D. McNeillie, was attired in grey crepade chine with condor hat of black hatters plush.

The best man was Mr. W. Robertson.

Mr. S., Collett, at the organ, played suitable music and during the service the hymns: "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "O God of Bethel" were sung.

A reception at the Hongkong Hotel grill room followed the service and Mr. and Mrs. Meffan then left for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's going away dress was of fawn. georgette with overdress of fuschiu. flowered chiffon and hat to match.

headline: EAST RIVER
text:
CHAN'S ARMY REFUSES BATTLE.

STRIKE AGAINST STRIKERS.

("W'ah Tsz Yat Po.")

As the Chan Kwing-ming army is retiring on its own account in preference to giving battle, General Cheung Kai-shek (the Cadet chieftain) has ordered Li Chai-sum (on the West River) to enter the East River war zone to establish himself at Tamshui. [Note: The telegram hints that the Reds fear being enticed into enemy territory and there being enveloped. General Cheung will take command in person.] Ex-Admiral Chan Chak (of Kongmoon and "Wing Fung" fame) has been appointed Director of Operations, under Chan Ming-shu, in the projected offensive against the Chan troops in the south of Kwangtung province. A general strike has been declared against the Reds by the merchants at Fu Mun (Bocca Tigris) and Tai Ping (on the opposite bank of the Canton River). Over 10 strikers' pickets were killed in a squabble over an embargo on saltfish and this has caused the strike. The Red civil authorities on the spot have cabled Canton.

text:
THE SERCURITY PACT INITIALLED.

ALL DISPUTES SETTLED.

headline: EXPORTING MONEY.
text:
TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE.

NOT CROSSING THE BORDEER

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who abandoned with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumuti was tendered at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempling to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force. Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERUTORY GAINED BY THE REDS:

RAILWAY REPORTED CLEAR.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwing-ming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Simechon, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by丙ontic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the fall of Wuchow the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

text:
Conflicting reports have been received regarding the fall of Waichow, the Chan stronghold on the East River. Some maintain that only the district capital by that name was surrendered to the Cube, but later reports claim that netted Cheging Kūi-shek's men are generally in the capital of the next seifure take of the same name as well.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
RESUMEES, EXCEPT ERITISH.

LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

From Our Own Correspondent.)

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Caneolian) and schools are still closed.

The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good.

H.M.S. "Mourhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of the strike.

There is a shortage of kerosine and' liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junks have seldom got through the strike pickets' cordons.. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed.
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates and established "themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaw and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hung-kai's remnants. Pirates have again been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "Mai Tain") have authority to pay for the before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-layn is brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa is at Chekhom and Yamping with his troops. General Li Chai-sum, the Red nominee, holds Sunning. Kungyick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Saiwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only import permitted from Macao but boats are low running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 20 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the "Kwok Ning" piracy (report) previously in the "China Mail").

headline: CANTON ITEMS. / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST PASSENGERS.
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the s.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hongkong. The prices charged by the junk and samparas operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing.

The "Honam" left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The "Fatshan" will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the "special tugs" which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high-handed actions. These clerks had spiked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Cantor.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Whichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: CHANGE OF FRONT.
text:
BETTER CANTON LANDING FACILITIES

MILITARY CONTROL

The “China Mail” reported a few days ago that facilities rather than difficulties were being placed in the way of passengers wishing to land in Canton from the “Honam.” From later reliable reports it would appear that this change of front is due to the action of the military authorities who in this and other directions are evincing their determination to curb the activities of the strikers, as the exercise of power of the latter since the absence of certain troops has incurred disfavour and is looked upon with suspicion.

The supervision of the craft which are now actually placed at the disposal of passengers wishing to land is now in the hands of the military—Whampoa cadets—and although nothing definite can be ascertained as to what transpires when passengers from the "Honam" and "Fatshan" are once ashore it is certainly a fact that no actual charge for transportation is being made. Prior to the handling of disembarkation by the military, a visit to strike headquarters was necessary for the purpose of payment of money for the privilege of landing. It is thought that a small sum has now to be paid at military headquarters instead.

The military have also taken control of outward bound passengers from Canton and greater facilities are thus "available, although a charge in excess of that paid by incoming passengers is said to be levied on them. As the strikers' pickets and the military are still at loggerheads over the matter, most of the sampans bearing outward bound passengers go alongside at night, but the greater freedom which is being exercised in the matter of the issue of passes is evidenced by the number of passengers brought from Canton by the "Honam" yesterday afternoon—150, a record number since the run was re-established between the two ports after the outbreak of the strike.

headline: MALARIA MENACE. / POOLS IN NEW EXCHANGE BUILDING.
text:
CONTRACTORS FINED.

Before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning, the Hongkong Engineering and Construction Co., Ltd. were summoned by the Sanitary Department for allowing pools of water to accumulate on the floors of the new Exchange Building in Des Vœux Road Central and thus providing breeding places for mosquitoes.

The Company was, represented by Mr. D. A. G. Alison. In imposing a fine of $40, Hia Worship said that he viewed the offence as a serious one in view of the prevalence of malaria in the Colony. He held the Company to be directly responsible in this matter, as the workmen who committed the offence were under its control.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED.
text:
TAIPING INCIDENT CLOSED?

With an armed escort and supported by soldiers, new strike pickets have entered the port of Ta' Bing (near Bocca Tigris, at the entrance to the Pearl River delta) and assumed duty.

As previously reported, a squabble broke out over trade in saltfish and the local merchants are alleged to have killed four of the pickets and wounded thirty-seven in a pitched fight.

Since then the trouble is stated to have been patched up, hence the despatch of new pickets. Trade between Tai Ping and Canton has resumed.

The bodies of the four dead strikers were conveyed with ritual to Canton and the wounded were sent to the Canton Labourers' Hospital for treatment.

headline: BITER BIT
text:
How strikers' armed launches carrying pickets were defeated in a running duel with a Chinese passenger vessel is related by a passenger who admits that he hid in galley of the merchant steamer and lay flat while the shooting was going on.

Having left Macao for Kwong Hoi city, in the Sze Yap districts, the s.s. "Ng Tai Chow" (meaning "Five Great Continents") was challenged in Chinese waters by armed launches. Pickets from Canton had already forbidden the ship to run as it was alleged that passengers had travelled by roundabout routes to get to Macao.

As the “Ng Tai Chay” ignored the strikers she, so the passenger states, was fired-upon. But the strikers reckoned without the arsenal carried by the merchant-man. The fire was returned and the pickets retired, defeated. Subsequently the quarrel was patched up and the “Ng Tai Chow” returned to Macao.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENT.
text:
COOLIES AND TABLE.

While proceeding along Pedder Street from Des Vaux Road to Queen's Road on Monday afternoon, a Chinese suddenly came in the way of a motor car driven by Mr. G. G. Thomson, of the Hongkong Electric Company, and was struck down by the mudguard. The man escaped injury, but a table which he was carrying at the time along with another was damaged.

headline: GOODS CLAIM / RESPONSIBILITY FOR PAYMENT.
text:
SALESMEN OR PARTNERS?

A dispute regarding responsibility for acceptance of an order for electrical fittings to the value of $230.80 occupied the attention of Mr. Justice Wood in the Summary Court this morning.

The firm which gave the order being no longer in existence, Mr. E. S. C. Brooks, on behalf of the firm which supplied them, used two men whom he claimed were partners in the concern.

Mr. C. A. S. Russ, for the two defendants, claimed that they were salesmen for the firm and not partners, and were therefore not liable for taking over and paying

headline: AIRSHIP CRASH. A COURT MARTIAL SEQUEL
text:
Washington, October 21. A court martial has been convened for October 28 for the trial of Colone) Mitchell for violating service regulations.

The court martial will consider his statements in connection with the loss of the Shenandoah that the result is almost due to treasonable and criminal conduct on the the part of the War and Navy Departments.

Moderate to fresh monsoon will prevail along the coast and over the Northern China Sea, " states the weather report. The weather forecast till noon is tomorrow in Beijing.

headline: “UNSOUND DEALINGS.”
text:
Legislative Control

Legislation to deal with the situation is not recommended by the Stocks and Shares Commission, the report of which was laid upon the table at to-day's meeting of the Legislative Council.

In view of difficulties involved in amalgamation, the Commission does not recommend the limitation of Exchanges to one. The obvious remedy is considered to be the reorganisation of Exchanges by their members by amending and adding to rules and strictly enforcing them. It had been given in evidence, stated the report, that there had been no recent case of a member of any Exchange being expelled, suspended, or even censured for failing to meet his obligations.

The members of the Commission have reason to believe that the share market has been carrying on its business for some time past on a thoroughly unsound basis and, even if the financial crisis had not taken place on the 22nd June, the time was bound to come in any case when a general slump in the market would have had very serious consequences.

After reviewing the growth of the three Exchanges and their rules, the causes for the large increase in speculative operations are referred to, this being attributed to the influx of Chinese money owing to interior disturbances, and the consequent cheapness of money. The balance sheets of many local companies reflected a certain amount of real prosperity leading to higher value of shares but in many cases prices of shares had risen beyond a figure justified. The causes of the collapse of the market in June were the following:

Dealing by unsound brokers with unsound clients.

Dealing by unsound brokers with sound clients.

Over-financing by native banks who, we are informed, were in the habit of advancing up to 80 per cent. or 90 per cent of the market value of the shares. Even 100 per cent. has been mentioned.

The general apprehension felt by the Chinese community as to the probable effect of the threatened strike and a boycott on the prosperity of Hongkong. At the last moment occurred the moratorium granted to the native banks, the closing of the Stock Exchange, the postponement of the Settlement and the sudden withdrawal of the extensive credit facilities—which had hitherto existed.

At the same time we are of opinion that if the first two factors, (a) and (b), had not been present the results would not have been nearly so serious and would not have affected so large a number of persons.

headline: CANTON NOTES. / REGULARS ROUTED BY MERCHANTS.
text:
STRIKERS' PERMITS.

Canton soldiers under General Li Fook-lam of Honam are stated to have been defeated by Merchants' Volunteers ("Man Tuen") at Kaukong when attempting to enter the district.

Permits from the strikers to leave Canton for Hongkong, and Maeso will be issued as usual as from October 20, states the "Wah Tsz, Yat Po."

Hu Han-min, the former Canton Foreign Commissioner, has reached Moscow where he spoke at the "Sun Wen" (Sun Yat-sen) University.—Wah Tsz Yat Po.

There is little appreciable change to-day in the quotation list issued by the Share & Real Estate Brokers Society of Hongkong, as compared with yesterday.

A cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" states that foreign warships are proceeding along the Yangtze River to Hankow to protect nationals in the event of trouble breaking out. Parents and friends of students at St. Joseph's College are reminded of the opening ceremony of the new reception hall and science laboratory, generally by H. E. the Children at Tzackie tomorrow. This is what he recalled was to have taken place in Yuhua but was not the first to be seen at the time.

headline: MR. HOLYOAK'S SPEECH.
text:
After the Colonial Secretary had moved the second reading of the budget Bill, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak said: Your Excellency.—It will perhaps be useful in discussing the draft estimates of revenue and expenditure for 1926, if in the first place I deal with your Excellency's speech introducing the budget before discussing in detail such points as appear to us to call for further explanation or special reference.

To commence with, we should like to congratulate you, sir, on the extremely able and comprehensive survey of the past year and the present situation, as well as upon the statesmanlike budget, taking which we have learned from successive budgets, to expect from you. Whilst sympathising with the difficulties of attempting any accurate forecast for the coming has naturally been a response that "for the present, the right course is to increase income and that there before you do not think it necessary to provide for additional direct taxation for the present." We were glad to hear from your Excellency that the Colony's revenue is already showing signs of improvement.

We most fully endorse your Excellency's statement that "you cannot believe that the intelligent people of Kwangtung—a race which has been famous for centuries for commercial ability and practical sense—can be content much longer to put up with the oppression of a régime imposed from outside and supported by mercenaries from other provinces," and we, too, believe that the traditional sound common sense of the people of Kwangtung, as well as the old-time deeply sincere friendship between the Cantonese officials and people and the British Government and its citizens residing in Hongkong and China must before long re-assort themselves, and conditions become once more normal for them—and us.

It is perhaps fitting at this stage to express the fervent hope that the conferences about to commence in Peking will materially assist in reinstating normal relations with China.

Turning now to the details of the Budget, we note for the first time that all junior clerks now come under the definite heading of Junior Clerical Service. Whilst appreciating the explanation that this has been done for the sake of economy in time and labour, we are not fully satisfied that it is not preferable to debit these salaries to the various departments concerned, that we may arrive at definite knowledge of the cost of running each department.

headline: China the Initial / ROBBERS BUSY.
text:
PROGRESS MAKES THIEVES!

HoiHow (Hainan Is.), Oct. 20. National Day (October 10) and Confucius Day (October 14) passed off without any trouble or demonstration. The Government schools have opened with about one-third of their usual enrol ment. The students seem very friendly.

The country is still very unsettled and robber bands are working in every district. In Vun Sang district the robbers are so bad that people are fleeing to the district city for protection or locking up their homes and sleeping hidden under bushes or trees in the open country at night.

It is reported that at Nam I recently, fifty miles south of Hoihow, a band of robbers burned about a hundred houses and killed over a hundred people. About fifty robbers were among those killed. It is an opinion among some of the Chinese that the rapid development of motor cars and roads in the island have driven chair coolies and burden bearers out of business and turned them into thieves!

A regiment in Dam Tsiu district rebelled against the Government and all the motor cars in the vicinity of Holhow were used to rush troops to that district. It is reported that the rebellion has been put down, fifty rebel soldiers captured, and the remainder forced to retire to the mountains. The local Government has a cartridge factory supplying all ammunition necessary and guns of an inferior quality are also made in Hainan. These facts are the recently constructed roads and the phones enable the quick despatch of troops and give the present Government great advantage in case of uprisings.

On October 3, Dr. Henry M. McCandliss suffered a slight stroke of paralysis from which he is making a good measure of recovery. He completed, last July, forty years of active medical work in Hainan under the American Presbyterian Mission. He founded the Hoihow hospital and has been at the head of it up to the present time building it up to one of the large hospitals of China. As soon as he is able to travel, Dr. and Mrs. McCandliss, who also leaves behind her a large record of work accomplished among the Chinese, will leave for Hongkong and probably for América, although their plans are not yet formulated. Dr. Clarence G. Salsbury is now in charge of the hospital.

headline: COOLIE TRAFFIC.
text:
Because of unsettled conditions in Hainan, last week two steamers took 1,700 coolies to Singapore. The coolie traffic seems to be normal and a large number of ships are calling at Hoihow. With a modern harbour and peace in the interior Hainan will have a brilliant prospect for progress on commercial lines.

In spite of business depression the streets of Hqihow are assuming the appearance of Hongkong streets. Instead of the old narrow byways, there are paved avenues lined on either side with clean new two and three storey buildings.

For the first time since the murder of Mr. George Byers in June 1924, the interior stations of the American Presbyterian Mission are now occupied. In Nooda are Dr. and Mrs. Stewart Seaton, Mrs. M. R. Melrose and Miss Mary Taylor, with Rev. J. F. Steiner dividing his time between Nooda and Hoihow. In Kachek are Dr. Bercovitz and family, Mr. D. H. Thomas and family, Miss K. L. Schaeffer, Miss Caroline McCreery and Mr. and Mrs. H. H. Bausman recently arrived from the States. Mr. Bausman is a graduate of Yale University and Divinity school.

The forthcoming wedding is announced of Mr Arthur Hevey, of No. 8, Knutsford Terrace, Kowloon, to Miss Florene Starrwall who is to arrive in the Colony by

headline: Customers' Appreciation.
text:
Appreciation of the milk supplied by the Company was shown by the increased number of customers and greater quantity sold up to the time of the strike, which unfortunately interrupted the progress made. I am glad to state, however, that a steady recovery is now being effected. The health of the herd is good. During the year 49 head were imported to cope with the demand, and the total now stands at 1,043 head. Early this year the Company's secretary was asked to visit Australia and New Zealand and I am glad to say the result of his visit proved as usual very gratifying and profitable to the Company. Whilst there Mr Manuk entered into agreements for the sole agencies in Hongkong and China of the "Daisy" brand butter of Messrs Presc�ts Ltd. and the "Anchor" brand butter of the New Zealand Co-operative Dairy Company. Both these butters are the particular brands exported from Australia and New Zealand respectively. Shanghai Science

arrangements just mentioned, your directors decided to open a branch of the company at Shanghai. This was done in June and is in charge of Mr. Letton, formerly a director of Messrs. Prescotts, Ltd. Mr. Letton was engaged for this purpose by Mr. Manuk during his visit to Australia. Mr. Letton has had 20 years' experience in dairy produce business, and under his management the Shanghai Branch has so far done very well and we expect greater results in the near future. I should like to say that your directors have found Mr. Manuk's annual visits to Australia to be of great importance and benefit to the Company and are well satisfied with the results attained. These visits enable us to keep in close and intimate touch with our suppliers and the market in general. Australia Visit.

The political unrest and boycott in June again taxed the resources of your Company to its utmost, but as you are aware we were able to cope with all demands and keep the colony supplied, thanks to our practice of carrying Heavy stocks of meat and butter, and also to the presence of your Secretary in Australia, who was able to secure extra supplies and freight space for our requirements. The European staff, and some of our Chinese staff, who remained loyal, worked most willingly throughout the trying period, and their services, have been suitably recognised by your Directors.

The Company's property and machinery are shown at a very conservative valuation in the balance sheet. You will be pleased to learn that the leases of our Pokfulam properties have all been renewed on a uniform basis and will continue in force for the next 31 years. We gave up certain building sites to the Government for which we received other sites adjoining our present property.

The Company's investments as shown in the balance sheet are well under their present market values, but as there are no official quotations we have refrained from giving the market valuation as formerly.

I need hardly reiterate the fact that everything possible is done to supply the Colony with pure food of the highest quality and the thanks of the directors and shareholders are due to the manager, secretary, and their efficient staff, for maintaining the standard of excellence which is always associated with this Company's supplies. With these remarks I beg to propose the adoption of the report and accounts. Seconded by Mr. P. Tester and carried unanimously.

Mr. Bridger proposed and Mr. Chan Tong seconded the re-election of Fr. Robert and Mr. R. M. Austin, the retiring directors. Mr. Makeham proposed and Mr. Abraham seconded the re-election of Mesars. Percy Smith, Seth and Fleming, as auditors, at a fee of $1,000.

headline: MACAO COUP.
text:
WARSHIP CAPTURES LAUNCHES

STRIKE PICKETS VANISH

A small Chinese gunboat, the "Ching Hoi," sailed round Macao harbour yesterday afternoon and collected eleven launches which flew the flag of the Canton Government. These launches were brought together and moored close to one of the Northern cruisers which were in Hongkong a few days ago. The launches now fly the red-white-red flag of General Chan Kwing-ming.

While the rounding-up process was being carried out, the strike pickets at Lappa Island disappeared from view.

It is rumoured here that Shekki is in the hands of General Chan's allies and that the Canton garrison has fled from the neighbourhood
