headline: LINER'S MISHAP
text:
STRIKES TANKER DURING

BEACHED THEN DOCKED.

The “Marella” from Australia, approaching Singapore yesterday afternoon, ran into a squall and came into collision with a tanker. The “Marella” was damaged amidships and the engine room became flooded; the holds remained intact.

The "Marella" was beached but eventually docked.

An Italian cruiser landed the passengers.

headline: SAFETY FIRST.
text:
RE-OPENING OF SHAMEEN

DUE PRECAUTIONS TAKEN.

The small Shameen gate, part of the larger one, was to be opened to day, Sir James Jamieson having communicated this intention to the usual meeting of residents at the Club.

When the smaller French gate was opened, zig-zag barricades leading to the bridge were placed leading from the open gate, and have remained there since, the object being to render impossible the success of any rush, however remote such a contingency may be. Similar precautions, it is thought, will be taken to-day at the British gate.

Discussion has centred round the possible opening of the gate and the removing of the barricades for some considerable time, many holding that the continuance of such measures are unnecessary and leading to the creation of bitterness. On the other hand it is held that there should be some measure of reciprocity by the Canton Government.

Acceptation of the responsibility for the safeguarding of Shameen against further attacks, the removal of pickets and restriction of movements of British residents in Canton are looked upon by them as the first essentials for the removing of the barricades. Again, there is the possibility that should an attack eventuate from the anti-Red forces in the north and the Red troops be defeated chaos may reign in Canton and measures of defence for Shameen will be vitally necessary.

The pickets outside the French gate have again resumed their activities and the importation of all food into Shameen is forbidden. The pickets claim the right, and exercise it, of searching all belongings of people entering. Americans also being subject to search. The American Vice-Consul was stopped as he was returning to Shameen with rice birds and these were taken from him.

The move which the Canton merchants have made in the direction of peace is the inevitable outcome not only of their direct losses in trade but of the taxation which has been particularly heavy because of the expenditure for the campaign on the East River.

There is in Canton money hardly sufficient for the feeding of the strikers for any considerable period and certainly none for clothing them for the winter.

headline: PEACE MOVES. / CANTON'S DELEGATION ARRIVES.
text:
TRADE RESTORATION WANTED.

Delegates from Canton's four leading commercial institutions arrived in Hongkong or Saturday, states the vernacular papers, to discuss with local Chinese merchants steps to restore communications between the two ports and to end the "strike.

It is stated that the delegates desire to ascertain in what way the Hongkong district commercial associations can assist in the matter. The Canton representatives are also mentioned as having expressed themselves as keen to take the matter up with their Government on their return as they particularly desire a resumption of trade.

According to the vernacular report the delegates sought an intellect view with Mr. Ho Kwong and Saturday and were to have preached the two Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council this morning.

headline: EARLIER CABLES. Berlin. October 24.
text:
It is anticipated that the ministers belonging to the German National Party in the Cabinet will retire, in consequence of a resolution by the Governing Board of the Party that the results of the Locarno negotiations are unacceptable. A Government majority for the ratification of the treaties is expected notwithstanding the defection. Although the decision of the Nationalist Party has caused considerable excitement, it is premature to speak of a Government crisis, as the final word is resting with to-morrow's decision of the German National Reichstag Party. Meanwhile President Hindenburg, Dr. Luther and Dr. Stresemann have cancelled their engagements and are remaining in the capital to negotiate with the Party leaders, with an aim to reaching a settlement.

Dr. Stresemann speaking at an election meeting at Karlsruhe vigorously repudiated the suggestion that the Powers represented at Locarhe intended to form an anti-Russian bloc, and declared that Germany would have nothing to do with such a policy, since she said the greatest value on her old relations with Russia.

headline: STRIKE NEWS.
text:
QUEER CANTON “OFFICIAL REPORT.

MERCHANT DELEGATION.

That a steamer from Bangkok had been detained by strikers at Canton is the gist of a report to hand. Neither the steamer's name nor any other particulars have been divulged. The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" is in receipt of a cable to the following effect from Canton: All grades of officials in the Kuomintang Government favour the settlement of terms to end the strike. In connection with the report that a delegation of Canton merchants has come to Hongkong to pay the way to ending the strike, it is now learned, states the "Kung Sheung Yat Po" that the news is premature. A Hongkong Chinese merchant has been asked to inquire as to the prospect of such a mission. TO DATE DOLLAR The following is the dollar and dollar terms used in this list.

headline: Shekki Position
text:
Passengers arriving from Macao yesterday are quoted as having stunted that there is little truth in

the report that anti-Reds have captured Shekki, the capital of the Heungshan district which, incidentally, is the birthplace of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The travelers are said to have added that all the fighting that took place there was between about 200 semi-bandit irregulars under Yuen Tai, who was once a notorious outlaw, and the armed strikers pickets near Chinshan, resulting in the strikers being disarmed.

Another special telegram to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" states that Canton has ordered General Li Fook-lam and Chu Pei-tah to recapture Heungshan.

Yet another report is that the Reds, being in great apprehension as to the outcome of the fall of Shekki-on account of its proximity to Canton and other important centres—have fitted out a naval and military force to retake the place. The report goes on to say that fighting is expected in a day or two.

In response to urgent representations from the magistrate of San On (the district just across

were fleeing, without offering battle, from 8,000 Chan troops. Some of the Cadets trekked overland, but a number took panic, commandeering native vessels. A few large junks each took away as many as two to three hundred.

Yesterday a fishing junk arrived in Hongkong. Forty-seven Red soldiers had gone aboard at Shanmei, ordering the crew of five to set sail immediately in spite of their being no provisions. Until the soldiers disembarked at a spot described as "the Chinese hill behind Cheung Chau," both crew and military had to subsist on one bowl of congee a day. When the crew tried to make for a Chinese Customs station they met with rough treatment. The Reds had aight machine-guns and ammunition with them when they left.

Among the seaplanites from H.M.S. “Hermes” exercising this morning were five machines flying in different formations to the bewilderment and evident enjoyment of the Chinese crowds in the streets.

headline: ALLEGED FRAUDS.
text:
CASE AGAINST EUROPEAN MANAGER

SUM OF $18,000 INVOLVED.

The trial of James Edward Atherley on six charges of alleged misappropriation of amounts amounting to $18,000 belonging to his employers opened at the Central Magistracy this morning. Mr. D. H. Blake prosecuted, and Mr. R. A. Wadeson appeared on behalf of the compradore of the firm involved. Mr. W. B. Hind was for the defence.

Mr. Blake said that the defendant was, for nearly four years, the manager in Hongkong of Messrs. Getz Bros. and Co. (of the Orient), Ltd., an American corporation with branches all over the Far East, and he was responsible to the head office of the firm in San Francisco for all business transactions, of which he had sole charge.

The business necessitated the employment of a compradore, and Chan Kan-yan performed this work for the past four years. It was his duty to make collections and disbursements, keep an account of all money transactions and also to make payments to the Bank on instructions from the manager.

The irregularities, Mr. Blake said, commenced in March 1924, but were not brought to light until a week ago when complaints were made regarding outstanding bills. In April of that year the compradore asked for instructions from the defendant in respect of a sum of money which he had available for paying. into the Bank, and he was asked to wait until the whole amount had been collected. Later, when the whole amount (5,981.93) had been collected, the defendant received the money and gave the compradore receipt under his own signature and the chop of the firm. Such receipts were made out from time to time by the manager, and he obtained the old and by including the amount in the new one on the lines of a receipt for $13,000 odd produced in Court. This was a common document to be passed between the compradore and the manager in case the money had not been paid into the Bank. The compradore in his position was bound to comply with the orders of the manager and had to pay out money without question. A sum of $1,500 paid to Mrs. Atherley to meet her expenses to the U.S.A. was also mentioned, the compradore being given a personal 10 U by the manager, who said that the money was a charge on the firm. Other payments made by the compradore were two bills representing household expenses of the manager, these also being stated to be for the firm's account.

In conclusion, Mr. Blake said that the books had been kept in English and Chinese. Without the assistance of the manager and through other causes he had had great difficulty in gathering together accurate proofs and getting the case to court as quickly as possible. For these reasons he could not actually guarantee the accuracy of all the details he had given.

During the outlining of the case, Mr. Hind asked His Worship to record. His objection to counsel's submission of documents and books which he contended did not constitute evidence.

The evidence of the compradore was next, taken and the case is proceeding.

headline: WORLD COAL
text:
STHILH HOILIDING OUR OWN

EXPERI S. OPINIONS.

Giving evidence to the Coal Commission, Sir Richard Redmayne said he could see no striking change on the world basis, detrimental to British coal interests.

Britain's could exports in 1024 were 51.2 per cent. of the world exports, compared with 49.8 in 1913.

He opined that in a quarter of a century there would be no oil in the United States, and the world supply of oil would suffice more than 80 to 100 years.

headline: POLITICS TABOO.
text:
MOSCOW'S SUN YAT-SEN UNIVERSITY.

The Chinese University named after the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen will be 'opened at Moscow at the beginning of December.

It will accommodate 250 Chinese students.

M. Radek, who has been elected Rector, said the work of the University would be strictly scientific, principally social and would be entirely free from propaganda.

headline: UNMOLESTED.
text:
SHAMEEN RESIDENTS AND ANTON

CANTON

ANITARY ARRANGEMENTS

No untoward incidents have taken place since the opening of the postern of the Western (British) gate on Shameen and residents walk generally unmolested and almost unnoticed in the City. Their presence there occasions no comment on the part of passers by and unless they bring parcels back to Shameen they are unmolested. Strike pickets claim the right to examine parcels and to prohibit the carrying into Shameen of foodstuffs.

It was inevitable that in the absence of Chinese workers the sanitary arrangements of the City have had to be left to individuals themselves and conditions as regards the streets and other public places have been of necessity not of the best. Since the arrival of non-Cantonese Chinese scavengers arranged for through the Sanitary authorities at Hongkong, things in this respect have improved considerably.

headline: “SERIOUS CHARGE.” / AMERICAN SAILOR'S FIREARMS
text:
An unemployed American seaman named Vertie Vlon Brunson was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, with unlawful possession of two automatic pistols and 52 rounds of ammunition.

Detective Sergeant O'Donovan said that he visited the Seamen's Institute yesterday evening on certain information received by him and arrested the defendant following the discovery of the arms in his possession.

His Worship told the defendant that it was a serious charge, and remanded the case for one week, bail being allowed on $2,000.

headline: “DISAPPOINTED.”
text:
GERMAN NATIONALS' PROTEST.

LOCARNO TREATIES.

The executive of the German National party in a manifesto outlining its attitude towards the Locarno treaties says that the pact greatly disappointed the party because of their principles regarding war-guilt and the state of the army. SATURDAY'S ACCIDENT:

headline: DRUNKEN BRAWL.
text:
R.G.A. MEN GET INTO TROUBLE.

ASSAULT ON POLICE.

Before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, Driver A. E. Blackman, of 38th Heavy Battery, and Gunner Kamm, of Victoria Barracks, were charged on four counts of damaging public ricshas, drunk and disorderly behaviour, and breaking the. cells of the charge room. Kamm was charged in addition with assaulting an Indian constable in the charge room.

The evidence disclosed that after 11 p.m. on Friday the defendants while in a drunken state damaged two ricshas left at the junction of Peel Street and Queen's Road Central. They were arrested by two Indian constables and brought to the charge room where the second defendant pinched one of the constables with his clenched fist.

Sub-Inspector C. McNab Wilson stated in evidence that he was in the charge room when the defendants were brought in at 12.30 a.m. They were both badly under the influence of liquor, and the second defendant was very violent in his behaviour, refusing to submit to a search or answer questions, and later knocking down an Indian constable in his presence. The first defendant walked quietly to the cell, but four European officers had to assist in placing the second defendant in the cell. The prisoners then proceeded to smash up the cells and tore off the flooring boards, keeping up a disturbance until 3:30 a.m. A military escort arrived later and took them away.

Both defendants accepted the evidence; Kamm stating that he did not remember any of the incidents of that night.

His Worship fined the first defendant $5 on each of the four charges, and a total of $5 compensation for damage to a ricsha and the cell.

Addressing the second defendant, His Worship said that he had aggravated his offence by striking down a constable in front of the Inspector, and he was not prepared to overlook this offence. He imposed a fine of $5 for damage to the ricsha and $4 compensation. On the charge of being drunk he was fried $5, and for damaging the cell he was ordered to pay $10 compensation. On the charge of assaulting the constable, defendant was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

headline: WHISKY A CURE?
text:
GARRISON SERGT. MAJOR'S EXPERIMENT

COURT MARTIAL SEQUEL.

Having heard, he stated in evidence this morning, that whisky was a cure for a minor ailment from which he was suffering, Garrison, Sergt. Major Henry Tye dosed himself for several days taking at no time more than four a day and mixing the alcohol with milk.

He was charged before a district court martial this morning with being guilty of conduct prejudicial to good order and military discipline in that he became unfit by reason of previous indulgence in alcohol stimulants.

He was not a spirit drinker, he said in his evidence this morning. His usual drink was beer, and the whisky evidently did not agree with him. He had, added to this, a close family bereavement which had preyed on his mind somewhat. He thought all this had combined to make the effects of the whisky more potent.

He was examined medically on the morning of October 19 and having been pronounced to be suffering from alcoholic poisoning was kept at the military hospital until October 24. For two days he was kept in bed, his condition having shown no signs of improvement. He was continually calling for drinks and the keys, said Capt. R. F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C.

Both Capt. Walker and Major A. S. Littlejohns, R.A.M.C. were questioned by Major Paton, who represented the prisoner, as to whether a long or short bout of drinking was likely to have brought about the state of priscner. He had only been in the hospital a short time and did not this go to show that he had not induced to any great extent asked Major Paton.

Both witnesses replied in effect that it depended on how much the man was accustomed to take in the ordinary way.

Evidence as to character was given and the prisoner's 23 years and 10 months' service, with only one minor offence against him was mentioned. Major J. Macready, D.S.O., Bfd. and Herts. Regt. also spoke as to prisoner's exemplary character since he joined the China Command in March of last year.

The Court assembled later for the purpose of trying Corporal Churn on charges of absenting himself without leave and failing to report when detailed for guard. His defence was that he had a pass to go and see the boxing and failed to hand in the half of it on his return. As regarded the absence from duty he had verbal leave from the orderly corporal. It transpired that when this latter was given the orderly corporal did not know that the prisoner was under open arrest in connection with the first charge.

headline: STAND OR FALL.
text:
FRENCH CABINET STATES POLICY

THE WAVE OF UNREST (Reuter's Service.)

The Government has decided to stand or fall on a vote of the Chamber on the Ministerial declaration which is to be presented to the Chamber this afternoon. The Socialists have decided to abstain from voting. The declaration stresses the financial problem, but does not reveal the proposed taxation, merely declaring that all forms of wealth will participate. It says the menace of Morocco has been removed.

The French occupy a strong northern frontier line from which suspicious movements can be watched and suppressed. Twenty-one battalions are returning to France.

It attributes the painful events in Syria to a wave of agitation sweeping from China to Morocco.

LUKEWARM RECEPTION. Paris, Nov. 3. One hundred and eighty, including 104 Socialists, abstained from voting the Ministerial declaration which generally received a luke warm reception. The Socialists were stonily silent.

The Right Centre was equally cold, though it cheered the reference to M. Briand's work at Locinto and Marshal Lyautey's and Yarshal Petain's achievements in Morocco. Following the announcement of the divisions, it was learnt that four Socialist leaders, M. Boncourt, M. Moutet, M. Auriol and M. Renaudel had resigned from the committee of the Socialist Parliamentary Group as a protest at the Party's decision not to support M. Painleve. The latter, on leaving the Chamber of Deputies to-night, remarked: "The present Cabinet will remain in office."

headline: AFTER 36 YEARS.
text:
THROUGH PLAGUE AND TYPHOON.

MN. J. KERR, A.S.P., RETIRES:

Thirty-six years' residence in any part of the globe, even with a stable community, would of necessity entail the witnessing of many changes, but to few places would this apply with such force as to Hongkong where the development has been so comparatively quick and Remarkable.

Mr. J. Kerr, Assistant Superintendent of Police, who retires at the end of this month with that amount of service here to his credit, will leave a very different Hongkong and Kowloon behind him than those in which he first set foot in 1890 when he arrived as a member of the Hongkong Police Force.

This naturally applies to Kowloon more particularly, which for some time after Mr. Kerr arrived, was practically all hills with a road as far as Austin Road. From here to any other spot in that direction one had to clamber over rocks and boulders. Kimberly Road led one then to the waterfront only. The New Territories were not then ceded, and Mr. Kerr remembers the bamboo border fence stretching from Kowloon City to Shamshuipo with Chinese "braves" on the other side attired in picturesque garb, their coats bearing Chinese characters. Their duties were connected with the Customs. The main ferry ran in those days from a point somewhere in the neighbourhood of the new main office buildings of the Wharf and Godown Company and there being no Salisbury Road in those days, loose boulders extended about as far as the, now, railway station.

One of Mr. Kerr's earliest and most trying experience was connected with the first outbreak of plague in Hongkong when deaths were taking place at the rate of 112 a day with some 3,000 in all. Public servants, the military and civilians combined in combating this terrible scourge and times were doubly trying for the police, for there was a certain amount of unrest. The plague was so virulent in its deadly effects that numbers were dying almost immediately on, admittance to hospitals and ignorance and superstition associated with foreign "devilry," the use of ice to bring down the temperatures of those affected being cited and there being much talk of open rebellion and violence. "Tung Wah hospital officials were, in fact, mobbed."

Mr. Kerr has still in his possession a medal awarded for services at this time. On one side of it are a patient on a stretcher, a nurse and doctor warding off the angel of death, a bucket of whitewash and brush and on the other side are Queen Victoria's head and an inscription. The whitewashing reference is to the method of stamping out the disease—the burning of all belongings of infected persons and the whitewashing of their premises.

Work of superintendence in connection with the removal of the dead in the typhoons of 1900 and 1906 also fell to Mr. Kerr's lot. The typhoon of 1900 was on November 10, the latest in the year one is known to have taken place here, and many craft were caught. The havoc wrought in that of 1906 was terrible, some 10,000 people, it is thought having lost their lives inside of two hours.

Mr Kerr's rise in the force has been steady; his appointment as Sergeant was in 1899, 3rd class Inspector in 1908, 2nd class in 1906 and 1st class in 1910. In 1915 Mr Kerr was appointed Chief Inspector and in 1922 he was appointed to the rank at which he is retiring.

Many years of active life should await Mr. Kerr who by no stretch of the word could be termed old although, "old" in the service of Hongkong. He intends settling down in Australia, his Home with Mrs. Kerr and his son. He had always been a "home bird." He confessed to a "China Mail" represals at various. He was looking forward to enjoying life "putting about on a piece of land," and doing what else he could. It make the best use of his time. The good with a man's friend was with the same

headline: PRATAS TRAGEDY.
text:
WATER DISTILLATION

From further advices regarding the tragedy enacted on Pratas shoal when over sixty Ningpo Chinese engaged on the construction of the wireless station were carried off by a terrible scourge of beriberi and others, conveyed to hospital at Amoy it is evident that although there is no natural drinking water on the island there was a condensing plant and had difficulty should have been experienced in obtaining pure water. It would appear that a Chinese Government representative made a visit last month when two cases of the disease were reported. The contractors at Shanghai who by their contract are regarded as liable for maintenance of communication with the mainland and medical attention, were advised that the employees should be taken off, the building construction now having been completed and the installation of the instruments being the only work outstanding.

In the meantime efforts were made to isolate the two cases until they could be removed but the spreading of the disease is said to have been caused through the disinclination of the two in question to separation from their fellows. Repeated efforts were made by the contractors to get into communication with Pratas but the rough weather made it impossible for the boats they sent to land. It was then that the Revenue cruiser put out from Amoy and achieved its object after a very rough trip.

headline: TRADE LOAN.
text:
AN OPEN LETTER TO THE COMMITTEE.

THE CHINESE VIEWPOINT

Gentlemen, I offer no apology for addressing you anonymously through the medium of the Press on the subject of the Trade Loan for this subject vitally concerns the public, and I feel that you will be interested to hear about the hopes and expectations of the Chinese regarding this matter about their anxieties and disappetments. But I do offer you my assurance that I am not being activated by any ulterior motive that I have no "axe to grind," and that, personally, I am in no way interested in the Loan. Now, what was the financial situation of the Colony prior to the announcement of the loan? It is, I think, no exaggeration to say that it was grave. The Banks—doubtless for good reasons, which I do not profess to know—refused to lend one money, irrespective of the amount or quality of the securities offered. Creditors were pressing debtors for repayment. The vitality of credit was gone. Cash appeared to have completely vanished from the market. The Chinese were driven to appeal to the Government for assistance. A Chinese Delegation, headed by the Chinese members on the Legislative Council, waived on the Government, and the whole outlook was exhaustively and impressively stated by their spokesman. Thanks to his masterly presentation of the case, and to the sympathy of Sir Edward Stubbs, the Government was, within the space of only a few days, able to announce that the Home Government would at once place at the disposal of the Colonial Government a sum of $23,000,000, which was the figure suggested by the

The effect of this announcement was marvellous and instantaneous. The whole tone of the financial situation at once improved. Faith in the Colony immediately revived. All hoped that with $3,000,000 available to be lent on good securities, of which there were ample, the nightmare of enforced sales and wholesale insolvencies would exist no more. Surely the money would be for the coming within one week? Two weeks? Three weeks? One month? Then as the weeks passed and still not one dollar came out from the loan to relieve the financial pension, people began to get uneasy, anxious and even in spedulous. As usual rumour, succeeded rumour. The Government would lend only to finance, business " not to ward off depreciative and rulorous sales. In any case, the ridiculous margins demanded by the Government would render the loan commercially useless. Indeed, was the money really available at all? And so, as the rumours increased, the situation gradually drifted back to the old days of despondence and financial stagnation. The catless men, believe me, every one opprearies that the task imposed upon you is staggering in its difficulty, and that the Government could not have found a body of men more qualified than yourself as to discharge the well-nigh superhuman task. I cannot therefore presume to offer you any notice. But I hope it is not presumptuous on my part if I were to give utterance to what I believe to be the views generally held in the Colony concerning this matter. I take it that the fundamental object of the Loan is to the words of the Secretary of State for the Colonies for the Federation of the financial credit of Hongkong. CANTON'S STEPS TO END STRIKE.

LATEST CABLE NEWS

Further news has reached Hong- ong with regard to the move- rents by Chinese merchants in anton to end the strike.

As reported in the "China Mail," the four leading commercial chambers held an informal meeting. The "Wah Taz Mat. Po" has now been informed by cable that a delegate has been appointed to interview. Wong Ching-wai, chairman of the Kuomintang Commission of Government, on the subject.

headline: China the Initial / HONGKONG, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1925. / PRAYA COLLISION.
text:
FIRE ENGINE AND MAIL VAN

PEDESTRIAN SEVERELY INJURED.

A collision occurred yesterday morning between a Post Office mail van and a fire engine which resulted in injuries to five persons, one of whom is now at the Government Civil Hospital in a critical condition.

The van was standing on the side of Connaught Road near the lane separating the Post Office building from the P. and O. offices. The fire engine with the usual crew on board turned from Pedder Street near the statue; and through some circumstance which is now being investigated struck the mail van in the rear. The force of the impact was so strong that the van destroyed an electric lamp post and ran a distance of about 30 feet before it was brought to a halt by striking the pillar on the pavement at the entrance to the P. and O. building.

The van being empty, and with

the brakes out of action, broke one of its front wheels in colliding with the pillar. The fire engine was completely disabled and very badly damaged. Special emergency equipment had to be brought to the scene, and the engine was taken across the harbour to the railway workshops for repair.

In addition to the Chinese pedestrian who was severely injured by the mail van in the course of its run, a Chinese officer on the engine, a fireman, and two others sustained minor injuries. The driver of the van who was on his seat at the time was not injured.

headline: A NARROW ESCAPE. / MACHINERY CATCHES WORKER.
text:
DRAGGED BY THE HAIR.

A Chinese girl employed at the Tai-Kuen Knitting Factory at Portland Street, Yaumati, had a narrow escape from death when she was caught by the hair and drawn into the machinery. With remarkable presence of mind, a workman brought the machinery to a standstill, and the girl was extricated. She sustained injuries to her scalp, and was taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital, where she is reported to be progressing satisfactorily.

headline: SOVIET CIVIL CODE. / PROPERTY RIGHTS RESTORED:
text:
The presidium of the Executive has considerably amended the Civil Code with a view to annulling restrictions as regards the right of inheritance, particularly the clause limiting the sum of inheritance to 10,000 roubles.

Property will only pass to the possession of the State in the event of the absence of a will and lawful heirs.

headline: MISS CAPELL'S PUPILS. / THEATRE ROYAL MATINEE.
text: Saturday's success was repeated yesterday and a large audience watched with great interest a programme of dancing demonstrating Miss Capell's abilities as a teacher and the cleverness of her pupils. Allison Mackenzie in "Jazz" came in for special notice and was loudly encored. But her companions were not a whit behind in what they did. This applies particularly to Winnie Henderson who, in "Rendezvous," showed what an artist she is. In addition to rousing applause, there were many gifts of flowers and chocolates received with evident enjoyment. Part of the proceeds of the two exhibitions are to be given to that excellent institution, the London shore held that she was a British ship. Yesterday the only British ship in Swatow was the "Dacre Castle" discharging oil. It is also said that the chief man in the port at present was formerly the chief of the Seamen's Union. This Union is now again at the height of its power, the committee comprising mostly freemen, stokers and sailors.

headline: SWATOW POSITION
text:
ANTI-BRITISH EMBARGO CONTINUES.

LABOUR CHIEF'S POWER

Three ships with Hongkong cargo on board—one Chinese, one Japanese and one Portuguese—were held up at Swatow Monday when ready to discharge.

On Monday night, the Swatow branch of the Seamen's Union held a meeting and it was decided that an.the consignees "had not given the Union sufficient notice," the merchants would have to pay $1,000 for each ship. On the money being handed over the vessels discharged on Tuesday without any further difficulty. On Wednesday the steamers were allowed to take on cargo, not for Hongkong but for Chinese ports in the South.

The 8.s. "Anhui" entered Swatow from Singapore. Her passengers were permitted to land but she was not allowed to take either cargo or passengers for Amoy as the strike pickets on

sentative at present Hongkong is a group of the Paracels group and if the report is favourable, work of building a meteorological station there in addition to that on Pratas will be immediately put in hand, direction being under the Chinese Admiralty. If conditions are favourable it is anticipated that the station will be in operation in about five months' time.

headline: STREET MISHAPS.
text:
EUROPEAN'S MOTOR CYCLE ACCIDENT

The efficient traffic arrangements made to cope with yesterday's holiday attraction averted any special accidents, two incidentals, attended with minor injuries, apart from the big collision on the Praya, being accidents of every day occurrence. Yesterday afternoon a tram car knocked down a Chinese at Praya East, near Bowrington Canal, and he had to be taken to hospital with internal injuries. In another accident at Praya East, a tram car overturned a ricsha on which were riding a lady and a child. The vehicle failed to get out of the tram lines owing to the excavation work on the roadside. The passengers, however, escaped injury. A motor lorry driver has reported to the police that he collided with a motor cycle the driver of the latter a European, being thrown off his machine. He picked himself up and continued his journey, apparently unsurprised. The excavation clanged was a moment for him morning. The value of this station will be considerable, principally to shipping south of Hongkong, in the neighbourhood of Hainan, which at present is without means of information of the movements of typhoons which take a more westerly curve than those striking Pratas. A typhoon of this nature often strikes inland and causes havoc at Canton.

headline: LOYAL DUBLIN.
text:
IMPRESSIVE ARMISTIC CEREMONY

VREATHS AND POPPIMS.

(Reuter's Service.) London November 11

In spite of previous agitation and the threats of the extreme Republicans, our account of which the Civil Guards were reinforced by Police Amistão's daily was collected in Dublin in a most tranquill manner. A cross is to be erected on a French battlefield in commemoration of the 16th 16th Division. It was temporarily placed on St. Stephen's Green and was unveiled in a simple impressive ceremony including two minutes' leverage, in the presence of the enormous crowd which cheered and wired Union Jacks.

After this unveiling the crowd joined in singing "God Save the King" started by Ex-Service men. Many wreaths were placed on the cross and poppes told readily.

Miss Maud Gonne, Mrs. McBride, and, other lady republicans, were removed from the crowd by the police for their own protection. They were carrying placards leading with prisoners in jail.

Fifteen people were injured in panics caused by the throwing of smoke bombs and fights between rival sections after the armishece celebrations in Dublin. Ex-Corporal, Oates, succumb to injuries.

After nightfall the Republicans demonstrated in the streets and broke the windows of the Masonio Hall.

Elaborate police precautions parented conflicts and detentives following the procession in a curfied over the heads of the demonstrators for the purpose of clengering the streets.

headline: TRAFFIC CLASSIC / RUSOLA SULSINDISUN CERTIFIED SEED:
text:
A RGW100N PRN(2)%。

In the prosecution of two rish coolies at the Rowlton Magistracy this morning for obstruction at the "Star" ferry wharf, it was stated by Sergeant Smith that European residents engaged public riches and valid by the r. nth. They are reported to the ferry and back home every day, and in order to meet these customers the coolies with their vehicles wait outside the fresh stand, thus causing obstruction.

The Magistrate imposed a fine of $2 each and remarked that people could take rieshas to the ferry and pay monthly, but were not allowed to subsidise vehicles for the homeward journey which necessitated the coolies having to wait near the ferry.

headline: REDS EXECUTED.
text:
NAVAL OFFICERS SHOT AT KONGMOON.

CANTON FLAGSHIP STIR

Obscurity shrouds the motive behind the execution of three Red naval officers at Kongmoon. It is believed that the three officers were attached to the "Chang Shan," (formerly, the "Wing, Fung" and renamed in honour of Dr. Sun Yat-sen), flagship of the Canton Navy.

When the Soviet influence reached its zenith a Russian commander, was appointed to the "Chang Shai." Since then several vague reports—not all substantiated—have been given in connection with her. One was a supposed mutiny in which the Russian chief was supposed to have walked the plank. A subsequent story was that the cruiser had disappeared!

Capt. Au-Yeung is the Chinese commander and it is thought that the executions were under his authority. "The officers are stated to be suspected of disloyalty but there is also a hint that a scramble for power behind the scenes may have some connection with the matter. Captain Au-Yeung is at Pickland, the port of Kongmoon, write the "China Mail" correspondence, is command of the Center River Defence Field.

headline: RED SCHOOL ROW. / AGITATOR STUDENTS AID POLITICIANS
text:
BIG SUMS COVETED.

By stirring up agitation among the younger students attending colleges and universities Canton politicians are alleged to be making a determined move to secure control of the very large sums tied up in endowment funds.

Several months ago the Kung Yee Hospital control was transferred to the Cukton University of which Chew Loo is the principal Dr. S. F. Lee of Hongkong was said to have given up his post at the Kung Yee because he did not concur with the decision.

Now organisations of junior students are said to be actively working on Red political initiative to get the properties standing to the name of the educational institutions out of the present holders' hands.

A telegram to the "Wah Tsa Yat Po" says that educationalists have been refused payment of 40 per cent expenses which they asked for. A general meeting is to be held which may decide to hold a strike in all schools, etc., in Canton on Monday if the request is not accepted to.

ANT-NORTH OFFERSIVE? Canton is also reported by the same paper to be forming bases on Kwanglung's northern friendlies for an offensive against the provinces of Fukken and Kiangsi.

headline: A SAD TIME
text:
MAGISTRATE'S SYMPATHY WITH FORESTERS.

AN ABUSED PERMIT.

During the hearing of a forestry case at the Central Ministry in which Mr. H. Green gave evidence, Mr. R. E. Lindseil struck a sympathetic note by remarking that he understood the department had been having a sad time. Mr. Green agreed that it had indeed been a very sad time.

The case was against ten women who were charged with unlawful possession of wood cut from the plantations in Wong Nei Chong village. It was stated that the first defendant held a permit from a contractor and the department to remove wood from a certain area. Under cover of this permit the others entered the plantations and were engaged in wholesale removal of wood until they came under the notice of an Indian constable.

His Worship was surprised to hear that all the defendants had readily furnished bail money of $25 each. This was explained by the fact that a crowd of friends and relatives followed the arrested women to the Police Station and bailed them out. They were stated to be fairly well to do and not of the ordinary coolie class. The woman who held the permit was discharged with a warning, and the others were fined $10 each.

headline: NO SHORTAGE OF FOOD.
text:
Reports that there was any shortage of food on Pratas and that this was responsible for the deaths amongst the coolies engaged on work there are entirely without foundation according to the definite statement of a high Chinese official staying in the Colony in whose hands has been the Chinese Admiralty's responsibility for the erection of the station.

There were 180 bags of rice untouched when the coolies amongst whom had spread the beri-beri were taken off by the "Haishing," he informed a "China Mail" representative. Wild reports that the men in question had lived on grass and seaweed for a week were absolutely false—in fact, reliefs which had been despatched from Shanghai some time before the beri-beri had spread and had proceeded to Frutas by the "Haishing" on the occasion of her last visit took no supplies with them, relying for the time being on the stocks left behind.

Asked whether...if there seemed a possibility that heri-beri had spread through the agency of the rice in question it was advisable that this rice should be used, the "China Mail" informant replied that this had been put to the contractors...who were responsible. They had since supplemented their supplies. The Chinese Government had also despatched to Pratas a very large supply of tinned stuffs from Hongkong, primarily for the Admiralty men manning the station, but for the others if needed.

With the last reliefs had also gone a certain number of planters with seeds in order that fresh vegetables might be grown. There were great possibilities on the island in this latter respect and Indian rice was already being grown. A large open space used previously for the laying out of fish and seaweed was a most fertile spot and the island was not the barren desolate spot it was made out to be, stated our informant. A few indigenous coconut trees were bearing fruit, also newly planted ones.

The men who had gone to Pratas for relief work were conversant with the position there and some of them had previously worked there, being part of a detachment which had been taken away as the work was nearing completion and their work, it was thought, would no longer be required. There had been two cases of beri-beri at that time and they were informed, together with the others, that it had'sprend. They had suitable medicines with them.

The number of deaths had been very much over-reported, stated the official in question. There had originally been 92 men engaged on the work of building, over 30 had been taken off on a previous occasion when there were two cases of beri-beri and as the work was nearing completion it was thought their services would no longer be required and a message he had received stated that over 30 were taken off by the "Hai-shing" when the disease had spread so rapidly. Presuming that all those not taken off were dead they only amounted to some 24 and not 62 as had been reported.

headline: CHRISTMAS MAIL.
text:
PARCELS COUNTER SCENES

The parents' counter at the General Post Office was literally besieged from morning by those anxious to deliver their packages before the last minute rush for the Christmas and New Year mail closing for Home at 5 p.m. to day. This mail is due in London on December 17.

Over 1,450 parcels had been received for despatch by the s.s. "Mantua" up till yesterday afternoon, and it is expected that last year's total of 3,050 parcels will be exceeded.

Although faced with an impossible task owing to shortage of hands and the calls on the parcels' staff to attend to inward deliveries, they are determined to get away all the parcels offering to-day even by working well into the night.

The Christmas letter will close on November 24.

Mrs. B. Thompson is in the French Hospital with malaria. Her friends will be pleased to hear she is making good progress.

Moscow, November 12. M. Karakhan goes to Peking at the end of the month to resume his post of Soviet Ambassador.

headline: TIT FOR TAT?
text:
ANTON SCHOOLS THREATEN STRIKE.

SEIZED STEAMER SEQUEL

Canton is not finding educational institutions and direct steamship communication such as easy matters as it had at first supposed. Last week the agitation by a section of junior students was reported to be culminating in a threatened strike of schools, colleges, etc., throughout the whole city. The latest news now is that if the Government does not pay certain arrears to the schools by tomorrow the strike will come into effect.

Then boycott of Canton is alleged to have been threatened by Cantonese merchants in Shanghai. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that on November 2, the s.s. "Hsien Wah" was "seized" by the military in Canton who claimed $20,000 damage from the China Merchants Co. for damage to a telegraph cable. The report continues that Shanghai has hinted that the company's steamers will not make the Canton call until the steamer is released. The Cantonese guild in Shanghai, therefore, has cabled the Kuomintang Government to release the ship pending discussion.

On inquiry from the local office of the China Merchants Co., the "China Mail" was informed that no report of any of the alleged occurrences had been sent to Hongkong.

headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
16 CANTONESE DUE TO-DAY?

LATEST STRIKE RUMOURS.

It was rumoured this morning that the Canton peace delegation is expected to arrive by the s.s. "Hônam" this afternoon, and that the committee of the Tung Wah Hospital and representatives of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and the Twenty-four Guilds will hold a reception.

The discussion will probably take place at the Tung Wah Hospital.

The delegation is to number 16 and is said to be representative of Canton's commercial interests, including also two representatives from the strike executive.

A cable received by the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" last night states that the Canton delegation's departure has been postponed till Friday.

Another message is that the Canton chambers of commerce have drafted a list of "terms" on which to base negotiations.

headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
SEDITIOUS CONSPIRACY CHARGES.

ORDERS FROM MOSCOW

The trial of the 12 Communists recently arrested on a charge of seditious conspiracy, was opened at the Old Bailey this morning, with two women as jurors.

All the defendants pleaded not guilty.

The Attorney-General, in opening the case, said the nature of the conspiracy which the prosecution undertook to prove was that the defendants were heads in Britain of an illegal organisation calling itself the Communist Party of Great Britain, the supreme control of which was in Moscow, with the object of forcibly overthrowing by arms the existing state of society and as a means thereto, seducing the armed forces of the Crown from their allegiance.

headline: "THE TRIAL IS A FARCE."
text:
A man who shouted "the trial is a farce" was ejected from the court.

The Attorney-General stated the Communists spent at least £12,000 annually on salaries and newspaper propaganda, and undoubtedly the money, or a greater part of it came from Moscow.

The Communists were therefore bound by orders from Moscow, which were illegal and criminal in England.

The Attorney-General's speech lasted over four hours. The trial was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: ROBBERY ECHO.
text:
A BID FOR FREEDOM FRUSTRATED

WOUNDED MAN IN COURT

An armed robbery committed at a pawnshop at Bulkeley Street, Hunghom, on June 30, and in connection with which two Chinese were sentenced to seven years' hard labour at the Criminal Sessions, was recalled at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with being concerned in the affair.

The present defendant was shot at and wounded by a constable during a raid carried out by the Police which resulted in the capture of the gang. Defendant had been in hospital since his capture. The case was remanded till Friday afternoon.

Arms Case.

A Chinese from a village near Shamshuipo was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour for unlawful possession of a revolver.

headline: TIME RIPE?
text:
SIGNS OF DESIRE TO END STRIKE.

LOVES BEHIND THE SCENES.

Although they are no more than straws in the wind, there are several indications that an all-round feeling exists in favour of ending the strike and boycott. Friday is, now stated to have been definitely fixed as the day of departure from Canton of a peace delegation to Hongkong. Over twenty merchants will be included, it is reported.

Yesterday the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce held a committee meeting which discussed the details of a reception for the Canton traders. Meanwhile representatives of Canton's four leading commercial associations—all designated as "chambers"—have interviewed Mr. Wong Ching-wai, one of the principals of the Kuomintang Commission of Government—and he is said to have lent a favourable ear. There is, however, a qualification Mr. Wong is quoted as having approved a mission to Hongkong, more for the purpose of ascertaining what can be done, than declaring an end to the present conditions.

Yesterday afternoon the Steamboat Co.'s s.s. "Honam" came down with about 400 native passengers—a "record number—who state that they made their way to the ship, when in Canton harbour unmolested by pickets.

Another sign of the times is a report from Canton that the present mercantile movement was engendered by the Hongkong Association of District Commercial Guilds, also that the sponsors of the Canton peace delegation, have put out feelers to the Strike Executive. The strike leaders, on the other hand, seem to be divided. One section is adamant and strongly disfavours any mission to Hongkong. Another party is reported to have declared itself as willing to abide by what the "majority of the people" say. In other words they will be guided by the Canton Government but they will not turn an entirely deaf ear to the merchants and middle class.

headline: BLIND HOME. / TO-DAY'S SALE OF WORK
text: A sale of work in aid of the Industrial Institution for the Blind, Kowloon, opened at the Y.W.C.A. rooms, Caine Road, this morning and will be continued till 5 p.m. Useful and舒適的 work in aid of the Industrial Institution for the Blind, Kowloon, opened at the Y.W.C.A. rooms, Caine Road, this morning and will be continued till 5 p.m. Useful and skillfully made articles of knitted woollens, embroideries and other goods adorned the tableau, and the blind girls made a striking appeal for sympathy by singing at intervals.
