headline: DANGEROUS
text:
The master of a fishing junk was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on two charges of unlawful possession of an old rifle and a quantity of detonators and dynamite. Evidence of seizure was given by Sergeant Carevel.

Pleading gully to the charge of possession of the explosives, Mr. C. A. S. Russ submitted that the junk occasionally visited the outskirts of British waters, but that the fishing was done in Chinese waters where there was no law against the use of dynamite.

A plea of not guilty was tendered on the charge of possession of the rifle. Mr. Russ explained that the weapon was kept on board as an assurance of security against possible molestation from strike pickets. The junk, he said, had at one time been used for the transport of vegetables to Hongkong from an outlying district and the owner had in fact held a permit to carry firearms while engaged on this mission.

His Worship convicted on both charges, among a fine of $150 for carrying explosives, which he considered was the more serious of the two, and $50 on the other charge.

Bangkok has been declared an infected port on account of cholera.

headline: DESERTION CHARGE
text:
NORTHERN CONSTABLE JAILED

A FAIR RECORD.

A Wei-hai-wei constable was charged before Mr. R. E. Lind-sell at the Central Magistracy this morning with desertion.

According to a record produced by Mr. W. R. Scott, 2nd Assistant Superintendent of Police, the man was sworn in last September to serve for three years, but deserted in July this year. He was arrested in Yaumati few days ago. Defendant's conduct during his short period of service was stated to be fair.

Sentence of four weeks' har labour was imposed.

headline: China" Initial
text:
No. 19,654

which might have grave consequences.

NO TIME FOR DELAY. In moving the amendment, cabled yesterday, Mr. A. Ponsonby thought the Treaty could be interpreted as the grouping of Western Powers against Russia, the result being the throwing ing of Russia into the arms of Asia.

Mr. Chamberlain, in replying, regretted the circumstances of the different Governments of the Empire precluded the possibility of a conference for them before the Home advisers entered negotiations with foreign countries.

He did not blame the Dominions, the governments "of which were unable to meet us at a moment's notice, but Britain faced the situation which had not brooked delay.

He emphasised the desire to pursue a policy full of harmony and in accord with agreement at every stage with the Dominions who had pointed out the right reserved to the Dominions to adhere or not adhere to the Treaty.

He hoped the incident would excite a keener desire over the Empire to find machinery whereby foreign policy would become in every act and every hour the foreign policy of the Empire and not, the foreign policy of Britain. (Cheers).

headline: MOTOR MISHAPS.
text:
YESTERDAY'S CAINE ROAD

APPRENTICE DRIVER HANED:

A chair bearer was accidentally knocked down at Caine Road yesterday by a motor car driven by Miss R. Mow. Fung. of Messrs. Gilman & Co. Ltd.

The coolie had to be taken to the Government Civil Hospital having sustained injuries to his friend and legs.

In another accident at Calne Rond, a Sanitary Board, coolie was struck down by a motor car driven by a learner. The coolie's injuries were not so serious in this case as to necessitate his removal to hospital.

The driver of the car was charged before the Magistrate this morning for using a road not allowed under his learner's licence. He was fined $10 and was ordered to pay in addition $5 as compensation to the injured coolie.

headline: PERTINENT QUESTION.
text:
Mr. Chamberlain warmly denied the Government's policy as being hostile to Russia. He declared that it was only perverted ingenuity to devise an argument that Locarno was establishing a new balance of power, namely, between Europe and Asia, and pointed out that Eastern nations were members of the League like the Western nations.

Japan, with whom we were happily on terms of intimate friendship and co-operation, was a member of the League.

He asked whether Mr. Ponsonby meant that Britain must not attempt to put relations with Germany on a better footing unless we received the sanction of the Soviet Government.

headline: DESTINY!
text:
THE NEW COMET AND THE STRIKE.

SIMPLE CHINESE BELIEF. Connection between the new comet and the local strike has been pointed to by some of the

simple Chinese in the Colony. Yesterday Reuter cabled the report of the discovery of a new comet in the constellation of the "Hunting Dog" by Yerkis Observatory, U.S.A. This comet is brightly visible through a small telescope.

A week or so ago local star-gazers were watching a “destiny” star from streets and housetops, shortly after sunset. The “discoverers” claim that they were even quicker, with the unaided eye, than the powerful apparatus worked by qualified astronomers. One even went so far as to maintain that the presence of this “broom” star (the Chinese colloquial for comet) would have a great influence over the settlement of the strike!

headline: LIFE OF CRIME. / HARDENED CRIMINAL AT SESSIONS.
text:
Having pleaded guilty to charges of theft from the Chinese Y.M.C.A. in Bridges Street where he had been shown into a room when he said he wanted to see a friend, also to the theft of three trunks and a rattan basket left in charge of a little girl on the Praya and to returning to Hongkong from which he had been banished for 10 years as an incorrigible criminal, a Chinese was sentenced to five years hard labour at the Criminal Sessions this morning.

His excuse regarding the latter charge was that he was returning to Formosa from Macao and had to come to Hongkong to get a ship and passport. There was delay regarding getting his photograph and that was why he was here for some time. With regard to the theft of trunks from the Praya He had given the little girl in charge money and told her to buy some stamps. He had then engaged a taxi to take them away. His Lordship (Sir Henry Cowper Gollan) remarking that the man seemed to have gone in for a life of stealing, passed sentence as stated above. Until noon tomorrow the weather forecast is N.E. winds moderate to

headline: DR. WU'S HELP. / HOPES OF ENDING THE BOYCOTT.
text:
MONEY EXPORT EMBARGO?

Dr. C. C. Wu (Wu Chao-chu) is now reported to be strenuously exerting his influence towards ending the present Canton boy-cott.

Among the. Kuomintang officials Dr. Wu is probably the "best. know and most respected diplomat. In the discussions between delegates of the merchants and the Canton Commission of Government Dr. Wu is reported to have used his good offices.

Another favourable report is that General Cheung Kai-shek's officers at Swatow are quietly supervising the strike pickets there and restriating them from any possible excesses.

Meanwhile the next step is eagerly awaited by Chinese merchants in Hongkong—the promised arrival of the Canton delegation to-morrow afternoon.

Passengers coming into Hongkong by train from Samchin state that the pickets just across the border have been exercising strict vigilance during the last two days in the matter of money and valuables. Those who take with them anything over $20 or excess jewellery have been sent back along the Chinese section of the Railway, or asked to deposit the surplus pending their return from Hongkong. No official notice has been given of any order by the Strike Executive regarding the export of money or valuables.

headline: MURDER TRIAL
text:
BUILDING

X YOUTH ARRAIGNED

The disappearance of it building implement is alleged to be the cause of a dispute between two employees, one an old man and the other little more than a youth. After high words had passed it is alleged that the young man who suspected the other of taking the tool, struck the old man with a knife in the abdomen. As a result of his injuries the man in question died at the Government Civil Hospital and the other is arraigned at the Criminal Sessions on a charge of murder.

He was represented this morning by Mr. H.S. Fitzroy and the Attorney General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., prosecuted.

The only alleged eye-witness is the man to whom belonged the tool which was the source of the trouble and on whose behalf the prisoner had taken up the cudgels. This man said that he saw prisoner strike the old man, with a knife and he (witness) then ran away. Later at a house at East Point he saw the prisoner who admitted that he had stabbed the man.

This witness was cross-examined, minutes by Mr. Fitzroy. Asked to account for the fact that it was he (witness) and not the prisoner who stayed away from work for two days and seemed to have most apprehensions, whereas prisoner went on with his work the witness replied that he ran away and hid because he thought if the police could not get the prisoner they would come for him. Witness maintained that he had heard the prisoner make the statement as to having stabbed the old man. This despite the fact that Mr. Fitzroy pointed out that another man who had heard the alleged confession stated in the witness box that he was the only person there at the time the confession was made. Medical evidence of the terrible nature of the wounds from which the old man died was given and cross-examined by Mr. Fitzroy witnesses said that they did not think that the wound could have been self-inflicted through the old man falling on the weapon clenched in his own hand.

The case is proceeding.

headline: PEACE DOINGS.
text:
INTERESTED PARTIES WORK HARD.

DELEGATION DUE TO-DAY.

Until the delegation arrives from Canton to-day it is not known what the nature of their discussion will be.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngnam, who at one time owned considerable property in the Colony, is the latest to have interested himself in a settlement.

Another good sign is the order by the Canton Government to their Police to disarm all pickets engaged in “protecting” transport (both of passengers and cargo at feels).

Then again Canton is desirous that another delegation go up frbn Hongkong.

A gentleman has received a letter, however, stating that even though the Canton delegates have the goodwill of the people in power, they may be placed in such a position that terms will have to be submitted again and that, consequently, the solution lies in a middle party finding a compromise.

headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
FREEDOM OF OPINION INVOLVED?

SEDITIONS OF THE MIGHTY.

... Sir Henry Slesser, counsel for defence, concluding a six hours speech in the trial of the Communists, said this was one of the most important cases submitted to a British jury in many years.

On the decision depended the liberties and opportunities of men to write and express opinions for many years to come.

Sir H. Slesser called only one witness who testified to purchasing at His Majesty's Stationery Office, copies of the Government report on Russia.

The defendant, Harry Pollitt, addressed the jury and was refused permission by the Judge to quote speeches by Lord Birkenhead, Lord Carson and Sir W. Joynson Hicks, the Judge remarking: "We cannot have their editions mixed up with yours."

headline: EIGHTH! / AMERICA AS AERIAL. POWER.
text:
$ x_{1} $

Two interesting witnesses at the Mitchell Court Martial, which is in its concluding stages are the world flier, Lieut. Wade and Captain Rickenbacker, who both sharply criticised the air service.

The former declared his intention of leaving the service owing to lack of opportunity.

Rickenbacker opined that the United States ranked eighth among the powers as regards aviation and was even inferior to Japan, Russia and Poland.

headline: STRIKE
text:
The strike threatened by the staffs of Canton educational institutions has been called off, it is stated.

Rehabilitation work progresses in the East River region. The dismantling of Waichow's city walls is almost completed and it is proposed to convert the historic Sai Wu Lake into a public park.

The capture of Lo Ting, by the Canton armies, in the southern sector, has been reported to Canton.

Chang Waiz, who governs that part of Kiangsi province adjacent to Kwangtung is said, according to a "Wah Tsz Yat Po" cable, to have ordered the army of the anti-Red (Gantonese) General Hung Shui-luo, to leave Kiangsi. General Hung-li-Sak, a�ulatory there after being defeated but Chang deems his presence a menace as he apprehends an invasion by General Cheting Kai-shek, the Cadet chief.

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
CHANGE IN OFFICIAL ATTITUDE?

"OFFENCES. EXPIATED."

It is significant that coincident with the moves that are being made in the direction of closer cooperation between Hongkong and Canton certain proposals have been mooted for a modification of the edict barring from admission to Government and Government aided schools students who were absent from study on certain dates.

The period of this suspension, or expulsion as it was then generally regarded, was not mentioned when the attitude of Sir R. E. Stubbs was outlined by the Chairman of the Education board and it is understood that the penalty paid during the period that has elapsed since their having been de-arred from entrance has been advanced to the Government as sufficient for the students to have expiated their offence. The end of the school year has been suggested as the date when such stringent measures might no longer apply.

The Government attitude is expected to be announced shortly.

It may be recalled that at the Education meeting at which Sir R. E. Stubbs' attitude was endorsed, nearly all the members who spoke were in accord with that attitude but a few thought it was too severe. Father Valtorta thought that temporary suspension and postponement of examinations would meet the case. Mr. J. M. Alves suggested the formation of a "humiliation" class of strikers in each school would be sufficient punishment and Dr. Wan spoke at length or "the need for taking a more liberal and considerate view."

Dr. Pearce thought that the balance had been struck between justice and generous consideration. Now, if ever, was the time for emphasising the importance of discipline. The matter should be left to the heads of schools. No one else could do anything in the matter.

The Chairman's final remark was that he thought that the matter could be safely left with the headmasters who, he was sure, would be sympathetic in their consideration.

headline: School Fees.
text: The “China Mail” also understands that the Government has under consideration the proposed raising of fees which was not the outcome of the strike but revision which was considered necessary in any event. Representations have been made that the present is hardly opportune for an extra financial burden to be imposed on parents and it is likely that the Government may postpone or mitigate the increases.

headline: "CORPSE FACTORY."
text:
THE STORY CROPS UP AGAIN.

QUESTIONS IN COMMONS:

The German corpse factory cropped up in the House of Commons. Sir L. Worthington Evans replying to Commander Kenworthy's request for information of the source of the rumour and to what extent the War Office accepted it, said the statement first appeared in the "Lokal Anzeiger," Berlin, and in two Belgian newspapers.

Later a German Army Order was captured, appearing to confirm the story.

The War Office saw no reason to disbelieve its truth but did not think that public interest would be served by further questions on the subject.

[A cable message from New York on October 25, said: In connection with the stir arising from the report that General Charteris, Chief of the British Intelligence Staff during the war, told the National Arts Club, at a recent private dinner that the story that the German boiled the bodies of dead soldiers for the purpose of obtaining fat was a deliberate invention, General Charteris told a Reuter representative before he left for England that he had been incorrectly reported. His references to propaganda, which were purely incidental, were made with the express purpose of emphasising the principle followed by the British that propaganda to be effective must be based on truth. He added that he only mentioned the case of the "corpse factory" for the purpose of emphasising that the report was not until and for propaganda when it became known that the soldier

headline: MISSING LETTERS.
text:
VIA SIBERIA ROUTE CHARGES.

ALLEGED TAMPERING.

Serious allegations were made at a meeting of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce of heavy delay and miscarriage of mails from Britain to the Far East via Siberia.

Delegates asserted that many mails are missing and letters are tampered with apparently when passing through Soviet territory. The matter was referred to the Postmaster-General.

headline: Railway Deadlock.
text: A semi-official message says: "In view of the refusal of the Chinese Government to sign an agreement regarding the through passenger communication between the Soviet railways and the Soviet and Japanese Chinese railway, the conference concerning the matter has been temporarily suspended on the suggestion of the Soviet delegates. The Russian and Japanese commission on goods traffic will begin work in a few days' time."

headline: CUTTING TREES. / OFFENDERS HEAVILY FINED:
text:
A SHAUKIWAN RAID.

Heavy penalties were imposed by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on a number of illicit woodcutters, the defendants being all women of the coolie class.

A large gang were engaged in the wholesale destruction of a plantation at Shaukijwan West yesterday afternoon. Guards from the Forestry Department, assisted by officers from Divisional Inspector Blackman's Station, pounced on the culprits and arrested some, whilst others made their escape. In a subsequent raid on huts in the vicinity, large quantities of freshly cut wood were seized, the total making up a full lorry load.

Five of the defendants were fined $50 each, or in the alternative four weeks' hard labour whilst others were fined $40 and $20, or imprisonment in default.

headline: BRIAND FAILS.
text:
CRISIS IN FRENCH POLITICS:

SOCIALISTS' DEMANDS.

M. Briand has declined to forin Government.

M. Doumer has been summoned. He has asked for 24 hours to consider the question of the formation of a Cabinet.

It appears the Socialists refused M. Briand's offer of three portfolios and claimed half the seats in the Cabinet.

M. Briand on leaving the Elysee, told the pressmen he would be delighted to include Ms. Herriot, Painleve, Klotz, Paul Boncour, and even representatives of the centre, in the Ministry, if Republican unity was capable of restoring the country's finances, but he was unable to obtain the support necessary to command a stable majority. M. Paul Doumer, President of the Senate Finance Committee, is Ex-Governor of Indo-China. FRANC FALLS, London, November 24. The French france in London

London, November 24. The French franc in London fell 126.65.

(E'arlicr Cables.)

One of M. Briand's main objections to the Premiership is his desire to remain at the Foreign Office to finish the work of the Locarno Conference. The Radicals are agitating for an Herriot Cabinet to include Socialists, but thirty Socialist deputies are opposed to participation in the Government, hence the Left Cartal is threatened with a spit. The solution of the crisis is therefore likely to be delayed owing to a difficulty in finding a stable majority whether either a Carter Cabinet or a concentration Ministry could be based. Reuter.

Miss Pit Wen Ha, the Chinese actress who is giving further performances at the Theatre Royal on account of delay in sailing, will present an autographed photo-graph to every holder of a $3

Qualified Eight Testing With Modern Equipment.

headline: BANISHEE CHARGED.
text:
DEFENDANT'S EXPLANATION IN COURT

STOPPED BY PICKETS.

A. Chinese was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning for returning from banishment.

According to the evidence of a Chinese detective, the man was escorted to Shumchun on September 30. It was stated that defendant had five previous convictions three for returning from banishment.

headline: BORDER INCIDENTS.
text:
RICE CARGOES STOLEN BY STRIKERS.

The peace of the border War disturbed by two incidents which took place on Monday morning. In the first, a party of strikers on mischief bent fired a couple of rounds in the direction of two European officers doing patrol duty on the banks of the Shumchun River. The fire was returned and the strikers took to their heels. This was followed by a theft of rice from coolies on the British side.

At another point near Lqkma-chau, armed men crossed the border and compelled some cookies carrying rice to take the cargo into Chinese territory.

headline: JAIL FOR REDS. / SEMITTOUS CONSPIRACY PROVED
text: The trial of the 12 Communist leaders at the Old Bailey has resulted in all the accused being found guilty. Five namely: Inkpin, Rus, Politt, Gallacher and Hannington have been sentenced to 12 months in the second division. The others refused to be taking over and were sentenced to six months in the second division.

headline: OBITUARY
text:
CHINESE DEATH AT 86TH BIRTHDAY

WELL-KNOWN METALS DEALER

Fifty-seven years a resident in Hongkong, Mr. Chin E-tin, the well-known metals merchant passed away at his residence, No. 23, Wing Woo Street yesterday at the ripe age of 86.

By a strange coincidence yesterday was the late M. Chin's birthday and it was after receiving congratulations from his many friends and relatives that he expired peacefully.

When Mr. Chin first arrived in the Colony he founded the firm of E. Hing & Co., now one of the oldest and most respected hardware firms. Many of the older members of the mercantile community will recall Mr. Chin, who from a very humble origin, rose to great wealth by integrity and shrewd handling of his business.

The funeral takes place tomorrow afternoon, and the remains will be deposited at the Tung Wah Hospital repository. The cortege passes the Yat Pit Ting, Kennedy Town, about 1.15 p.m.

News from Canton to-morrow is that alleged strike pickets have forcibly exercised a censorship of mails, particularly on letters and/or packages to Hongkong. It is stated that a number of men called at the office declaring themselves to represent the Strike Executive and conducted themselves in such a manner that the Canton Post Office has had to make representations. A message to the Wah Tez Yat Po" says that Mr. Yeung Sai-ngaam has been appointed, by the Canton Government, "special investigator to Hongkong and Macao."

headline: Governing Cabinet Suggested.
text:
Tuan Chi-jui summoned another special meeting at his residence last night, which was attended by most of the members of the Cabinet. He again advocated resigning and suggested the formation of a governing Cabinet under Huang Fu, as after the coup d'état of last year. Most of those present opposed, and urged Tuan Chi-jui to remain for the sake of the conference. No decision was reached.

The students are arranging a big demonstration to-morrow, at which in addition to the demand for unconditional tariff autonomy, they will urge the abolition of Tupanships, placing provincial control in the hands of Civil Governors, and disbandment of superfluous troops. It is not expected that the police will prevent the demonstration.

Feng Yu-hsiang's third division arrived at Nanyuan from Kalgan last night. Half are remaining at Nanyuan and half proceeding to Changsintien.

Tuan Chi-jui has sent his aide-de-camp to see Lu Chung-lin. He said he would take personal responsibility for political suspects and requested the immediate release of Tseng Yu-chun. The latter was accordingly released on bail this morning.

headline: Japan's Attitude.
text:
It is understood that official circles consider Chang Tso-lin virtually eliminated unless an unexpected coup is sprung. Japan is not likely to reinforce the Manchuria garrison.

The Japanese Consult General has cabled to Tokyo for two more warships, following an emergency mass meeting of his nationals, who hold that the situation is menacing. Reports are continually arriving of banditry and looting in the interior but foreigners have apparently been unharmed, although many have come here for safety.

The city of Tsingtao is outwardly calm but the police have issued an ultimatum demanding four months back pay. This has alarmed the civil authorities who have ordered the Chamber of Commerce to raise the necessary $300,000.

headline: Generuls' Demands.
text:
Chang Tsung-chang is reported to have wired to Kuo Sung-ling saying he approved the latter's action and if assured of the Tupanship of Shantung will declare independence and co-operate with Kuo Sung-ling and Li Ching-lin to pacify the country.

Kuo Sung-ling has wired Mukden conveying his demands which are stated to be that Yueh Weichun shall have Shantung, Feng Yu-hsiang Chihli, Li Chinglin Jehol, while Kuo Sung-ling shall have Manchuria

A correction states that Tseng Yu-chun has not yet been released. Lu Chung-lin has informed Tuan's aide-de-camp that Tseng Yu-chun is not really a prisoner. He had merely prevented his leaving for Tientsin.

Taeng Yu-chun therefore remains at Lu Chung-lin's headquarters. There was another meeting at Tuan Chi-jui's residence this morning. Tuan Chi-jin declared Muiden events would not cause his resignation which was added to the upon Fene Yu-nina. He would therefore move to the Haigang Testingγ

headline: SECOND MISSION
text:
WAIT FOR HONGKONG."

LATEST ADVICE FROM RELIABLE

That a second "peace quission" from Canton-comprising two delegates—was coming down by river steamer today, was the gist of the latest message received regarding the "strike settlement." Mr. Yeung Sai-nguam and Mr. Kan Kum-shek are the two gentlemen expected. Mr. Yeung has been reported, according to Canton vernacular cables, as having been appointed special investigator by the Provincial Government. He was formerly a well-known merchant and at one time owned extensive property in Hongkong. Mr. Kan is one of the principals of the Canton Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Co. He was one of the last delegation and is quoted as having said that the present trouble is due to a class war the world over.

It is also gathered that Mr. Young and Mr. Kan have no

special duties to perform in connection with their visit.

The "China Mail" informant said: — Canton is probably waiting for Hongkong to make the next move. Meanwhile Messrs. Young and Kan. will sustain and add to the good feelings already express

headline: $20 A STRIPE? / CHINESE HAVILDAR IN TROUBLE
text:
ALLEGED PROMOTION SQUEEZE.

Holding a rank similar to that of sergeant-major, Havildar Major Chan Chu-fat, a Hakka Chinese, of the 40th Coy., Royal Engineers (native personnel) was charged before a District Court Martial (in the R.E. Theatre) at Wellington Barracks this morning with “receiving a valuable consideration in respect of a promotion.”

The alleged offence related to the promotion of Lance-Naik Leung Tai to Naik (corporal). Major J. F. Drake, 1/East Surreys, was President. Other members of the Court were Captain J. W. McCardy, R.A., and Lieut. J. H. Smith, M.C., R.A.

Lieut. A. J. L. Whyte, R.E., prosecuted and Mr. L. D. Turner defended

Corporal Gore, R.E., told the Courthastak Naik Leung Tai had complained to him about accused wanting money on the Naik's receiving a gratuity at the end of October. According to the evidence the Naik told witness that the Havildar Major would lead him a dog's life if money was not paid.

Acting C.S.M. Pitt was the second witness. On November 9 he said, Naik Leung Tai reported to him that accused had demanded $50 for getting him the second stripe; that morning $20 had been paid. Witness asked the Naik if there were witnesses and the Naik replied that he had five. Accordingly, witness reported to the officer, commanding the company. The case was proceeding as this

The case was proceeding as this edition went to press.

headline: WIRELESS STRIKE
text:
ACTION BY BOARD OF TRADE.

REGULATIONS RELAXED.

The strike of wireless operators does not involved the land stations, but the Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists, which called the strike, claims as members 98 per cent. of the wireless operators aboard British merchantmen.

Wireless operators have been instructed to report to the union as ships come into port and not to sign on for fresh voyages, but ships already at sea are not endangered as existing contracts will not be broken.

The opinion is expressed that if the Board of Trade insists on the full observance of the regulations with regard to the carrying of wireless operators, many ships must be held up.

headline: CREATING RIDICULE?
text:
The Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists says that approximately 200 operators up to the present have refused to renew their signatures on ships articles and asserts that one Liverpool, one Glasgow and two Hull boats have been held up.

The Association criticises the Board of Trade relaxation cabled earlier as a move in favour of shipowners which will create suspicion and ridicule of Government regulations.

The two ships held up at Hull later sailed with Board of Trade clearances.

It is reported from Liverpool that operators on the White Star boat "Celtic" are among those who refused to sign but the Cunard, Alfred Holt and Brocklebank lines are not affected as they employ their own operators and have not given notice of any reduction in wages.

An earlier cable stated: The Telegraphists Association has issued strike notices in the case of all wireless operators aboard British ships, land have instructed the men not to sign for further voyages pending a settlement of the dispute regarding conditions of service, including the proposed reduction of wages of 22s.6d. monthly.

headline: TRADE POINTS. / BRITISH AND GERMAN INTERESTS.
text:
CONFERENCE HITCH

It is semi-officially stated that negotiations between the British and German delegations on questions arising out of the Anglo-German trade agreement have been provisionally broken off owing to differences of opinion with regard to the interpretation of various points in the protocol, although understanding was reached with regard to the application of the respective customs tariffs.

The disagreement related to the interpretation of a clause in the protocol of the Anglo-German commercial treaty whereby the British Government pledged itself not to impose duties especially detrimental to Germany.

The German delegates claimed that the British customs duties on many German exports, especially musical instruments and planos, should be abrogated or considerably reduced in view of this clause.

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
CANTON TO APPOINT DELEGATES? THE NEXT SOBE!

THE FROSPECTS ARE ROSY

To day the "salient point in the movements towards a settlement of the "strike" is that everything now hinges on the appointment by Canton of a delegation to negotiate with Hongkong's representatives.

This morning the "Chinn Mail" was authoritatively informed that the departure of the Colony's mission, namely, the Hon. Sir Paul Chater, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shouson, the Hon. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. D. G. M. Bernard, will be fixed when, Canton, he announced the constitution of their body. In the best informed circles it is considered that the report published of actual appointments is premature. Interviewed by a vernacular paper representative at a private Cainese club last night, the spokesman of the second merchant mission "emphasised that he had come down to Hongkong on private business and in a purely personal capacity.

In reply to a query he indicated that the prospects were rosy and that favourable intelligence would be available shortly.

It is believed that the sailing of Messrs. Yeung Sai-ngaam and Kan Kim-shek from Canton was delayed from "Saturday" to yesterday owing to their being called to an important conference almost on the moment of embarking, though the discussions were stated to be of an informal nature.

Since the return of the first Canton, “unofficial”, delegation many steps have been taken behind the scenes.

The Hongkong Union of District Commercial Associations has written to Mr. Wong Ching-wai (chairman), Nationalist Provincial Government) outlining the recreation accorded the merchants here and laying stress on Hongkong's cordiality and friendliness.

The merchant delegates also got in touch with the Kwangtung authorities and Mr. Wong is reported as having consulted Dr. C. C. Wu on the matter.

Another noteworthy incident is the return to the Colony on Saturday of Dr. S. W. Ts'o who maintains that his trip to Canton was entirely in connection with private affairs. On Sunday he was one of those who met Messrs. Yeung and Kan at the Steamboat Co.'s wharf.

This morning the "Wan Kiu Yato" published a cable from Canton, dated yesterday, to the effect that in connection with the ending of the strike, the labourers would select a delegate and the merchants one. The merchant nominee, however, would act strictly as a third party, using food offices as mediator and not participating in the actual deliberations.

This afternoon the China Mail was informed that a meeting of the delegates will be held at 4 p.m. at the Chinese Merchants' Club, when interesting developments were expected. Confirmation has been obtained that the report of 'Canton's approvalments' was premature. It is admitted that Messrs. Yeung and Kan are down here in connection with the negotiations. They were acting strictly as individuals—not even could their visit be described as "semi-official," it was stated—but in their personal capacities they were assisting in bringing matters to a head. Chinese gentlemen who have received correspondence from members of the last delegation declare that most of the pioneering work is accomplished. Accordingly more definite information is anticipated.

TO-DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, on demand, to-day was 2/47/18

Later during the proceeding the speakers urged the formation of a revolutionary army to overthrow the Government.

A parade was organised and the demonstrators laredl succeeded in setting fire to the offices of the "chen Pao," causing some damage before the fire. brigade extinished the blaze. The police arrested the self-confessed leader of the incendiaries.

headline: FAKLIEK CABLES
text:
Peking, Nov. 20. A mandate issued accepts the resignation of Yen Kung-cho and approvals Kung Hsin-chan as acting Minister of Communications. To-day's demonstration had a decidedly Communistic tendency, the students assembling being not only Kuomintangites but also a large number of workers, ricsha and other coolies. No national flags were observed; the students carrying the Canton flag and the workers had left. The workers were all armed with stout sticks and accompanied by motor cars with doctor's and nurses. The demonstrators are now parading the streets and distributing pamphlets, demanding itter also the overthrow of Tuan Chi-juli, to kill Chu Shen and shoot all traitors; to dissolve the Tariff Conference and arm all the people for a popular revolution and a real national conference. So far there is no violence.

This afternoon's student demonstration for the purpose of receiving Lu Chung-lin's reply to demands made was not so largely attended as yesterday's gathering, probably because yesterday's display of violence aroused misgivings among the more timorous as to the likely consequences. "The immediate dissolution of the Tariff Conference" was one slogan prominently displayed this afternoon and the list of Tuan Chi-jui's alleged crimes against the people was posted up.

Pleading indisposition Lu Chung-lin refrained from attending the gathering and the students proceeded to discuss plans for the next move which threatens to include an attack on the “Chen Pao” on account of its anti-communistic tendencies.

The Manchurian situation is clarifying, Kuo Sung-ling's van-guard in twelve trains arrived at Chin Wang Tao yesterday, he claims to have occupied Shan Hai Kuan and his headquarters will be at Chin Wang Tao. The Chang-Tso-limits have a division and a half and Chung Tsien-so two divisions at Chinchow. The Jehol army is going to Chinchow to assist Chang Tso-lin and the first clash is expected at Wanchatun near Shan Hai Kuan. The twelve aeroplanes which Kuo Sung-ling seized have now flown to Mukden and are being used to drop propaganda pamphlets over Kuo's troops.

The advance of the Hongenroops into Shantung continues. Chang Tsung-chang is concentrating at Weihsien and Chinchowfu, and is apparently preparing to leave Shantung with the remnants of his army and go by gunboat to Manchuria. Shanghai, Nov. 29. Kuo Sung-ling has issued a manifesto against Chang Tsung-lin, which he declares that it is possible any longer to see his brethren working suffering and

fighting for nothing but the glory and selfish ends of a few persons. Therefore, in compliance with the will of the people he is directing a military movement toward Mukdan, as it is proper that he should overthrow the ruling caste of the Mukdan "minds whose brutal militarists, such as Chang Tao-lin especially, have been poisoned by the cruel doctrine of militarism." He is determined to bring forth upon Manchuria a new government in which the governed will govern themselves and he must strive to achieve per mantra's people not only in Manchuria but in China. Engels, Glenn, who is reported to the public health depot to the conference that has been released under the Act. The report noted to be

LUKEWARM RECREATION CONCEDED FINANCE THE PROPOER (Router's Service)

M. Brind's Cabinets having a lukewarm reception. The Right and Centre hold the opinion that the Cabinet tends too much towards the Left and regret that M. Briand has not formed a ministry of "national union." The Socialists are disgruntled owing to their exclusion while the radicals, who have secured a majority of the portfolios and some of the most important, would have preferred M. Herriot as Premier.

M. Loucheur's appointment to the Finance Ministry is received with considerable reserve. His ability is not doubted, but his versatility is regarded as being too chameleonic.

The decision to create an Advisory Committee of the Finance Ministry is universally approved. Generally the parties are inclined to withhold judgment pending a disclosure of the Government's financial programme, on which the Cabinet, like its predecessor, will stand or fall.

headline: KOYLOON COURT.
text:
HAWKER'S COMPLAINT TO MAGISTRATE

At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning a Chinese stallholder was charged with hawking without a permit.

The defendant stated in evidence that the consiste attempted to take a turnp, and became angry when this was refused. Defendant was then assaulted by the constable, who also broke a dish.

Other, stallholders corroborated defendant's story, and on being discharged the defendant submitted a written complaint, which was endorsed by the Magistrute. Among other cases dealt with, a number of Chinese were charged with unlawful possession of pine wood. Fines of $35 or six weeks' hard labour were imposed, the penalties coming under the new Ordinance which allows a fine of $250 instead of $10 under the previous Ordinance.

headline: MISSING COAL
text:
LAUNCH MOVEMENTS AROUSE SUSPICION.

COURT SEQUEL:

The manoeuvres of two launches lying outside Bailey's shipyard in the early morning of September 8 aroused the suspicions of Mr. Edwards, an engineer in the employ of Messrs. W. S. Bailey and Co., and as a result of his observations four men appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning, one charged with misappropriating coal and the others with aiding and abetting him.

The launches in question were the “Poseidon” and the “TaiYuk Fong,” the former being a Blue Funnel (Ocean Steamship Company) launch operating from Holt's wharf, and the latter the launch of Watson and Co., Ltd.

The coxswain of the “Poseidon” was charged with misappropriating five tons of coal, at the Criminal Sessions this morning, whilst the engineer and 2nd coxswain of the same launch, also the coxswain of the “Tai Yuk Fong,” were charged with complicity.

The respective systems under which the coxswains of the launches were engaged were referred to by Mr. G. K. Holmes, Crown Solicitor. The coxswain of the "Poseidon" had coal supplied to him direct by his employers and the coxswain of the "Tai Yuk Fong" was paid $360 a month out of which he had to pay the crew and find the coal.

The “Poseidon” coxswain had 12 tons of coal supplied him on September 6 at which time there was approximately 4 tons in the bunkers. Between that date and the morning of September 8, 2 or perhaps 3 tons, at a liberal estimate might have been used, said the Crown Solicitor.

At about 7 o'clock on the morning of September 8, Mr. Edwards noticed the two launches together lying outside Bailey's shipyard. Baskets were passing from the "Poseidon" to the "Tai Yuk Fong" which when he went to the water's edge to see more clearly he noticed contained coal. The "Tai Yuk Fong" took a list towards the "Poseidon" as loading progressed and then went to the other side and when it eventually steamed away it was on an even keel.

The coxswain and others on the "Poseidon" were arrested as a result of police investigation when the "Poseidon" arrived at Holt's wharf, Mr. Fraser, of Bailey's, having, telephoned to Captain Griggs. The coxswain of Watson's launch was arrested later, the launch on investigation by the police having been found to contain her full coal capacity.

The case for the Crown proceeded no further than the outlining of the case at the Court this morning, the judge, Mr. Justice Wood, counsel, the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., (instructed by Mr. D. McCallum) and Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed to defend Watson's coxswain by Mr. Remedios) all proceeding in the launches to the scene where the alleged misappropriation took place.

headline: EXPORTING MONEY / TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE
text:
NOT CROHING THE BORDER.

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who absccaded with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumati was tendered at the Nowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempting to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force.

Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERNITÓico GAINED BY

RAILWAY REPORTED OLEAB.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwingming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Samchun, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by frantic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the full of Wu-how the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

headline: THE BOYCOTT
text:
LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Candjan) and schools are still closed. The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good. H.M.S. "Moorhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of

There is a shortage of kerosine and liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junkshares seldom got through the atrike pickets' cordons. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed:
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates, and established themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaws and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hungkal's remnants.

Pirates have often been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "M.F.T.en") have authority to patrol as before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-lam (a brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa) is at Chekhom and Yanping with his troops. General Li Chici-sum, the Red nominee, holds Summing, Kungvick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan Ming-shu.

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Sanwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only-import permitted from Macao but boats are now running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 29 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the “Kwok Ning” piracy (reported previously in the “China Mail”).

headline: CANTON ITEMS / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING.

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the a.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hong Kong. The prices changed by the junka and sampans operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing. The “Honam” left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The “Fatahan” will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the “special tugs” which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high handed actions. These clerks had walked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Canton.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Wichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: ENVOY TO CHINA?
text:
HOME GOVERNMENT AGAINST PROPOSAI.

The appointment of a special envoy, a man of high prestige and standing, to discuss with Peking the grievances the Chinese, have against the British, is a proposal which has found favour with a considerable section of the London press.

According to diplomatic correspondents, however, this idea has not commended itself to the Government who consider that the circumstances may best be met in this respect by arranging for the return to the Legation at Peking in the middle of September of Sir Ronald Macleay who is at present undergoing a cure of the continent. A well-known merchant in the City of London spoke as follows to an "Observer" representative:

The trouble, he said, is in as Canton is concerned is the result of intimidation by the Bolshevik party there, and the danger jo. The men working in Hongkong receive orders from Canton to leave their employment and at the same time the threat is uttered that if they do not obey them their families will be killed. Alarmed by these threats they dare not continue to work, even if they would.

Immense Chinese business interests have been just as badly hit by the strike as the British firms themselves. The Bolshevik movement in fact, was aimed against capital, irrespective of nationality, whether Chinese or British.

headline: SNUB FOR REDS.
text: The members of the left wing made an attack on Mr. Ramsay MacDonald in connection with the Zinovieff letter which they say proved a flasco, at the Labour Conference this morning. A composite resolution on the subject was introduced demanding inter alia that an apology be sent to the Soviet Government and Zinovieff, but it was overwhelmingly rejected on a show of hands.

headline: COMMUNIST LEADERS CANNOT THROW STONES.
text:
The Labour Conference overwhelmingly defeated a Communist motion to refer back the section of the Executive Board's report dealing with unemployment. Mr. Gallagher, of Paisley, submitting the motion, asserted that the movement was being handed over to the middle classes. Mr. MacDonald, replying, said that it was a libel to say that the labour leaders had blank cheques from Moscow and that it was time that such slanders were faced. He declared that nobody was less entitled to point the finger of scorn at himself or anyone else from the viewpoint of vulgar display of wealth or riotous living than the present British Communist leaders. (Cheers).

Shanghai, September 30.—When nearing the upper Yangtze port of Tuchow on the 27th the American steamer “Chichuen” was fired on by a large contingent of soldiers ensonced on the heights overlooking the gorges. The firing was kept up for an hour when steamer was struck at least two hundred times. A Chinese member of the crew was slightly wounded. The American gunboat “Palce” was ordered to escort the vessel through the soldier ridden area to Chungqing. The miscreants are believed to be fleeing soldiers of General Yangsen. The “Chichuen,” which was flying the American flag, belongs to the Yangtze Rapids S.S. Co. The skipper was the only foreigner aboard.—Reuter.

headline: ABNORMAL FANATICS
text:
One feels convinced after a few weeks in Russia that only a small minority of the Communists believe in anything but their own power and advancement, writes a correspondent of the "Daily Telegraph." Many of the leaders are, no doubt, genuine Communists. Of the sincerity of Chicherin, for instance, there can be no doubt: he refused a great inheritance in his early years for the sake of his principles, and at that fateful meeting in London, where Lenin split the Socialists into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks, he voted with the former. But not one, looking into his pale eyes with that strange glitter in them, could regard him as normal, Dzerhinsky, too, produces the impression of a cold-blooded fanatic. "You cannot make revolutions in white kid gloves," he answered a more squeamish acquaintance, and the same spirit has carried him through ruthless seas of blood as through fifteen years in a dungeon for the sake of his convictions.

The “screwed-up” expression of the great Bolsheviks, especially of Lenin and Trotsky, has often been commented on, and the galleries of portraits with which Moscow abounds show this phenomenon to be characteristic. Rykoff is almost the only prominent Communist who has the face of an ordinary human being. For this very reason, perhaps, and because of his moderation, his influence is small, and since he gave the Third International some very sound advice on the folly of persecuting the nephew, or private traders, out of existence, he has made himself disliked by the extremists. It would seem that the screwed-up face and glinty eyes are symptoms of abnormality, and no real Bolshevik leader can be regarded as quite normal. Lenin was certainly a great man, of tremendous driving power; yet in the official bulletin of his autopsy it was announced that, instead of grey matter in his brain, they found green slime.

headline: SWARMS OF SPIES.
text:
The extremists now in power have taken the bit between their teeth, and miss the controlling master-hand. None of the moderate men appear to be strong enough to check them, and they are capable of overriding any reasonable arrangement made with a, foreign country by the Government on the grounds of political expediency. Yet the officials with whom foreigners come into contact seem not only reasonable, but civil and courteous; their hands, however, are so entwined in the meshes of an endless tangle of red tape that business is as tedious as it is difficult. Yet this very red tape is necessary as a check, for they cannot trust one another; all are thinking of lining their nests against a rainy day, and survivors of pre-Communistic days are always on the look-out for a chance to recover, regardless of means, some of their lost property.

In Russia the individual dares very little. Spies swarm everywhere, and the more prominent and more responsible the man, the more his actions are watched and recorded. The leaders spy upon each other, and the powerful "Ogpu" spies on everybody. Foreigners are watched, and the inquisitive spoon-fed, so that it is very difficult to form a genuine opinion. In the hotels thecomings and goings are registered, as well as interesting conversations. As a rule this is done without attracting attention, but occasionally a clumsy fellow, when eavesdropping, will betray himself. Natives dare not visit foreigners, and if foreigners visit Russian friends it is certain to bring suspicion upon them. The postal censorship is an old Russian institution, and it is certain that the Bolsheviks have continued this legacy of the Tsars, with many other of the worst features of the old regime, and it is unwise to write from abroad to friends in Russia.

WORSE THAN TSARIST TYRANNY. But the tyranny of the Tsars was liberty, indeed, compared with the tyranny of the Bolsheviks. Then at least one was allowed to live and trade and work, so long as politics were not touched. Russian broadmindedness, the child of their boundless plains, allowed greater freedom of action than does public opinion in Britain. To-day everyone lives in constant dread. Many people never go to bed before two a.m., so as to be dressed when the agents come, for that is their favourite hour. It is characteristic of Russia that the old saying, when a chance silence falls upon a party, it is not that an angel is passing over, but "a policeman has been born."

Intolerance is the keynote of the Communist system, which might be defined as the very anti-podes of the policy of "live and let live." They loathe Democracy, for the Dictatorship of the Proletariat is incompatible with the greatest good of the greatest number, and means exclusive power in the hands of the minority—another characteristic in common with the old régime. They openly treat as enemies all who are not members of the party; they make use of them so far as it suits their purpose, but once they have ceased to be useful they are better dead.

It is told that in 1923 Moscow was a gay city, but in 1924 the swing to the left and the economic distress made themselves felt. Seats at the Bolshoi Theatre, opera, and ballet cost too much. There are few people in Moscow to-day who can afford ten, or even fifteen, gold roubles for stalls, which are patronised chiefly by an occasional member of some foreign mission, a concession-hunter from capitalistic Europe, or nephew who has not yet received the usual short notice of expulsion. Yet, as during the terror in the French Revolution we read that the theatres were crammed, so to-day during the terror which few see, but everybody feels in the air in Russia, the harassed and nervous public flocks to the theatre and the cinemas to forget for a moment their anxieties and fears.

Still, the Russian temperament shows itself often enough in laughing faces in the streets; yet this laugh has a hollow ring about it; it is the spirit of "let us eat, drink, and be merry, for to-morrow we die," that spirit which is truer of the Russian than of any other nationality in Europe, for everybody lives from hand to mouth, nothing knowing and little caring what to-morrow may bring forth. The only man I saw in Moscow who seemed genuinely happy had no legs. Both had been amputated above the knee. He came stumping cheerfully into a grocer's shop, with a healthy glow and a cheerful smile on his bronzed and bearded face. I instinctively drew out a few kopecks, when to my surprise he fished out of a capacious pocket a huge pile of small change, both paper and that not unpleasing "hard valuta" now in circulation, which was evidently his day's takings. He changed it for five and ten rouble notes, for he found begging a lucrative business, he cracked jokes with the salesmen, laughed uproariously, and after a vigorous discussion about vintages, bought a bottle of "port-vin" for three roubles, stuffed it into his pocket, and stumped out into the street, whistling a cheerful air.

headline: FORLORN CHILDREN.
text:
If the other beggars in Moscow were as merry, it would be a cheerful city, indeed, for scarcely even on the Galata Bridge at Stamboul can one see so many maimed and distorted beggars as in the capital of Bolshevism; and not all are cripples; ragged boys are a perfect nuisance, and it is impossible to buy a packet of cigarettes at a kiosk or come out of a restaurant without being persecuted by a batch of these important young ruffians. I was surprised at this phenomenon, and made inquiries, as I thought that under the proletarian regime all the poor were provided for. I was told that many found it a more paying game than working, while others could not produce the indispensable "dokument" which is so dear to the Russian official. Another characteristic feature is afforded by the swarms of forlorn children. The years of social disturbance, mortality among parents, and general life.

moralisation, especially among the youth of both sexes, have produced a big crop of parentless children, who live God knows how, begging a bit, stealing a bit, sleeping huddled up together among ruined and uncompleted buildings. To their credit, the Soviet authorities are endeavouring to cope with this evil, and among the very numerous appeals to one's purse when sitting in cafés and restaurants the one to which one gives with least reluctance is the fund for these poor waifs.

The concentration of the government in Moscow has led to a shortage of lodgings which is probably more acute than in any other city in Europe. Directly the frost breaks building proceeds vigorously. One huge skeleton structure near the Arbat was condemned as unsafe in the Tsar's days, and a lengthy lawsuit ensued. Now the Bolsheviks regardless of the architects' verdict, are hurrying on its completion with all possible speed. The only comment I heard was: "Thank God, only Communists will live there, so it will be a good thing if it does collapse." Rooms are almost impossible to secure, and few are worth having. A limited definite space called "ploshchad" is allotted to every person and heavily taxed. No body is permitted to stay in the city unless he can give a good reason, and many, a family has been deported at a few hours' notice to remote villages in the Arctic Circle. Few flats or lodgings remind one of civilised Europe. The "paradni," or front entrance, is invariably closed, bolted, and barred. No one can afford to keep a dvornik, or hall porter, and all use the "black" entrance, or back door. When calling upon an acquaintance it is necessary to wander about a courtyard, usually immense and always untidy, to find the tradesmen's entrance, which admits to a dark and gloomy kitchen, and then through dingy passages and corridors littered with boxes, stacks of old furniture, broken statues, and musty pictures, all recking and never ventilated, to the single room that is all that most families can boast it. This is usually over-furnished, and always depressing; an old rug may conceal a bed and make it look like a sofa, but a washstand, especially a Russian one, is never an elegant object. Worst of all is the Russia's dread of fresh air.

Only when spring timidly shows itself and the earliest flowers are hawked about the streets usually at extravagant prices can the Russian brighten his dingy quarters with a sprig or two of mimosa from the Crimea or lilac from Kieff, to remind him that Nature is still beautiful.

headline: POSITION OF WOMEN. / OVERLAND CHINA MAIL
text: The Municipal Soviet exercises a fatherly supervision over its citizens; as in the old days, it is forbidden to enter or leave a tram when in motion, and the fine of a gold rouble for so doing is enforced; penalties, too are exacted for throwing about those long cardboard cigarette ends with which Russians are apt to strew the country, and big receptacles, labelled "dlia okurok," are placed in all public buildings and in the streets. But the latter are defaced by the shrieking propaganda, which gets on one's nerves until they are dulled; the effect produced by this incessant appeal to the eye is one of insincerity.

A rather surprisingly puritanical feature is the "struggle with prostitution," for which an active propaganda is maintained, visible in great posters. This seems odd, when they have tried to abolish Christianity, and Soviet marriage is a mere formula of registration; as easy and inexpensive to undo as to enter. But woman's position in Soviet Russia is in no way inferior to man's; she serves upon the General Staff of the Red army, and the tripe-woman of Marseilles has found her modern counterpart in the female executioners of the Che-Ka. The Communist women endeavour to distinguish themselves from their bourgeoisie sisters by eccentricities of dress or affection of masculinity, which completely destroys their attractiveness to the eye. It is often hard to tell the sex when one sees a young person with close-cropped hair, check jockey cap with a huge long peak, a cigarette end hanging on the lip, and the hands deep in the trousers pockets. The figure is that of a veritable female apache straight from the variety stage.

headline: BRITAIN'S PRESTIGE
text:
The "Telegraph" regards the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities and minimise personal outrages on British subjects as threatening the prestige of Britain in the War East. The treatment in Canton of two Hongkong journalists is referred to in this connection.

In editorial comment, Mr. Percival Landon's review of the situation in China is regarded as bringing out very clearly the painful fact that the Chinese politicians regard Great Britain and other Powers as their enemies. It is very difficult for British readers to realise this. There is no hostility towards China in England. We are sorry for her; we lament the misery that the collapse of her Central Government has brought upon the oldest of civilised peoples; we are anxious to give her effective help in recovering her ancient peace, though we do not know how to set about it. But of enmity or even dislike there is no trace on our side. Those who concern themselves with Chinese affairs are much readier to blame our Foreign Office for its supposed faults of commission or omission than to denounce the Chinese. It is surely remarkable that the deliberate insult offered to the British Iseigation at Peking by subjecting it to a boycott and constraining the Chinese servants to leave the premises should not have excited public indignation at home, although the Peking Government, in permitting the boycott to continue, has disregarded Treaty stipulations as well as the ordinary diplomatic courtesies. The disgraceful incident at Canton recently, when two British journalists from Hongkong, relying on the Canton Government's assertion that there was no boycott of British shipping, landed on the quay and were immediately seized and thrust into a filthy jail, would have stirred our fathers and grand-fathers to violent wrath. They, in their day, expected British citizens to be treated fairly in every part of the world, and they would have looked for something more than the evasive apology proffered at Canton—an apology not for the unlawful imprisonment, but for the use of the chains in which these unfortunate journalists were led through the city and exposed to the jeers of the mob. But the benevolence with which Great Britain is determined to regard Chinese doings, and the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities because all real power is in the hands of military chieftains, may cause even these personal outrages on British subject to be minimised and overlooked, though nothing could be worse for our prestige in the Far East. Yet, in spite of all our resolute manifestations of goodwill towards China, we are reminded by Mr. Landon that the friendliness is all on our side. The Chinese politicians, led by Mr. Wang, who's Moscow's warmest friend at Peking, regard us and the other Powers as enemies, and will enter the coming Conference with the object of doing us harm.

headline: UNPLEASANT FACTS
text:
It is better to face the facts, unpleasant though they are, than to blind ourselves with illusions. China's hostility is bad enough, but the impotence of her self-styled Government is worse from a diplomatic standpoint, because it affords the Powers no hope of remedying her grievances satisfactorily. If President Tuan Chijui and his Cabinet really controlled the Eighteen Provinces the Powers might easily come to terms with him, as Great Britain, America, and Japan are most anxious to restore good relations with their Chinese customers. But the truth is that the President is but the head of a shadow Government, a mere simulacrum of sovereignty, a marionette whose strings are pulled by the inscrutable "Christian" General Feng Yu-hsiang, whose troops occupy the capital, and who receives his munitions by way of Mongolia from his Bolshevik paymasters. Outside Peking and the border Provinces of Shensi and Kansu, which constitute Feng's present zone of occupation, his puppet President is virtually unrecognised, except as the giver of honorific titles to the military leaders who obtain temporary control in the several provinces. The Powers, in negotiating with the nominees of Tuan Chijui, will be dealing with men who have no power to implement their promises, but who undoubtedly will use the Conference as a means of inflaming the anti-foreign movement. As Mr. Tandon points out, the Powers may agree to the proposed increase of the Chinese tariff on

foreign imports, which the Conference has been summoned to discuss. But they will be asked by the Chinese to go further, and to consider the complete abolition of the fiscal treaties and of the extra-territorial rights possessed by foreigners in China. If they refuse to do so the aglators will have fresh material for their propaganda. Yet no discussion of these matters can be helpful while there is no protection for foreigners and their property outside the Treaty ports. Even the tariff question is complicated by the prevailing disorder. As Mr. Landon says, if the Flowers allow the Peking Government to raise some additional millions out of the Maritime Customs they will give fresh offence to all Feng's rivals. He would receive the money, through his obedient servants in Peking, and would spend it in spreading the Soviet agitation. The other Tupans, or Tuchuns, with armies of their own, would want to know why the Powers were thus subsidising Feng against them. We should thus be assisting our bitterest opponent and annoying all the other powerful chiefs. Yet it is difficult to see how the Powers could insist on supervising the expenditure of the new Customs revenue if they agree to its being raised.

headline: CHINA UNITY PROSPECTS.
text: It may be that some Chinese Napoleon will arise and restore the unity of the Empire. But the recent history of China's civil wars warns us that provincial discussions and the lack of moral sense among the generals make the task of a Chinese Napoleon extremely difficult. Chang Two-lin, the Manchurian ruler, still has what is nominally the largest army, a quarter of a million strong, and exercises control, as far south as Shanghai. His chief rival, Feng Yu-hsiang, who was once the leading commander under Wu Pei-fu, the former over-lord of Central China, and who rose to eminence by betraying Wu in his last struggle with Chang, is now, with Moscow's help, at the head of a force almost as numerous as the Manchurian host, and perhaps as well armed. Whether and when these two potentates, Chang and Feng, who depend respectively on Japan and on Russia, will come into collision no one can say. Nor is it safe to conclude that the victor in the duel, if it came, would necessarily gather Central China, to say nothing of the unruly South, into his fold, and make China one again. Chinese domestic politics are not so simple as that; the fierce animosities existing between the provinces are complicated by party feuds and personal ambitions, so that military victories, real or supposed, have hitherto had no definite results. We may suppose that the anarchy which is wasting China and ruining her trade will come to an end sooner or later, and that force will have to be used to restore order. But to assign a date to this consummation, or to suppose that Chang or Wu, or any other personality now prominent in Western eyes, will achieve the desired end would be very unwise. Our chief hopes must rest on the innate good sense and untiring industry of the Chinese people. If they could somehow be persuaded that the foreigner was not their enemy but anxious to be their friend, and to resume the trade which has benefited all parties engaged in it, they would soon bring about a revival, as they have done many times before in their long history. But how this change of view is to be brought about, in face of the persistent Bolshevik campaign throughout China, is the real problem to which Western diplomats need to address themselves in earnest before still worse mischief has been done.

headline: COAL STRIKE.
text:
The country is completely unruffled over the anthracite coal strike which has been proceeding for six weeks. The miners themselves are enjoying a prolonged holiday fishing, camping and touring. Some have taken temporary employment. A number of foreigners are profiting from the opportunity to visit their homes. The owners similarly are unperturbed. They believe that the strikers will return when their money is spent. In the meantime the country is carrying on with accumulated stocks which however will soon disappear with the approach of winter. The Government hitherto has been reluctant to intervene until the placidity has passed off.
