headline: A Shadow Government.
text:
The first point to be borne in mind is that the Allies—if the term may be allowed, without indicating in any way an identity of interests—are dealing with a shadow Government that has no power either to conclude a treaty or to enforce any part of it, except by permission of and at the direction of a military autocrat. At the moment it is the Soviet Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang—whose outbreakings of war and slaughter against foreigners will be fresh in the memory of Englishmen—who has the Peking Government under his absolute control. Without his assent from Kalgan or Kansu not a clause will be accepted by the Chinese Government or put afterwards into force.

The second point of practical importance is that the conference will be held in a hostile capital. In itself this characteristic distinguishes this conference from any other international discussion in recent years. In the event of a dissolution of the congress without achieving a satisfactory result, this fact is worth while bearing in mind. To judge by the insults already directed against our own Legation and that of the United States, incidents may occur which may seriously complicate subsequent relations. In respect of these insults, the shadow Government has turned a deaf ear to protests, and a similar attitude on the part of the military autocrat might precipitate grave trouble. Such behaviour as sanctioning the action of those who are terrorising the Legation servants into desertion is inconceivable in any civilised Government, but the fact remains that the Government still tacitly endorses this intimidation, and that consequently the strike continues. It will be in an avowedly anti-foreign atmosphere that this debate will take place. The real enemy will not be directly represented, but every move in China's game will have been suggested or sanctioned from Moscow and played across the council-table by Mr. T. Wang, the ablest of Chinese politicians, and the most thorough adherent of the Soviet Government in China. No doubt he believes that he is merely using Moscow as a tool, but the recent experience of the unhappy Hu Han-min in Canton should teach him that he who sups with the devil needs a loor spoon. But for the moment it is only the avowedly hostile driving force behind the Conference that I wish to emphasize. Thirdly, it must be remembered that additional revenues from the increase of Customs distractions, to which the Allies are, of course, pledged, will in itself cause acute

dissension in China, even before a treaty is signed. To give it to Peking is tantamount to giving it through Feng, for the spread of Soviet propaganda throughout the Chinese Republic. The other Tupans would only see in the grant a subsidy given by foreign influence to Peking for their undoing. Among these latter Chang Tso-lin himself must be ranked, unless he manages to obtain at least his full share of the increment by a private arrangement with his inevitable enemy Feng. Moreover, we should not overlook the recrudescence of activity from Yochow, whither Wu Pei-fu has been taken himself. On the one hand, nothing is so likely to arouse civil war as the handing over to Peking and Feng Yu-hsiang of any large share of the proceeds of these increased duties; on the other hand, nothing will exacerbate anti-foreign hatred more than any attempt of foreigners to control or deal in any way with this new surplus. It will be useless for foreigners to pretend that, after securing the loans, the use made of the extra revenue is no affair of theirs. The time has gone by when indirect responsibility can be repudiated in China. Certain European nations who used this excuse for pouring arms and ammunition into China during recent years are now regretting their action. If the Conference uses its unquestionable right to assign these extra revenues to Peking—the prisoner of each military autocrat in turn—it cannot plead irresponsibility if the civil war which it has been the constant endeavour of all foreign diplomacy to extinguish blazes up again more savagely than ever.

headline: $ ^{1} $ JAPAN AND RUSSIA
text:
THEIR RELATIONS WITH CHINA.

Whilst the ex-Kaiser chooses to see in the Far East, possibilities of a Russo-Japanese alliance against Europe with particular reference to the development of China, the "Belfast Telegraph" thinks that the end has not been seen of rivalry between Japan and Russia in this area. "If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast tomorrow," states this "journal," she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the possibility of German intervention and possibly that of the United States at a later stage.

The "Bolfust Telegraph" article in full is as follows:—

The strike at the Japanese factories in Shanghai, which has been the pretext for so much anti-foreign irritation in China, has now been settled but the trouble else where is still far from being at an end. A good deal of the unrest which is visible in many parts of the world to-day arises from the stirring up of racial feeling; noticeable in various ways of late years, but specially through the Great War. Some 200,000 Chinese were on that occasion in the service of the Allies in munition work, the manning of ships, or making roads behind the lines. The number of Hindu troops sefting, in the war was very large, and their losses, especially in Mesopotamia, were heavy. Although Britain did not employ African negro troops on the Western front, the French did so to a large extent. It is certain that these members of black or "coloured" races brought back to their homes changed views as to life in general and a certain amount of dissatisfaction with their lot, the desire being felt for a more ample scope for existence. There is a demand for more room, as it were, which finds vent in a blind striking out in all directions. Of this we have examples in China at the present time. There are aspects of the situation which are not wholly to be deplored. There is an undoubted danger to the white race in some parts of the globe, like Australia and California, of being "swamped" by Chinese or Japanese settlement. The Chinaman has always been looked upon as an economic danger whenever his labour comes into competition with that of the European. "The Chinese coolie," says an American writer, "is the ideal industrial machine, the perfect human ox." He can live in almost any variety of climate, and once he gets unchecked admission is likely to drive out the white man. To some extent the same applies to Hindu coolie labour. If Hawaii is being "swamped" by Japanese, the island of Mauritius has been taken possession of by Hindus, who now form two-thirds of the whole population. Only for the enactment of an Exclusion Law recently, something of the same sort would have happened in Natal.

WAR SERVICE RESULTS. During the Great War, as in the wars of the middle of the eighteenth century between France and Britain, the conflict was not waged by whites alone. The "black" races of Africa, the "browns" of India, and the "yellow" of Japan took part in the actual fighting to a greater or less extent, and the services which they rendered in defeating the Germans were not allowed to sink into oblivion. The movement now visible in China is part of a world-wide stirring amongst the "coloured" races against white domination. All the benefits which the European has bestowed are ignored, but it is also forgotten that China is not yet at the stage at which she can dispense with extraneous guidance, whether from the European or the scarcely less unpopular Japanese. The attitude adopted by the Soviet Government at this juncture is true to the traditions of the "Czarist" Government, of which it is in many respects the true heir. Bolshevik intrigues may help to keep alive the agitation against the foreigner, but the real object in view is the regaining of that ascendancy in Manchuria which the Czar's advisers gained only to lose it in battle with Japan. If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast to morrow she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the pros-

text:

There is hardly anything more certain in our uncertain human world than that a new factor has taken prominent place in the complicated equation of current events. The East—Near and Far: from the Pacific through to Egypt, and so across North Africa to Morocco—this far-flung East no longer is to be treated as was natural enough in those earlier generations when, obviously, it scare more than stirred uneasily in its age-long slumber under the impact of restless aggression from the other side the globe. "It is very much awake, now. It has become distinctly self-conscious; is fast growing as consistently active as for so long it has been persistingly passive. More and more it is playing a part, with increasing resistance to being played upon. Above all, from the Straits of Gibraltar to those of Tsushima, it is insisting on being its own master. In a word then our times must provide immediately some readjustment of relations between the civilisations of East and West, or the smouldering discontent of to-day may to-morrow flare up into the blaze of open widespread trouble.

In the actual fighting Japan won the first round, but the Russia Bolshevik diplomacy is now seeking to revenge the disasters of 1904 by striking at Japan and Britain, whose moral support contributed not a little to the victory of the former country on that occasion. JAPAN'S EXAMPLE:

Whether the Chinese will continue to lend themselves to be used for this purpose long enough to suit the designs of Moscow is a doubtful question. In the case of Japan's awakening she proved her capacity to develop along the lines chosen by her, retaining foreign assistance up to the point at which it could be dispensed with safely. No discrimination was exercised against any particular European nation, and an absence of violence characterised the proceedings. Japan's circumstances were, and still are, vastly different from those of China. The latter country, with her vast area and population of over 400 millions, offers a wide field for industrial development. The construction of railways, the opening up of the great coalfields and other mineral resources would give lucrative employment to many Chinamen now on the verge of starvation, and there are extensive areas in the west which could be made productive by cultivation on up-to-date lines. The men who have made such a tragic muddle of splendid opportunities in Russia are not likely to lead the Chinese along a safe path to national regeneration. Japan could do so with a fair amount of success, but she would be certain to exact a heavy price. Britain, which is being assailed most vigorously of all the supposed enemies of the "New China," is the best qualified to be the friend of that country. If the present attitude of certain sections of the Chinese people is persisted in, it will be a tragic blunder from the point of view of the whole country, and the consequences will be regretted in days to come when it is too late. There is enough intellect amongst the Chinese people to avert such a cost of strenge if it is properly brought and led in the right direction.

headline: CHINA'S AMAZONS:
text:
FORMER LADY PIRATE.

Recent reports of the participation in fighting or piratical attacks of bobbed haired, bare armed Amazons of China, leads Bassett Digby to the following comment in the "Singapore Free Press":—Many unravelled Britons who derive a sneaking delight from conning the red-bloodedly male

surprise—and disappointment—of the appearance of lady pirates in the devious and muddy estuaries of chaotic China.

This is no development, however. Lady pirates have ever been a commonplace institution of the Far East, though their functions are less specialised than those of their male colleagues. Theirs is a pleasantly diversified and domesticated piracy—throat-slitting, rocking the cradle, setting captured junks ablaze, cooking lunch, opium smuggling, mahjongh, and the throwing overboard of slaughtered victims, interspersed with a quiet half-hour or so of gossip with the other girls, and a shampoo. True words, if spoken fippantly, may I assure you. There are numbers of lady pirates, too, among the ranging proas haunting the remoter byways of the Malay Archipelago, worthy wives and mothers, good plain cooks, skilled needle-women and navigators, deadly wielders of the dirk and most unpleasantly efficient with the cutlass. "You probably do not realise that, only a couple of centuries ago, we had some very workman-like—or, should I say, workwomenlike—lady" pirates of our own

There was demure little Mary Reell, for instance, who adopted the career at the age of thirteen and dying in jail some years later, slightly before sentence of death by hanging, was to be carried out. In her crowded, and not very brief career on the Spanish Main she set an example to adventurous young women that deserves better than the slowly descending dust of oblivion.

headline: Posed: As Boy.
text:
Mary's "mother," who was married to a sailor, bore a son shortly after her husband left England on a voyage from which he was destined not to return. When the boy was a year old the mother took him away with her from her late husband's prosperous relations, with whom she had been given a home, for a stay with her own friends, who were poor. While away, the boy baby died. The mother, loth to risk being cast off by the family that had been pensioning her, adopted a girl baby—Mary—dressed her in boy's clothes and passed her off as a lad.

When her mother died, Mary, who was thirteen, got a job as boy attendant upon a French lady. Her next job was that of cabin boy on a man-of-war, after which she turned up in Flanders as a cadet in an infantry regiment. Failing to land a commission, she changed over to the cavalry and was getting on very nicely when disaster befell her. She fell in love with an army comrade. They both left the army a few months later and were married. Her husband lived only a short time. After his death Mary, impatient with domesticity, dressed again as a man, went to Holland and joined an infantry regiment. It bored her. She joined a ship sailing for the West Indies which fell into the hands of British pirates who fired her enthusiasm for the career. She joined the gang.

For a while the pirates, taking advantage of a royal amnesty, lived peaceably ashore. But money began to run low. Faced with the dreadful prospect of honest and ill-requited toil, they made strenuous efforts to secure some employment that would be more congenial and lucrative. They signed on with one of a group of privateers that Captain Woods Rogers Governor of Providence, was sending down to Central America to rob and harass the Spaniards. Mary was among them.

Doubless Rogers deemed himself, "canny" in "staffing." His raiders with experienced Union pirates who could be relied on not to become the prey of "deficate moral scruples," but human nature asserted itself, and "no sooner had the yeasels sailed than the piratical crews promptly locked the officers in their cabins and took charge of things.

headline: PROUD MEMORY.
text:
I have valued my association with you more than I can say and it will always be one of my proudest memories that you have unanimously and repeatedly shown your confidence in me by asking that my term of office should be extend. If your request had been granted I should have been happy to remain, but, as this has not been found possible, I can only express to you my heartfelt thanks for paying me so striking a compliment.

I have also to thank you, gentlemen, one and all, for the invaluable help which you have given me during these years by your advice and criticisms. It has been a cause of admiration and wonder to me that in a Colony such as this, where there is no lessured class, it has always been possible to find able and hard-working men who will sacrifice their time to the gratuous service of the State. Membership of this Council has been no sinecure, and the Colony has cause to be grateful to all of you and to those other former members of the Council, who have been taken from us—such men as my dear friend Alexander Stephen, Montague Ede, Arthur Lowe, Lau Chu-pak, Ng Hon-tsz and Chow Sul-ki.

I owe a special debt of gratitude to those of you who have served on my Executive Council, for I fear that I have on many occasions taxed your patience to an

unprecedented extent by long sitings. I have often felt that, although you did not say so, you must have thought that I was wasting your time in long discussions and by bringing before you matters which there was no statutory obligation to refer to the Executive Council. If so I can only ask you to forgive me for taking advantage of your goodwill. My reason has been that I have always believed that it is better to discuss things before they are done rather than after, and whenever possible to make sure that all aspects of a question are considered before a decision is taken. I am not so vain as to believe that I have made no mistakes, but I do feel justified in claiming that I have avoided many by this policy and that those long meetings have served the public weal.

headline: COLONY'S PROGRESS.
text:
In addition to the messages of farewell to H.E. Sir R. E. Stubbs, reference was also made at yesterday's meeting of the Legislative Council to the services of Sir Claud Severn, the meeting in question being probably the last Council meeting... he will attend and certainly the last at which he will reply to points on the budget raised by Unofficial members.

H.E. the Governor in thanking Sir Claud Severn for the highly efficient manner in which he had served as Colonial Secretary for some 14 years in this Colony, referred to the entirely adequate manner in which he had taken the place of Governor during temporary absences. (Hear, hear)

Sir Claud Severn mentioned that this was the twelfth debate on the Budget in this Colony in which he had taken part, and he had had the honour of introducing the estimates for the years 1914, 1919 and 1923. The progress and development of the Colony and its general prosperity during the 14 years he had been here had, of course, been extremely gratifying to him as well as to the whole community. He had watched the progress of the Colony with the greatest possible interest, and although there was now what he was sure was generally felt to be just a temporary slackening of that development, he felt that if he was able to return to "this Colony" after a comparatively short time he would find all the big works that are in contemplation and had progress in full swing again and ample revenue to make provisions for them.

headline: RIVER MINES?
text:
EMPLOYING UNQUALIFIED PILOTS?

A floating object, black, round and smooth, which might have been a mine, is reported to have been sighted by the s.s. "Honam". and to have passed halfway between Sampan Chau and Fish Stakes.

A Harbour Office's notification is posted to this effect and reporting that other vessels passing up and down the river have sighted similar objects, the French gunboat, "Argus" having met two within the last week.

Mishaps to steamers in the Canton river, reports of which have been received in Hongkong, are believed to have been due to the engagement of unqualified men as pilots. As most ships proceeding to Canton to discharge cargo do not call at Hongkong they have been at a loss to secure good pilots and the mishaps are the consequence.

There have been no serious accidents up to the present, the majority of groundings being cases of small steamers touching mud and coming off at the next high water, or after the cargo has been discharged in part. In some cases, however, vessels have been hard and fast for the best part of a week it is stated, and the work of lightening them is proceeding. Two that have been refloated are the "Nanyo Maru" No. 1 and the "Yei Maru," both of which were frequent callers at Hongkong prior to the boycott.

headline: MORE STRIFE?
text:
Managua, Nicaragua, Oct. 26. Ex-President Chamorro, the leader of the Conservatives, entered the city and seized the fortress of Ta Loma, unopposed by the garrison which joined the movement. Conflicts between the Constabulary and the Conservatives resulted in two of the constabulary being killed. Nine Conservatives were killed and 13 wounded.

The Conservatives occupy the upper part of the city where they have erected barricades. It is understood that President Solarzano has agreed with the Conservatives demand for the dismissal of the liberal members of the Cabinet in order to avoid further bloodshed.

headline: SERIOUS CHARGE
text:
ALLEGED MISAPPROPRIATION OF FUNDS

EUROPEAN MANAGER IN CUSTODY.

Before Mr. S.B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon, J. E. Atherley, manager of Messrs. Getz Bros. & Co. (of the Orient), Ltd., was charged with alleged misappropriation of $13,400 belonging to his employers.

Mr. D. H. Blake prosecuted, and Mr. A. H. Hall appeared for the offence.

It was submitted by the defence that the case was one for the Civil Court, but His Worship did not agree with this view.

Hearing was fixed for tomorrow morning and the afternoons of the two following days. On the question of bail, which had been fixed at $20,000, His Worship said he could not make a reduction in the amount. The sum would be in cash or in two sureties to the satisfaction of the Court.

headline: CHIA DI AND ALVIC
text:
Carles Casella of Turin is in the unusual position of being both dead and alive. His troubles began in 1917, when he was wounded and taken prisoner during the Caporato disaster, and was unable to give only account of himself during the next fourteen months. After the Armistice, he came back to Italy, rejoined the army and was duly demobilised in 1919.

Casella first realised his double existence in 1927, when, wishing to get married, he applied to his native place, Suluzzo, for the necessary documents. A note from the syndic informed him that, so far as Suluzzo was concerned, Ienrico Cassella had been killed at the front, and his name occupied an honoured place on the local war memorial. By personal intervention and by the help of further corroborative evidence, Cassella succeeded in persuading the authorities that he was sufficiently alive to take a wife, but he could not get them to remove his name from the memorial. They said it would not be the look of it.

Having secured his papers, Casella applied for the bonus of one thousand a/w, to which all ex-soldiers are entitled. Here again he found himself confronted by a statement of his own death and War Offices being notoriously hard to convince, he has only just managed to secure his money.

Casella said nothing of these things to his bride, as he thought she might not like the idea of marrying a man officially supposed to be dead. So it is easier to imagine than to describe her feelings when in 1922 she received a communication from the Ex-Soldiers Association asking for a photograph of the "dear departed" to place in the album of those who had fallen for their country. It took her husband some time to make her see the humour of the situation. Shortly afterwards, an aunt of Casella's was invited to go and receive a war medal to which her dead nephew was entitled. The dead nephew went himself to fetch the medal, but was not so foolish as to try and prove himself alive. He said he was his own brother, and the medal was handed to him with suitable words of sympathy. Casella is a good-tempered man, and he had resigned himself to the anomalies of the situation. What has really proved the last straw and has induced him to make his wrongs public, is the fact that the tax-collector has found him out in his modest abode and persists against all official evidence in considering him as very much alive.

headline: EUROPE'S TANGLES.
text:
'' ・

In his recent remarkable outburst M. Chicherin, the Soviet Commissar for Foreign Affairs does not seek to hide his chagrin at the successful outcome of the negotiations for the holding of a conference to discuss the European Security Pact. It was well for the maintenance of that spirit of goodwill which has marked the earlier conversations at Locarno that the publication of Chicherin's speech was followed by a prompt and strong denial on the part of Herr Stregemann that Germany was seeking an Eastern orientation. Although German's chief delegate dissociates himself, so "hotly" (in the words of the cable) from the suggestion that Germany seeks to bring pressure to bear on the French and British delegates by using the possibility of a Germano Bolshevik alliance as a lover by which to obtain special treatment, it may be that a useful purpose will be served by Chicherin's reminder of an alternative to a satisfactory settlement. It must be borne in mind

that Germany has already a trade agreement with the Soviets, and although it has proved of little or no use to Germany, an extension of its provisions might quite conceivably be considered by Germany as the lesser of two evils in a choice between it and crippling undertakings with the Allies. The Treaty of Rapallo between the Soviets and Germany, the provisions of which Chicherin so grandiloquently promises to extend to matters military in the event of the Locarno Conference not concluding favourably for Germany, was concluded during the Genoa Conference of 1922 at a time when German business men believed that economic and political penetration of Russia was possible. But several German firms are said to have burnt their fingers as a result of it. Whether the prospective advantages for Germany in a Bolshevised Asia in the event of such an agreement as Chicherin holds forth being accepted would prove less mythical than the trade “advantages” of the Treaty of Rapello is extremely problematical but the decision of Germany to risk it must be considered as a distinct possibility if the hands of the more moderate of the delegates at Locarno are forced by the attitude of a section to impose demands solely with an eye on the sanctions which may be enforced in the event of non-compliance. It would be jingoistic to predict an early division of the world into two camps fighting on a European-Asiatic front if Germany should decide to throw her lot in with a Bolshevised Asia, but it is obviously the ruin of Western civilisation that Chicherin and his myrmidons have set before themselves as an ideal, and they are sparing neither themselves nor their own country in their efforts to bring such a state of affairs to pass. The actual decision as to whether she will throw in her lot with Europe against the forces of Bolshevism rests, of course, with Germany but her attitude may be largely determined by the policies of France and Britain towards her. The complete accord which Mr. Austen Chamberlain and Mr. England arrived at and the conciliatory tone of the French notes

calling of the Locarno Conference may well be regarded as indicating France's pacific intentions, and if France and Germany agree on the details of the proposed arbitration treaties between Germany and her neighbours, practical and general agreement may well be in sight. It is sincerely to be hoped that the goodwill which has animated the delegates in the preliminary discussions is an augury of final success in this effort to unravel the tangle of European affairs.

headline: 4 REBUFF.
text: derived from the refusal of the Chinese to take part in the judicial enquiry into the shooting at Shanghai on May 30 is the evident sincerity, or determination of the Peking Government. They know their own mind and their contentions, in all the circumstances, are reasonable. There has been an inexcusable delay; first in deciding on a judicial enquiry, and secondly in appointing members to the judicial board. There may be reasons for the latter: the slowness in matters of modern diplomacy; the absence of Britain's representative at Peking with no one left in charge in a superior position, adequately to represent the nation. This latter has been the cause of pointed strictures at Home, and no good will be done in blinking facts, and in ignoring the harm done by those facts. The conceding of these points does not for a moment mean approving the action taken by the Chinese. The outbreak of what we may term hostilities against the British, was due to the unfortunate fact that a British police officer at Shanghai felt it necessary to give the order to shoot which resulted in the deaths of numbers of Chinese. What has followed needs no repetition. Mob law, boycott, looting, and striking need strong arguments to justify them. Nothing has arisen to justify what has taken place in these respects. An enquiry has been held and evidence taken and recorded. "Most of the requisite evidence has become unobtainable or has disappeared." On this we must qualify our admission of "evident sincerity" on on the part of the Peking Government. It suggests to the impartial mind that one party, having made outrageous statements and accusations, is now willing to let matters remain in a state of passivity, so that on proper occasions the innuendos and indictments of the hot days of June and July can be trotted out and used as "evidence" of foreign methods. The action of foreign Governments who have sent judicial representatives will be awaited with some interest. A rebuff and an insult have been tendered. It is impossible to think that in spite of the Peking Government's Note, the enquiry will not be held. It should be held, and it must be held.

This policy naturally commended itself greatly to the public, since the Governor was able to promise that under it, for many years, to come, materially increased taxation could be avoided, even if the revenue from opium should cease to figure in our returns.

That was the outlook this time last year.

How different it is to-day as a result of the strike and boycott can be seen from the budget speech Sir Edward Stubbs delivered in the Legislative Council this afternoon. An estimate of revenue is necessarily at any time a rather uncertain thing, he observed, being at best an expression of belief or an aspiration, but in the present case he could not claim that it was anything more than a guess—“whether a good guess or a bad one we cannot hope to tell until long after I have left the Colony.” Instead of speeding up development work as planned in the last budget, the Government is now making “every possible effort to effect economies,” and while “cannot hope to close the year without a heavy deficit,” it is comforting to note that “in any case our balances are sufficient to cover any possible deficit this year and to leave us a margin which should enable us to carry on through the year 1926 without imposing additional burdens on the taxpayer unless the situation should become materially worse than it is at present.” What are the prospects of the situation becoming materially worse? Next to the immediate financial question, involving as it did possible further taxation that question represents the most important side of the budget speech. How long does the Government from its special vantage point consider the trouble will last?

Our calendar laconically explains: "Birthday of Confucius." Not a Chinese house in Hongkong this morning, palatial home of wealthy merchant or squalid novel of humble coolie, failed to observe the religious ceremony that begins the celebration of the birthday anniversary of China's greatest sage. Moreover, everywhere in China this same ceremony has been performed. With deep solemnity and venration, the whole nation's newly, the memory of its most famous philosopher. Born in 551 B.C., King Ch'in Chaucer, the leader of the people who made the does not claim place among the founders of religion. He claimed to be "a transmitter and not a maker, believing in and loving the ancients," and his interest lay not chiefly in religion but in correct conduct and statecraft. The works of the ancients Confucius loved were not primarily religious although regarded with religious veneration. His own autobiography he summarised as follows: At fifteen my mind was bent on learning. At thirty I stood firm. At forty I had no doubts. At fifty I could trust my ears. headline: THE MAN AND HIS MESSAGE.
text:
The human appeal in the utterances of Confucius is an all pervading one. It affects the foreigner just as much as it affects—or ought to affect—the Chinese who, to-day, throughout all the provinces will pay tribute to the great teacher's memory. "While reading the works of Confucius," says one who followed him, "I have always fancied I could see the man as he was in life." Many are the princes and prophets that the world has seen in its time glorious in life, forgotten in death. But Confucius, though only a humble member of the cotton clothes, makes remains among us after many generations. He is the

the supremacy of his principles is fully and freely admitted. He may indeed be pronounced the divinest of men." Professor Giles calls him the Socrates of China, a very apt description. He taught virtue for its own sake, he tells us, and the discourses fully bear this out. It may not be difficult to understand the reverence with which the Chinese regard their ancient sage. He was one of themselves. He suffered as many humans do, from the wiles of those who knew not virtue, and his "like passions" were shown in a tendency to sadness. In the old days Confucius "became the idol of the people." History is repeating itself. The intense feeling of the present day, the source of much of it to be despised, is tending to the making of idols. And with this making there is a grave suspicion that the foundations are not always sure, not always good, or, to be more explicit, that the motives leading to this idolatry are not quite of the purest. It has been said that if Britain had been purely Christian, or practised an absolute pure form of Christianity, there would have been no great war. Can it be said that if China had practised implicitly the teaching of Confucius, we should have witnessed the disruption of the Chinese themselves, to say nothing at all of political disturbances which have found an outlet in strike, boycott and indignity on those of other races? The Master's definition of Charity was to love one another; his definition of knowledge to know one another. Perhaps the danger—it applies to the "idols" of other countries and those who pretend to revere them—is in the mere acceptance of Confucius, without an understanding of the man and his message, and, which is worse, without the practising of his precepts. What seems to be needed throughout the length and breadth of the land is not that the name, as of old, shall fly "in songs through their mouths," but that there shall be something less of lip service and the bowing of the head, and more of tilial piety: respect abroad: garnestness: truthfulness: love to all.

headline: VIA SIBERIA.
text:
One of the signs of the return to normal after the war was early considered to be the "Via Siberia" mode of travelling to the East, or the direction to this effect written on correspondence. Only this week is it given as a piece of interesting news that a mail from Home arrived in a record transit of twenty days. Information of this sort was fairly common before the war, and the Via Siberia route was becoming a fairly popular one with those who either were "no sailors bold," or with whom time was of some consequence. As a mail route, the Russia way has yet to be equalled—unless it will be equalled and surpassed, as seems probable by air mail routes—for it has meant the early confirmation of cables, contracts, and orders, and has made home seem just round the corner. It is only recently that the line has again been open for traffic and there is on record the interesting experiences of those who have essayed the journey since the Soviet became responsible for the control of the line. These experiences were interesting to say the least, but not encouraging to those who contemplated a journey across Europe. The news now cabled out will effectually dampen any ardour that would be

travellers had in this connection. A judge, the son of a judge, feeling the restraint of Soviet hospitality, freely acknowledged, feels called upon to recount his and his fellow-passengers' experiences during a journey home. Three times held up by the overhealing of an axle, may not be a matter worth complaining about; but a considerable delay due to the work of bandits, is a reasonable cause of complaint, more so when the work of these outlaws results in the loss of lives of railway workers, and is likely to do so in the case of passengers belonging to different countries. The incidents mentioned by Mr. W. W. Grantham, K.C., point to serious facts which cannot be blinked: Russia's internal affairs are by no means settled or secure. Counter-revolutionaries appear to be carrying on a sort of guerrilla warfare, and this suggests that "Red" activities now so well known under the word Bolshevikism, are not generally appreciated. Nor are they, we imagine, likely to be appreciated. Thus we may still expect the removal of bolts and pins from railway-lines, more or less as a matter of course for some little time to come. The statement that the railway track and rolling stock are both in a "shocking state," suggest a laxity of control due either to indifference, or to what is probably more correct, to the fact that the Government has its hands too full as a result of its interference in things which it can be argued do not concern it in the least. In the Far East the work of Russian politicians is well known. The fact of it is self-evident. To Bolsheviks, we ascribe all our present troubles, and in spite of denials to the contrary, there is a vast deal of truth in what is said. This pointed warning from home will certainly have the effect of hesitancy or abstention. Sympathise as we may desire to do with counter-revolutionaries, sympathy stops short at the possibility of being killed by them in their efforts to remove from the earth those who apparently are doing no good on it. Mr. Grantham's warning will probably be misconstrued and misinterpreted. But it will do good in drawing attention to the

fact that there are British ships comfortable and speedy and routes, effectively controlled by a British navy, which give all that the most exacting traveller can desire.

headline: Good Work.
text: The local Police Department should have just reason to be proud of their efforts when the statistics for the year come to be published as the measures taken since the commencement of the strike four months ago have resulted in a remarkable falling off in the number of serious crimes which in normal times fill the daily registen This happy result has been achieved by hard work on the part of the officials of this department and to some extent through other causes. These latter include the valuable assistance of special constables, the quietening effect on evildoers by the presence of the mobilised Volunteers, and the stoppage of the Canton traffic, which enabled the authorities to exercise more efficient control on Chinese passengers by ships. Added to these is the good which resulted in eliminating the lawless element by periodical raids on suspected houses and dwellings in general.

Mr. Thorne says that he met Lord Birkenhead in a London tube station when he (Mr. Thorne) was about to set out on his wartime visit to Russia. “Hello, Thorne,” said Lord Birkenhead (then Sir F. E. Smith). “I’ve been reading about your going to Russia as a delegate. Do you know it is very cold out there?”

Mr. Thorne replied that he only knew of what he had read of Russia.

"Oh!" came the reply. "You had better take this coat with you."

Despite the Labour member's protests, Lord Birkenhead insisted on lending his magnificent coat there and then.

Lady Astor regarded Mr Thorne with special favour because he gave his corner seat in the house of Commons to her.

“Just after this incident,” he relates, “she presented me with two gold-cased pencils and a beautiful diamond and pearl tie-pin.

"When I was ill in Aberdeen she sent me roses from her own garden. During my wife's illness she also sent her fruit and flowers, as well as to my son when he was in hospital in Falmouth."

Mr. Thorne was later a guest at one of Lady Astor's political dinners, but he would only go on condition that he could wear his everyday clothes.

The last page of the book contains a pathetic reference to the author's late wife.

"During the 30 years of our married life," he writes, "I had many ups and downs, all of which she shared with me. She was a thrifty and economical Chancellor of the Household Exchequer.

"Her foresight was revealed to me in a way I never realised when, after her death, I found that she had left me 2450, which she had saved, and of which I knew nothing."

headline: REDS IN COURT.
text: SCRIM MAGE IN STREET. (Reuter's Service.) London, October 23. Twelve arrested Communist leaders were charged at Bow Street with unlawful conspiracy to publish seditious libels and inhale mutiny. A large crowd was outside the court, including fashionably dressed women and many young men and women yearning red badges. A section of the crowd sang the "Red Flag." During a scrimmage the police took into custody a man carrying a red flag. Mr. Tom Mann was present in court. Sir Trayers Humphreys, prosecuting, said the accused was being prosecuted as the leaders and principal executive officers of two illegal organisations, namely the Communist Party of Great Britain and the Young Communist League which received orders from Moscow. The prosecution's view was that all persons die, seminating the doctrine of Communism were liable to prosecution for sedition. Communism as explained by the accused persons was illegal because it involved the forklift overtook of the government, the creation of a class war and seduction of the armed forces of the Crown from their allegiance.

headline: PUBLIC SERVICE.
text:
Our stipendary magistrates do well, when occasions arise, to pay tribute to those who perform acts of public service. Unfortunately the occasion too seldom recurs. More often than not the individual is moved to action when he has been placed in danger as the result of another's doings, and a prosecution has, more often than not, followed. In the more rare cases where the individual is not involved, but the community as a whole is concerned, the urge to act in the public interest becomes weak and is often ignored. Happily there are exceptions, and presentations made by the Government through the Police Department to those who have served the public interests by acts of personal courage witness to this fact. In other cases, a sense of civic pride has prompted others to take action to prevent wanton damage being done by trespassers, and to spend time in a police court to bear witness to what they have seen. It is this form of public service which is as worthy as any that can be made. If such rare examples could be followed generally, crime statistics and the work of the police would be much lessened, and there would be a saving of the Colony's natural beauty, and a saving in

money, where, as sometimes happens, the work of depredation has to be made good. Whilst we are not advocates of the community forming itself into bands of-what-may be called "Peeping Toms"—there should be a quickening of the civic sense on the part of the members of all the communities. It is time, for instance, that the proper usage of ricshas should be insisted on. There are byelaws, we believe, which decree that they shall be used for no other purpose than that of conveying human freight. Only once do we remember a case being voluntarily brought on a question of an infringement of this regulation. The street fountains are designed to save precious water during a famine. The waste of water on the part of unthinking users is a scandal and a shame. Of the bringing to book of "road hogs" there is nothing much to be said at this late stage. Those who act in a sense of righteous indignation in this connection do a service to the cause of what we may call clean motoring as well as to the general safety of those who have no desire to be propelled out of this world, or seriously injured, by a motor vehicle recklessly driven. Hitherto complaint has been made at the apathy of Chinese in coming forward to testify in cases of robbery and the like. The condemnation has alike been general and uncomplimentary. It has not shown much knowledge of Chinese psychology. It is probably easier to be brave outside a Chinese quarter of the city, than it is to be in one. Instruction in civic duty must come from the "elders" of the Chinese, and we should certainly like to see some action taken in this direction. But we are not certain that the foreign community as a whole accepts the implied obligation of citizenship, by being jealous of the privileges of citizenship.

headline: SHAW'S WORK
text:
INTERESTING UNIVERSITY LECTURE

PLAYWRIGHT AND JOURNALIST.

Before a large and very appreciative audience, Prof. Simpson delivered a lecture on Wednesday night in the University Union Assembly Hall on "Bernard Shaw." Prof. J. Fenton presided at the meeting.

In his opening remarks, Prof. Simpson dwelt on the life of the great author who was born in 1856, pointing out his Socialistic tendencies, his joining of the Fabian Society in 1884, and his activities both as a street-orator and as a pamphleteer. He took to journalism and criticised music and pictures. He found this too exacting and turned novelist but this resulted in failure and so he went on to play writing. The theatre having fallen on evil days, producers were looking about for fresh blood and Ibsen succeeded in bringing out his "Doll's House." This gave the stimulus and Shaw came forward with "Widowers' Houses" which ran two nights. In 1892, "The Philanderer" was written, but was found unsuitable for acting. Shaw's idea was to forsake the career of journalism and resort to writing plays of a new type.

headline: NEW IDEAS
text:
Another reason is that the play is the natural evolution of the essayist—the trouble is that he seldom lives through this because of the strain. Shaw survived and was able to write plays giving the amplest scope for criticism. He aims more at the propaganda of new ideas through his prefaces and explanations of plays than through actors; for he believes theatre-goers are unable to think sufficiently. Careful descriptions of scenes and appearances of actors are given. This style has been rapidly followed by such great writers as Sir James Barrie, Galsworthy and others.

Shaw being a follower of John Stuart Mills, did not believe much in intuition and tried to place before people the bare facts of life. Traditional feelings are attacked bitterly and rudely. Like all Victorians he is bent on forwarding Mill's Doctrine of Investigation.

"UNPLEASANT" PLAYS. The first plays of Bernard Shaw were called the Unpleasant Plays. In "Widowers' Houses" he tried to treat on the economies of unearned incomes derived mainly from ill-constructed and poorly furnished houses let out to the poor. The socialists liked this but not so the independent income-earners.

“The Philanderer” treats of marriage and is without a plot whereas the third play, “Mrs. Warren's Profession,” attacks the employment of women and the low pay in those days.

In the next series, the Pleasant Plays, “Arms and the Man” and three others, Bernard Shaw was greatly helped by William Archer who gave him good reviews and this seemed to be the bridge that admitted him into West-end London and Society.

NUTCRACK NIGHT, beliefs still linger in remote country districts. Most of these have to do with love, courtship, and marriage, as, for example, the one which decreases the roasting of chestnuts on the bars of the grate in order to find out if a girl's lover is true or false. Because of this the anniversary is known as "Nutcrack Night". In the North of England, if the nuts crack or jump it is a bad omen. The loved one is faithless. But if they burn clearly and steadily, without spluttering, the lady need have no qualms.

The ultimate aim was the thing, no matter how crooked the way to them. But the dead past had buried its dead. The dawn of a new era beckoned, and the promised land of contentment loomed in the distance. A guide there had been. Wise, discreet, other guides there were; men of knowledge and experience, yet not all blessed with a knowledge of the sure path. The old road had been pleasant—broad and comfortable. Fruit trees lined it on either side. Luscious—almost free for the plucking. A very easy road on which many tarried plucking not wisely but too well. Forgetting the thirsty ones; the toilers and those who put off the robe of opportunity for that of procrastination, the fruit gatherers waxed fat; the others thin. There was discontentment. But the command to “work together” seized the people and they bought up the opportunity. Their, bartering was done on equitable lines. They lived, not in palaces of exorbitance, but in places which taxed them not unduly. The one saw that though they were not here for their health's sake, they were here for things more enduring than money. The others glimpsed the new spirit and example again proved itself better than precept. All saw virtue in honest dealing and frank intercourse on problems that mattered. The departing one had seriously and studiously set himself to tasks of good government. At times of hardship he had set alleged economic facts at defiance, and the people benefitted. His departing message was “work together” and on the eve of the advent of yet another proved leader with a diversity of gifts, but the same spirit, they took the message not merely to heart, but to themselves, individually, collectively. CONSTITUDES AND FOREST THIEVES A COMRADE DEATE Over zealousness on the part of an Indian and a Chinese constable to curb the activities of forest, thieves led to what Mr. Whyte Smith, Crown solicitor, termed the committing of a very foolish action. They left a mother Indian constable who was with them in charge of a prisoner they had already captured and set off in pursuit of others.

When the two constables returned they found that the revolver of their commude had been taken from his holster and was lying 40 yards along the forestry path. The constable was lying face downward with face and abdomen wounds which proved fatal and the erstwhile prisoner was nowhere to be seen.

The murdered constable was of poor physique whilst the man the constables had left in his charge was a much stronger man, commented Mr. Whyte Smith. The revolver of the deceased man when found had had three rounds discharged.

The only witness who saw anything of the incidents after the departure of the other two constables was a stall-holder who, emerging from his hut some 820 yards away saw two men struggling and saw that one was an Indian constable and the other a Chinese. He heard a police whistle blown and immediately afterwards a shot. He ran to the residence of Mr. Knopp nearby and together with the latter went to the spot. They heard another shot and by the time they reached the scene of the struggle the constable was lying face downwards and there was no one to be seen.

Mr. Whyte Smith said that the defendant had absconded from his residence and crossed the border and it was when he was returning to carry out negotiations for some property he owned in Kowloon City that he was arrested at the bridge at Eo Wu. At an identification parade he was recognised as the man who was arrested by the picket.

After evidence at the "Central Magistracy yesterday, the case was adjourned.

headline: O. M. S.
text:
The "Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies" is meeting with a divided press. If anything it is what is known as a bad press. We can understand several of the arguments against it and the suggestion of the possibility of it taking on a Party bias. The idea of the O.M.S. has sprung out of recent happenings at Home and, among other things is described as the latest manifestation of the fear of Communism. There is room in Hongkong for an O.M.S. as we have previously suggested: Arguments which may apply at Home, do not, and cannot apply here. A strike in this Colony as we well know, is likely to reach out into unheard of directions. The cause of a strike, real or imagined, can become lost in the mists of racial prejudice and anger, when the foreigner is faced with things he cannot adequately grapple with—intimidation, fear, boycott. This Colony, no matter what the cause of any strike or boycott may be, should not be at the mercy of these forces to the danger of the proper maintenance of its supplies. Hongkong is an island surrounded by something more than water as some of the preceding words indicate. When let the future take care of

itself. Without raising a hand to make our supplies safe? In the term supplies we may well include essential "services" — the ferries, trams, electric lighting, etc. Our record in the past in some of these matters is deplorable—showing a lack of foresight and a crass in-difference to the mental outlook of the many who outnumber the supposedly thinking ones. Indication there is that some attention will be paid to the possibilities of the agricultural development of parts of the New Territories, so that food supplies of certain kinds will be assured us: But this is a long way ahead and likely to be retarded by the indifference of those who, apparently, have no need to worry at the moment about the source and the cost of food. There is an urgent need for the firm establishment of an O.M.S. in the Colony. Whether it should be organised by the Government or the community needs to be decided, but it matters not so long as staps are taken—and at once—to initiate this movement. There is a clear call here for the Unofficial members of the Legislative Council to be up and doing. Some of them may know "every hill, valley, bay and inlet" of the place, but do they know how to press a button that will call each of us to concerted action to maintain supplies and services, should the time again arrive for a display of solidarity?

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
Received just after the) “China Muil” had gone to press yesterday was the notification that Mr. Sutherland Stewart of the Taikoo Sugar Refinery had passed away at the Government Civil Hospital. It was then thought that he had succinbed to acute malaria which had affected his brain.

Mr. Stewart leaves a wife and three unmarried daughters to mourn his loss and the sympathy of all will go out to the bereaved family. Mrs. Stewart is resident in Hongkong and Miss Jean, the eldest daughter, is a teacher at the Quarry Bay School. The late Mr. Stewart was a native of Greenock, Scotland.

It was only last Saturday that Mr. Stewart was admitted to the Government Civil Hospital where he passed away after an illness of less than a week. For the last six and a half years Mr. Stewart had been with Tailoo arriving in the Colony from Africa. He was forty years of age and had travelled forty extensively. Described by his colleagues as of a nice quiet, unassuming nature, never in the least way offensive, he was very popular with those that came into contact with him. On the last STRIKE INCIDENT ON CANTON RIVER.

In a race against time the Kowloon (Chinese) Customs has been asked to rescue a dozen souls murooned on a rock, outside British waters, in the Canton River, others having already perished.

The night before last a junk put out from Su Cheng to pick up a ferry to Hongkong by evading the cordon drawn by the strike pickets. In the dark the junk crashed against the well-known river landmark of Tai Chaam and foundered.

Two people are known to have drowned at the moment. About a dozen were carried, clinging to wreckage, into British waters (near Deep Bay) and saved by the s.l. "San Hang On." The remainder were last seen off a precarious foot, hold with a strong wind blowing, hence the necessity for urgent rescue.

text:
The policy Sir R. E. Stuesslaid down with regard to striking students was that those who had absented themselves on certain dates were not to be re-admitted to Government and Government-aided schools. The heads of all other schools agreed to co-operate in this. The Chairman of the Education Board, in announcing the Government's measures, softened what some of the members considered undue severity by stating that in spite of the apparent definite nature of the in

late Headmaster took the view that it would be prejudicial to the maintenance of discipline that there should be taken back senior students to whom the situation had been explained and who were assured of protection in respect of threats to which they had been subjected. Whether, from Sir R. E. Stubbs' decision, suspension or expulsion was to be inferred is not clear from the wording of the resolution sent to the Education Committee, but there are indications that his successor is inclined to the more lenient view, and that during the period in which the door of local schools has been closed to them, the schoolboy will be considered to have explained their offences. The wisdom of such a course is evident, having regard to the fact that the students have already suffered as a result of their action—the rude awakening of certain students who thought that it was free education they were to get in a neighbouring so-called educational institution has already received publicity—also taking into consideration the state of genuine fear into which many of them were worked as a result of very extensive propaganda amongst them Hongkong educational institutions are necessary, quite apart from their general educative value, as a means of combating the Bolsnevik propaganda which is being so extensively organised in China to day and it would be a mistake to admit defeat and

It into the schools. The Reds Coast that they have captured all the Normal Schools of the country, and in a recent article, the Rev. A. W. Lochhead, resident in Honan for the past twenty-one years, states there is much to indicate that their boast has some foundation in fact. In North Honan he had had bitter personal experience that the Normal School was the centre of the most violent and anti-foreign propaganda and he had heard that one hundred and twenty Middle School teachers in the provinces had been dismissed because they were not Red. headline: MEMORIAL SERVICE
text:
FUNERAL OF THE QUHEN MOTHER.

FRIDAY'S OBSERVANCH

A "Government Gazette Extraordinary" issued yesterday announces.—

"Whereas the day of the funeral of Her late Majesty Queen Alexandra is to be one of Public Mourning," His Excellency, the Governor in Council directs that Friday, November 27, 1935, shall be observed in this Colony as a dies non, under and with the effect mentioned in section 7 of Ordinance No. 5 of 1912. A memorial service will be held in St. John's Cathedral at 10 o'clock to which all classes of the community are invited. A limited number of seats will be reserved for the Legislative Council, Consuls, Navy and Army Officers, Government Officials, heads of business houses and soldiers and sailors. capacity of the Cathedral is 700 with additional standing room for about 300.

The congregation is asked to be seated by 9:15 a.m. Music will be played at 9:50.

At St. Andrew's Church, Kowloon, a memorial service will be held at 10 a.m. to tomorrow and the Rev. J. Horace Johnston, of Union Church, will take part.

A special memorial service will be held by the Parsee Community of Hongkong to-morrow at the Parsee Church when the head priest will hold a Jason ceermony and recite prayers and invocations in memory of the late Queen Mother. In these the Parsee Community will join.

headline: LABOUR'S SENSE
text:
ALIVE TO EMPIRE NEEDS.

The Labour Party Conference carried the Executive's resolution, moved by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, declaring that only upon avowedly Socialist principles could the workers' claim be a fair and decent livelihood be met.

An amendment by Mr. Ferguson, of Glasgow, declaring it was necessary to organise the workers for a vigorous struggle to over-throw the capitalist class, was overwhelmingly defeated.

The Conference also passed a resolution declaring that unemployment was only preventable by the scientific co-ordination of nations and economic resources of industrial undertakings for the public good, instead of private gain and demanding the national adoption of this principle of a living wage as a first charge on industry; adequate maintenance of all unemployeds, and their dependants; pensions for aged and incapacitated workers and widows with children; raising the school leaving age to sixteen with maintenance grants; provision for training unemployed, and demanding that the Government take steps to assist in a revival of overseas trade, and closer relations with Russia. The Labour Conference adopted a resolution moved by Mr. J. R. Clynes urging that steps be taken to ensure closer political economic relationship between Britain, India, the self-governing dominions and other States of the British Commonwealth of Nations, requesting a survey of land resources of the Empire, the training of emigrants, and condemning the capitalistic exploitation of natives in the tropics; demanding Government controlled bulk purchase of food supplies, and raw materials of the Dominions in order to secure stable prices, expounding a scheme to encourage home production of food assistance to British farmers, and recommending periodical conferences representing the Socialist movement in the Commonwealth.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
NEGOTIATIONS MOVING RAPIDLY.

The Franco-American negotiations are moving, rapidly, it is stated. The Americans have reduced the proposed annuities by $20,000,000 and also agreed to insert a clause in a subsequent agreement providing for revision in the event of evidence forthcoming that the French capacity to pay has been over estimated.

headline: EMPIRE NEWS.
text:
A complaint of insufficient Australian news published in Britain was the burden of a resolution moved by Sir Hugh Denison, New South Wales, advocating co-operation between Australian newspapers with the object of supplying the British Press with a service similar to the present service from Britain to Australia. Mr. Holtz, Victoria, in second-ing, advocated that other Dominions should be similarly linked up. Mr. Turner, Britain, moved an amendment pledging his conferees to do their utmost to secure the publication of more Empire news and stated that agencies and correspondents already gave British papers more Dominions news that they could use.

Several delegates argued in the same strain.

Mr. Woods, Canada, in supporting the amendment, agreed that this was the most that could be done. Lord Burnham lengthily explained the difficulties of British newspapers as regards cabled news and showed the difficulty of giving effect to the scheme embodied in the resolution. Sir, Denison accepted the amendment and as a substantive motion it was finally carried that in view of the growing importance of overseas Dominions, and in order to promote a better inter-Empire knowledge and understanding, members of the Conference pledge themselves to the utmost efforts to secure the publication of more Empire news than hitherto. Douhing with the release of Swatow from Red control and the probable effect that the success of this section of the Kuomintang will have on the prospects for settlement of China's political dissensions and disunity, the "Peking and Tientsin Times" comments as follows:—

moderate advance will be made in the direction of Canton, A great dent of preparation and re-organisation will be necessary before the anti-Bolshevist troops in eastern Kwangtung can hope to challenge the more efficient and well-armed units under the direct control of Borodin and his henchmen. The Peking Government, for various reasons, of which fear of the expansion of the influence of the present regime in Canton is the foremost seems anxious to help the moderate wing of the Kuomintang, and to give Chen Chiang-ming the assistance his army needs. But there are difficulties on both sides. The separatist tendencies of the Kuomintang have not been eliminated. Even though so-called moderates seem to be determined to continue this policy to compel the Central Authorities to give them a large share in the Government. The Citizens' Conference is obviously the faintest means of a settlement of China's political discussions and disunity, but the Kuomintang are not more sincere than the Anfuities in the proposed use of this instrument. Each wants to pack the Conference with arbitrarily chosen nominees who will serve the interests of the respective parties before they will consider the higher concerns of the nation. Peking cannot very well co-operate with the Kuomintang in a war on the Bolsheviks and refuse to co-operate in the Citizens' Conference. On the other hand, many of the Kuomintang leaders, who dispute the authority the Central Committee, have to walk warily. Both extremists and moderates are courting the favours and support of the numerous branches of the party in the provinces, and the Right Wing apparently feel that even a temporary alliance with the present Peking Government would deprive them of much of the sympathy they might otherwise obtain from the provincial committees. The tradition of separatism which has developed since the Republic—partly political and partly psychological—is not an easy thing to break down, in spite of all that the province has suffered since it broke away from Peking. There are internal differences, for which handicap prompt and effective action by the moderates. We cannot understand the hostility that still exists to Chen Chiang-ming, whose action in refusing to participate in Sun Yat-sen's much-mounted but fantastic Expedition against the North was perfectly right, as same as his chief's course was insane. But the hostility is there, whether it be justified or not. The Party leaders have done their best to make his name anathematic throughout the rank and file, and they cannot very well turn round admit they were wrong, and openly support his campaign. This attitude is based on no punctilious moral grounds. The stigma they have attached to Chen Chiang-ming others have attached to Marsha Feng Yu-hsiang, but that has no prevented the Kuomintang from carrying favour with the latter.

The whole situation is very complicated, and it is probable that the Kuomintang moderates will conduct their own propaganda campaign against the Reds, persuade Peking to keep its own counsel, and, if help must be given the troops now at Swatow and other parts of the province not directly under Canton's authority, to give that help secretly. If there were any evidence of disinterested and patriotic statesmanship, we might look to the Citizens' Conference to provide an amicable solution, but he Tuan Government, which has cunningly used the anti-foreign agitation to perpetuate its enjoyment of office, is not likely—without pressure from abroad—to use the instrument it has created for unselfish purposes. Every approach to unification hitherto has been marred by sordid motives. It will never be achieved that way.

headline: MR. LLOYD GEORGE AND AMERICA.
text:
Mr. Lloyd George visited the Eisteddfod at Fwlhelli, and received an enthusiastic welcome from a great crowd of people assembled in the Eisteddfod pavilion. He was accompanied by Dame Margaret Lloyd George, Miss Megan Lloyd George, and the Bishop of St. Davids.

Speaking partly in Welsh and partly in English, Mr. Lloyd George, referring to the success achieved by English choirs at the Eisteddfod, said that was for the good of Wales. "We were relying too much upon our established fame, upon our natural facility and genius for song. It was about time our English friends came to stir us up." The political changes of the day, he proceeded, were not nearly so great as the changes in the habits of the people and their attitude of mind towards questions. Whether they were changes for the better or the worse God alone knew, but the real danger of change in a community was that the people in seeking something which was better might lose something equally good. The Prime Minister would have been delighted to have attended the Eisteddfod had it not been for the exigencies of the political situation. The next day they were to have a very distinguished Labour leader (Mr. J. H. Thomas); that day they had a simple countryman whose opinions did not fit quite comfortably into any political mould. (Laughter).

Later Mr. Lloyd George addressed the Overseas Welsh visitors at a reception given by Mr. David Davies, M.P., president of the Welsh League of Nations Union. Speaking particularly to the United States visitors, he said, "I appreciate the particular difficulties which you have in America in regard to the League. I am looking forward to the time when there will be such modifications and adaptations of the original scheme that your difficulties will be removed, and it will be possible for the United States to join in the great confraternity of nations to act together to impose peace on the quarrelsome nations of the world. (Cheers). Until the United States, with its vast and growing influence—an influence which to-day is almost incalculable, and in the coming years will be a dominant influence—can see its way to join some sort of confraternity of nations that will ensure peace and goodwill amongst men, I despair of the possibilities of civilisation in the future. I had a good deal to do with the direction of the war, and was the only Minister throughout the world who went through it from beginning to end. I should not like to see another. It was a horror. It was something that humanity, whatever its faults, imperfections, and sins ought not to be subjected to again.

should never happen again, but what do I see? Nations arming, nations utilising their power and resources with a view to perfecting, increasing, and intensifying the mechanism of human slaughter and misery. Well, unless you in a. Continent which has great advantages over us come to the rescue of civilisation I am afraid of what will happen. I honestly do not believe European civilisation could survive another war. I saw the thing growing in destructiveness year by year, the machinery becoming more shattering, terrible, and devastating. When the Armistice was signed there were inventions ready to be hurled into the mass of humanity which would have been destructive beyond imagination. Since then science has been working; some of the most ingenious brains at the command of the communities have been at the task of working out something still more

terrible. What happened in the last war is nothing to what would happen if there were to be war in the world to-day. America can save us; We have our quarrels in Europe. The weeds of hatred, racial, national, religious—every conceivable form of human passion, anger, wrath, and ferocity are deep down in the soil of Europe. There is not a frontier in Europe which has not been traced in red—fought and re-fought. You are free from that in America. For God's sake keep America free, but do not abandon Europe, and do not ring down the fire curtain so that the flames should not consume you. You cannot say 'Am I my brother's keeper?' No great country can have the brand of Cain on its brow and go through the world. Remember you belong to the same fraternity as poor Europe and the best you have got came from Europe.

"I appeal to Welshmen of every country and every clime," Mr. Lloyd George concluded, "to do their best, each in his own way, to influence the lands they will return to and of which they are citizens, and to which they owe their first loyalty—to influence them to come to assist in the great common task inherited from the founder of our great faith, the redemption of mankind!" (Loud cheers).

headline: CHINA CABLES.
text:
TELEGRAMS TO INLAND PLACES

The Eastern Extension Telegraph Co. notifies that:—

Telegrams to Amoy, Fooahow and Shanghai as well as to all places in North China (Chihli, Shantung, Manchuria, Mongolia, etc.) are accepted and transmitted as usual.

Telegrams to Hankow will be accepted either with abbreviated telegraphic address or with full address and will be forwarded by wire to Peking and thence posted direct to addressees.

Telegrams to other places in Central China than Hankow and to Inland places via Shanghai, Amoy and Foochow will also be accepted and will, if fully addressed be posted direct to addressees from Peking, Shanghai, Amoy or Foochow respectively but if bearing abbreviated address may be retained until normal conditions are re-established.

All telegrams to places affected by the dislocation of the Chinese Telegraph Administration's service are, however, accepted at the senders' risk-only.

Warsaw, September 30.—The visit of Chicherin who is en route to a health resort in Germany was marked by a notable reapproachment between Poland and Russia. Chicherin was received and entertained by the President of the Republic, the Presidents of the two Chambers and the Prime Minister. He had a two hours' conference with the Polish Foreign Minister. The German Minister who was suddenly recalled from leave tried on several occasions to see Chicherin, but calls at the Soviet Legation were fruitless owing to Chicherin's other engagements.—Reuter;

London, September 30. — The Bakers' and Allied Traders' Association has sent a letter to Sir Kingsley Wood asking for an extension of time before the enforcement of the new regulations in regard to the use of boric acid in egg yolks imported from China. The association say that they propose to try out two new methods of preservation by packing in England and sending to China and then re-shipping here in order to see the effect of the various climatic conditions on the contents of the barrels. Sir Kingsley Wood, in reply, regretted that he was unable to hold out any hope of a further extension of time.—Reuter.

headline: COMMITTEE MEETS.
text:
The following letter from the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce to the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council, is self-explanatory:—

September 80, 1925.

"Sirs,—I have the honour to inform you that at a meeting of the General Committee of this Chamber held on the 25th September, the following two resolutions were passed, and to ask you to transmit them to the Government:"

(1) That this Chamber respectfully expresses its profound gratitude to His Excellency the Governor and the senior officials for the great sympathy they have shown in the matter of their petition for Government financial assistance, and the readiness and despatch with which they have secured a loan of £3,000,000 from the Imperial Government to relieve the existing financial stringency.

(2) That this Chamber also respectfully expresses its deep gratitude to His Majesty's Secretary of State for the Colonies for the kind interest and practical sympathy he has shown for Hongkong by at once approving of the said loan of £3,000,000 to the Colony.

he Hon. Messrs. Chow Shou-ron and R. H. Kotewall
