headline: MOSQUITO SCOURGE
text:
The invaluable work and pressing needs of the Ross Institute for Tropical Diseases, Putney Heath, moves Home newspapers to eulogise a fresh the research work of Sir Ronald which resulted in the probing of the secret of the malarial parasite and in this connection the following article is of particular interest.

A very dangerous creature is that lady anopheles which, without so much introduction as "Excuse me, sir, your bite next," falls upon you and leaves with you a tiny germ that may lay you up with malaria for many days and possibly end your career. And pretty as dangerous, with the long tapering limbs of a bullerina of the world of diptera, guazy lanceol wings, and brilliant eyes. "The mischief she has done in times past, and is still doing, and will continue to do it not carefully watched, is colossal. She terrified the Malay States by hiding in the still waters, and emerging when a victim opportumely appeared. She rendered little the first attempts to cut the Panama Canal by sedulously infecting the imported labour. She gave the name of "white man's grave" to West Africa. She waylaid and scourged one-third of the entire population of the tropics every year, and accounted for one-third of the inmates in the hospitals. So much mischief and other siren probably ever did.

The has many sisters and brothers, no more estimable in the social sense. One confers yellow fever upon you and another elephantiasis. Yet others bring you plague through the distributing agency of rals, and typhus fever, and sleeping sickness—no end of deadly complaints to render life a torture. An active, sedulous criminal investigation department was badly needed, and by and by it came, but slowly, and only after infinite patient labour was the scourge checked. Then it was possible to compete the Panama Canal, to remove the topographical stigma upon West Africa, to lighten the work of the tropical hospitals.

The real caus of the scornage to be eradicated was a mystery. The midget enemy was unsuspected. First the partial etfieacy of quinine was discovered. But even then, and for very long afterwards, everybody but a few specialists believed that malaria was due to bad air from noxious murses. It was not until 1878 that a French army surgeon discovered the malarial parasite in the human blood, and then Sir Patrick Manson formed the theory that there might be a development of the parasite in the mosquito. But war had to be fought against those wedded to the old false idea—a little war, but prolonged, within the greater war.

headline: JAPAN'S ALARM.
text:
Plans which Chang Tso-lin, the Mukden warlord, has in hand for developing Manchuria and opening up rich land for more direct trade are thought by Japan to be a menace to its hold on Southern Manchuria and, incidentally, by Russia to constitute a menace to its hold on more northern districts.

The Tokyo correspondent of the "Daily Mail" states:—

While China, from Peking to Canton, is racked with anti-foreign rioting, boycotts, and demands for “freedom” from foreign supervision, Manchuria is proceeding calmly in its development, with the aid of foreign capital as well as foreign engineers and the use of foreign material and machinery.

Chang Tso-lin, the Ruler of the Three Eastern Provinces that go to make up the vast dominion of Manchuria, is boldly carrying out a scheme of railway construction that will treble the wealth of his provinces and give him an independence of communication that will double his military strength.

One line is to connect Mukden, Jehol, and Kalgan, and to consolidate under his rule the territory he gained in his recent war with Wu Pei-fu, which made him paramount in China. This line will furnish a new route into Peking. British engineers are now laying out the line, and material for a start on its construction has been purchased.

Take a map of North China and the two main Manchurian railway lines are seen to form a great "T" with the Chinese Eastern, from Manchuli, on the Siberian border, running south-east to Pogranitchafa, on the Ussuri border, forming the upper line of the letter, and the South Manchurian running south-west from Changchun to Dairen, as the vertical stroke.

headline: Rich Land.
text:
The traffic of this richest section of China, one of the greatest undeveloped corners of the globe, has been shared so far between Russia and Japan. Now its owner, ruler, the progressive Chang Tsollin, proposes to run a series of lines east and west, connecting with and feeding into the Japanese line, but capable of being linked up ultimately as an independent, self-sufficient system.

Two new lines are under way, one being the Taonan-Tsitsihar spur, to tap the territory of the Chinese Eastern, the other an extension of Chang's own main railway from Mukden north-east to Tungliac, via Changwu.

It can also later be linked up with the Chinese spur lines to the north and give Chang'an independent connection with the Chinese Eastern. Thus his plans not only threaten Russia's hold on North Manchuria but also Japan's hold upon South Manchuria as well.

The Taonan-Taitsihar line is one the Japanese desired to exempt from inclusion under the Consortium, claiming priority in any loans made for it.

Another line Japan fought to retain but ultimately abandoned, on the surface at least, is one to connect Mukden and Kalgan to the north of the Great Wall. This line will, besides opening up a vast territory of rich land, said to be particularly valuable as a poppy-growing country, yielding a superior grade of opium, be of the highest strategic value.

Through the Great Wall

When the line is built it will command all the roads from the north into Peking through the mountain passes and the Great Wall. It will also give control over the routes from Urga, over which now is believed to be passing Soviet military supplies for the "Christian General," Fang Yushian, alleged to be Moscow's ally against Japan, who, at least is playing Moscow's game to-day in China against Great Britain. It must necessarily be years before this line can be built, under present financial conditions in China, but the first link has been completed in the spur running from Chinchow, on the main Chinese Mukden Tientain line to Chaoyang, over which trains will be operating by the end of this year. headline: SHANGHAI COMMENT
text: One of our Hongkong contemporaries is waxing righteously — indignant in regard to a practice that is becoming increasingly prevalent in the Crown Colony as a result of the strike which has affected Hongkong so much, notes the "North China Daily News." When the general exodus of Chinese employed by foreigners took place in June, the house servants at Hongkong were among the first to go and, as it is now much easier to get into Canton than out of it, many of those who left Hongkong so light-heartedly three months ago cannot get back if they would. A certain number have, however, returned, but by no means a large proportion, and the shortage of servants—or at least trained ones—is still neutally felt. Now there come complaints that people whose servants have not returned are enticing away other peoples' servants who have either managed to get back or did not go away at all, and it is stated that even Government staffs are being preyed upon. The process adopted is an eminently simple one, and one that is most likely to make appeal to Chinese of the servant class—the offer of higher wages. The practice is strongly being condemned in Hongkong, where in view of the special circumstances of the Colony, it appears to be a lowdown practice and one that must be condemned. With those remarks, no reasonableண்டு can find fault, as also the statement that if things go on in the same manner wages will soar and domestic economies remain seriously on of joint long after the boycott bus finished. Certainly the practice of persons able to pay high wages, enticing the servants of people who are not, perhaps, able to pay as much is a mean one. Apparently, however, it is one of those things that nothing will ever stop, whether conditions be normal or otherwise. Servant-enticing is by no mean an unknown sport in Europe and America, and appears to be one of those phases of the Tenth Commandinent which will be violated so long as there are desirable men-servants and maid-servants for people to covet.

headline: “RED” MENACE.
text:
In an article appearing in "The Pubriot," Harriet Osgood Taylor, whose name is well-known in Hongkong through her former residence here—she is the wife of a former Harbour Master—and her appeals in connection with the work of restoring devastated areas in France, urges the Governments concerned to combat more resolutely the insidious influence of Bolsheviks in China, which she terms as the gruesest possible menace to China and civilisation itself. "The various wars between North and South," she states, the constant strikes (far too friendly handled by the British Government in Hongkong, as those who know say there) are all symptoms of the same disease—the virus of Revolution injected into body already disordered.

The article is headed "Renping the Whirtwind in China" and is as follows:

It is small satisfaction to one who still owns a house and other interests in the British Crown Colony of Hongkong and sees their value deteriorating steadily under the weight of trade depression caused by Chinese strikes and British Governmental weakness to be able to say, "I told you so," as regards the cause. But eighteen years residence in the Far East, in the Philippines, Japan, and Java, as well as in China, has shown me that until the several Governments concerned meet the challenge of the insidious force which is making for disintegration—often than not in the guise of wished-for reforms—civilisation itself as well as same government is threatened.

headline: ROOT TROUBLE.
text:
In one way or another the whole East is smouldering, ready to blaze. In the Philippines the United States now understand that they must clear out or govern. Unable at such a distance to do the latter, they will probably retire without loss of face —so important in the Orient—by selling the islands to Japan. This would be excellent for everyone, especially the Filipinos, who would be governed firmly and unsentimentally, while the Japanese, overcrowded to bursting it home, would here find room for national expansion, causing to arouse suspicion in America's, Australia's, and Holland's neighbourly breasts. The Dutch in Java live on the oversizzling lids of political as well as physical volcanos, and China's complete Bolsheviks would doubtless destroy them more effectively than even another Krukton eruption would. The French in Indo-China, the British in Singapore and Burma are equally threatened. Japan, the only Eastern nation which has realised the danger, but who, owing to the success of the sinister plot which ruptured the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and betrayed the British Navy in Washington three years ago, has at last been forced into the arms she wished to escape—of the blood-smeared Bolsheviks. The writings in China, as at home, have been many. Bolsheviks are now working openly where formerly they acted through secret societies. Flabbiness in dealing with the dangerous situation which has been permitted thereby to develop has hastened the crisis. Much nonsense is talked and written about "National Aspirations," "Reenochment of Foreigners," "Factory Conditions," "Child Labour," and all the rest of the formula to incite and excuse revolution. There may be some de-hided people who really believe in them, just as there were when Ireland was dismembered and the veins of the British Empire opened to ensure her slow but not painless demise. No one worth arguing with...believes it is anything but Bolshevism that inspires this trouble, which, wittingly or not—again as in Ireland, Egypt, and India—our own Government has complacently helped. In spite of a truncated navy, an unbuilt base at Singapore, a weak army, without our ally Japan, and, I fear, with false friends working against us in China, we must nevertheless act. Bolshevism must be destroyed, or it will destroy us. In finding a remedy for all ills, physical, moral, or political, the first thing to do is to discover the cause. Does China's history show any previous outbreaks of the virulent disease now ringing there which would suggest a remedy? The answer is overwhelmingly affirmative. The revolution now commencing there is like cancer; and just as the two men who recently announced the discovery of a virus which, in conjunction with an already-discussed state, in-line probable cause of that world scourge, so Mrs. Webster, in her remarkable series of books dealing with revolution, has discovered the germ by which, in conjunction with an already-discussed system, revolutions may be propagated. surviving civilisation in the world, but it is not civilised to-day—it is barbarous. Its unnumbered millions are ignorant, superstitious, and oppressed as no other people; except Russians, are oppressed. China's whole history—in spite of its contributions to art, literature, and philosophy—like that of Egypt, is of a succession of conquests. She has been eternally ruled by aliens, who, conquering as much by the weakness and corruption of her own people as by force of arms, have in turn themselves been displaced by the same combination of degeneracy and venality at home, force and guile from outside. Modern history in China, as elsewhere, has been repeated itself, and although, after the Opinion Wars of 1840 and 1860, the war with Japan in 1894 and the Boxer rebellion in 1900, her nominal ruler was allowed to remain on the throne, her inner monde steadily deteriorated, and the secret power, silently working like poison in the body politic, prepared the unhappy country for its worst rule of all—the Republic and the brigands and Bolsheviks who have succeeded it. China's only honest rule in recent years has come from outside. The extraterritoriality granted to foreigners—briefly, that they should be tried by their own and not by corrupt Chinese Counts—has been, and more than ever now, a vital necessity. All her recent troubles have been propagated through secret societies, and, although this is well known, there seems to be a conspiracy of silence in the Press regarding it, especially in the present crisis. The Boxer Rebellion, with its outbreaks of anti-foreign feeling, was in itself as factitious as it was fatal to the policy it advocated of turning out foreigners. The Revolution, of 1911 was, from the Chinese point of view, braving of view-breaking up by civil war an empire which had existed for thousands of years—even more stupid. The nation has been warring against itself ever since—helped always by agitators working through trade guilds as well as through secret societies. As for the ostensible reasons for the present crisis, they can be dismissed as absurd and in China's own interest, should be. No one who knows conditions in China itself, as well as in the foreign concessions, believes in them. But things are too serious now for further yielding and sentimentality. If the Bolshevik agents who are organising this business are not destroyed, China itself will be. If any foreign States concerned, through apathy, jealousy, self-interest, or blindness, refuses now to face the ngry facts, yields in the smallest degree to the preposterous demands of the agents of that secret controlling force, Bolsheviks will slowly but surely triumph over the whole world. Not Treaty Ports and Crown Colonies will go down but whole civilisations. It is a world issue.

headline: FATES OF NATIONS.
text:
LOCARNO AND THE WORLD.

The peaceful little town is agog with excitement at the arrival of so many prominent foreigners for the conference.

The place is swarming with journalists of all nationalities.

Special police have been drafted in to maintain order and protect distinguished guests.

All the delegations have now arrived and everything is ready for the conference to-morrow.

Herr Luther, in an interview, expressed confidence that the conference would produce decisive results if the negotiations were carried on in a spirit of mutual goodwill on the basis of equality and reciprocity.

Herr Stresemann said the conference should aim at the re-establishment of sound finances and the promotion of technical progress.

He pointed out that the hegemony of Europe had been definitely destroyed and no single Power any longer was able to pursue a policy of isolation.

He denied hotly that recent conversations with M. Chicherin showed that Germany was seeking an Eastern orientation.

[Locarno is a town in Switzerland, on the upper end of the Lago Maggiore. Its appearance is wholly Italian. The Protestant inhabitants, expelled in 1553, settled chiefly in Zurich, where they introduced the silk industry.]

headline: CHICHERIN'S OUTBURST.
text: Signs of the Soviet's anxiety at Germany's participation in the Locarno conference are forthcoming in an interview with M. Chicherin published in the "Berliner Tageblatt," wherein the strongest anti-British sentiments are expressed. Chicherin said the present situation in European politics was the result of British enmity towards the Soviet and that England's Pact policy was part of her fundamental anti-Soviet activity. That was why Russia watched with growing concern how Germany was falling in the wake of the British plans. No doubt it was against the wish of the German Government, but it was questionable whether England would not succeed in forcing her anti-Soviet policy on Germany. So far as the pact campaign was concerned, England's aim was to obtain the position of arbiter of the Continent. Chicherin said he found comfort in the belief of the impending signature of the Russo-German trade agreement, which was clear proof of Germany's determination not to deviate from the principles of the Rapallo treaty.

headline: A THORNY TASK.
text:
Messages from Berlin and Locarno indicate that Dr. Luther and Herr Stresemann's task at the Pact Conference is rendered more difficult by the critical attitude of German newspapers and political parties.

The former particularly are protesting at the report of a possible German abandonment of objections to France's standing guarantee for the Eastern Pact in return for French concessions as regards the occupation of the Rhineland.

The Nationalists have even sent a prominent Reichstag supporter to Locarno, apparently to apply a, restraining influence on the German delegates' actions, if deemed desirable,

A Locarno message says that the German delegates are prepared to accept clauses dealing with general arbitration on all Franco-German questions of a. politico-juridical character.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
A substantial part of the western security pact has been completed and it is expected that the jurists will add the finishing touches to-day; but the glass is not set so fair in regard to other subjects to be considered and it must not be forgotten that all questions are inter-dependent.

Newspaper despatches from Locarno foreshadow a tug-of-war with the German representatives, particularly on the question of the Eastern pact.

The "Echo de Paris" says that the optimism with which the conference opened has been replaced by greater reserve. It adds that it is beginning to be realised that the Germans will play an extremely keen game, and Poland and Czecho-Slovakia are apprehensive on that score and that France will not desert them.

"L'Ere Nouvelle" says that the shadow of Russia dominates Locarno. The question is whether Germany is locking west or east. "According as this question is answered affirmatively or negatively the Locarno pourparlers signify the commencement of the construction of Europe or the inauguration of a dubious situation, heavy with peril for the Allies."

“Le Journal’s” correspondent says that French circles in Locarno declare it to be inadmissible that the proposed pact will suppress or weaken existing treaties. Should Germany try to go back on the engagements into which she entered, in the course of the negotiations before the conference, the responsibility will rest entirely with her.

headline: SNUB FOR REDS. / AMERICAN LABOUR'S SENSE.
text:
HOLDING ALOOF.

(Keuter's American Service.

The position of the American Federation of Labour in regard to the Russian labour movement was vividly indicated in a reply by Mr. Green, President of the American Federation, to an address by Mr. Purcell, M.P., representative of the British Trade Union Congress, who criticised the Americans as being the slowest in accepting the new social and political ideas, and hoped the American Federation would send delegations to Russia to establish close and fraternal relations with the Russian workers.

Mr. Green, amid the greatest enthusiasm, announced that the American Federation would never affiliate with the present Russian labour movement, and added: "We are not willing to pay the price of casting in our lot with a class that would destroy us if it could."

General Von Arninn, unveiling a regimental monument, referred to the "loyalty to our military oath which we swore to our war lord" and alluded to Germans' gratitude and unswerving loyalty towards the Kaiser.

headline: "VIA SIBERIA"
text:
One of the signs of the return to normal after the war was early considered to be the "Via Siberia" mode of travelling to the East, or the direction to this effect written on correspondence Only this week is it given as a piece of interesting news that a mail from Home arrived in a record transit of twenty days. Information of this sort was fairly common before the war, and the Via Siberia route was becoming a fairly popular one with those who either were "no sailors bold," or with whom time was of some consequence. As a mail route, the Russia way has yet to be equalled—unless it will be equalled and surpassed, as seems probable by air mail routes—for it has meant the early confirmation of cables, contracts, and orders, and has made home seem just round the corner. It is only recently that the line has again been open for traffic and there is on record the interesting experiences of those who have essayed the journey since the Soviet became responsible for the control of the line. These experiences were interesting to say the least, but not encouraging to those who contemplated a journey across Europe. The news now cabled out will effectually dampen any andour that would be

travelers had in this connection. A judge, the son of a judge, feeling the restraint of Soviet hospitality, freely acknowledged, feels called upon to recount his and his fellow-passengers' experiences during a journey home. Three times held up by the overheating of an axle, may not be a matter worth complaining about; but a considerable delay due to the work of bandits, is a reasonable cause of complaint, more so when the work of these outlaws results in the loss of lives of railway workers, and is likely to do so in the case of passengers belonging to different countries. The incidents mentioned by Mr. W. W. Grantham, K.C., point to serious facts which cannot be blinked. Russia's internal affairs are by no means settled or secure. Counter-revolutionaries appear to be carrying on a sort of guerilla warfare, and this suggests that "Red" activities now so well known under the word Bolshevism, are not generally appreciated. Nor are they, we imagine, likely to be appreciated. Thus we may still expect the removal of bolts and pins from railway-lines, more or less as a matter of course for some little time to come. The statement that the railway track and rolling stock are both in a "shocking state," suggest a laxity of control due either to indifference, or to what is probably more correct, to the fact that the Government has it hands too full as a result of its interference in things which it can be argued do not concern it in the least. This happy result has been achieved by hard work on the part of the officials of this department and to some extent through other causes. headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text:
How political enemies become very human in their everyday relations is illustrated by Mr. Will Thorne, the Labour M.P., in his autobiography "My Life's Battles," which Messrs. Newnes publish at 3s. 6d. Mr. Thorne says that he met Lord Birkenhead in a London tube station when he (Mr. Thorne) was about to set out on his wartime visit to Russia. “Hello, Thorne,” said Lord Birkenhead (then Sir F. E. Smith). “I’ve been reading about your going to Russia as a delegate. Do you know it is very cold out there?”

Mr. Thorne replied that he only knew of what he had read of Russia.

"Oh!" came the reply. "You had better take this coat with you."

Despite the Labour member's protests, Lord Birkenhead insisted on lending his magnificent coat there and then.

Lady Astor regarded Mr. Thorne with special favour because he gave his corner seat in the house of Commons to her.

“Just after this incident,” he relates, “she presented me with two gold-cased pencils and a beautiful diamond and pearl tie-pin.

"When I was ill in Aberdeen she sent me roses from her own garden. During my wife's illness she also sent her fruit and flowers, as well as to my son when he was in hospital in Falmouth." Mr. Thorne was later a guest at one of Lady Astor's political dinners, but he would only go on condition that he could wear his everyday clothes.

The last page of the book contains a pathetic reference to the author's late wife.

“During the 30 years of our married life,” he writes, “I had many tips and downs, all of which she shared with me. She was a thrifty and economical Chancellor of the Household Exchequer.”

"Her foresight was revealed to me in a way I never realised when, after her death, I found that she had left me £450, which she had saved, and of which I knew nothing."

headline: GLOOMY PICTURE.
text:
BRITAIN'S COAL INDUSTRY OUTLOOK.

There was a large attendance of the public at the first sitting of the Coal Commission at Westminster Hall which was attended by representatives of the Miners' Federation and the Mining Association.

Mr. Ernest Gowers, Permanent Under Secretary of Mines, stated that the present demand and consequently the present output of British coal had descended to the level of 20 years ago, but the industry was employing upwards of a quarter of a million more persons.

The consumption from customers in Russia. Germany, and Austin had been reduced by 46,000,000 tons.

Replying to Mr. Reveridge, Mr. Gowers mentioned that seven men were now employed where previously it had been six. It was agreed that the pre-war standard of wages was only multinational by increased output per head of the employers, or the material increase of prices of coal to other articles. Mr. Gowers said he realised he had a very gloomy picture.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
For the first time since the Conference opened, M. Srzynski and M. Benes, the Polish and Czechoslovakian Foreign Ministers, participated therein. This morning Sig. Musolini is rushing to Locarno in a motor car from Milan in an effort to participate in the conference before it closes. It is understood that altogether five documents will be signed, namely the Pact itself and four arbitration trenties, Franco-German, Germapo-Polish, Germano-Czechoslovakia and BergGerman.

headline: FRANCE'S REDS.
text:
COMMUNIST MAYORS SUSPENDED.

ARHESTS IN PARIS.

A Communist demonstration outside the Bolshevik Pavilion at the Decorative arts exhibition was forcibly dispersed and 40 arrests were made.

The Communist Mayor of Saint Denis has been suspended for a month for grave dereliction of duty in allowing public services to be held up on the 12th inst., when the Communists attempted a general strike.

The Communist Mayor and Deputy Mayor of Halluin in department Nord have also been suspended for abusing the privileges of their office.

headline: JUDICIAL INQUIRY. / INSPICTOR EVIDENCE.
text:
At the Federal Equipment Design, the report of Hanson, replying to Mr. Dusnee Dindley Johnson, said that he did not believe that the events of May 20 would have been averted by detailing the original mob of students who thronged the charge room when the first four were arrested. He did not believe that they were preventing them from joining the outside mob the temper of the crowd would have been better. He had no special instructions from his superiors to take precautions against risks previous to May 30. An American missionary, Mr. Cities, giving evidence said that he was among the crowd at the time of the shooting. The mob was excited, waving banners and throwing leaflets in the air. From his position in the crowd witness did not realise any necessity for shooting.

Sub-Inspector Shellsworth said he was on duty at the Ninking Road and Chekiang Road corner. At about three o'clock he saw a "howling mob" surrounding a policeman on point duty. Witness, accompanied by three foreign police, attempted to break up the crowd, whereupon the mob pulled down. Unstable Cole and Stevens to the ground. Witness then ordered badons to be drawn, and the police slowly retreated toward the Station, pressed by a violent crowd. Witness heard the cry "Kill the foreigners," and was of the opinion that both volleys were necessary to repel the crowd. Had witness been in charge of the Station he would have done the same as Inspector Elverson.

headline: NEW AIR FEAT.
text:
London, Oct. 15. The first experiments in England with the use of a dirigible ax can aeroplane carrier were carried out at Pulham this morning. The R 33 left her mooring must with a light aeroplane fixed by a special apparatus under her hull. The R 38 cruised for a quarter of an hour and then a 1553 monoplane, piloted by Flight-Lieutenant R. L. Haig, chief test pilot of the Royal Aircraft establishment, was released from a trapeze slung beneath the airship, but in attempting to re-attach itself to the dirigible the aeroplane was slightly damaged and the pilot decided to land.

It transpires that the aeroplane unhooked from the airship and flew for some time. It then re-hooked but tie propeller of the aeroplane was slightly damaged by striking a wire. The pilot then unhooked successfully for a second time and descended.

headline: MURDER CHARGE / SEQUEL TO PAINTERS' QUARREL
text:
KOWL00N CASE

An argument arising out of a dispute over the disappearance of a painter's tool was alleged to be the cause of the death of Ip Kamlum when Mr. T. S. Whyte-Smith prosecuted for the Crown at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday in a charge of murder against another painter named Cheung Hi. The man died in hospital as the result of an abdominal wound which brought on peritonitis.

The case was adjourned after evidence had been called by the Crown.

The Treasury were not represented at the police court proceedings at Harewood End, near Sellack, Harefordshire, and no legal representative made an opening statement for the prosecution against Richard Louis Wreford Brown, of Sidonia, Sellack, a farmer and ex-officer of the 1st Welsh Guards, who was committed for trial at the County Assistance for the murder of his father-law, Dr. Walter Carless S. Ayne, a professor of obstetri-at Bristol University, at Sidonia on August 14.

Wreford Brown received the committal unmoved, but there was a pathetic scene when his mother, who had sat through the hearing, went across the court to him and they embraced each other affectionate for some minutes before the son was taken back to prison. When the proceedings opened, Mr. George C. Swayne, solicitor and brother of Dr. Swayne, said: "I represent Dr. Swayne's family, and I identify myself with the defence, and express great sympathy with the accused in his distressing circumstances and mental affliction."

headline: STRIKE OVER.
text: The southern's strike at British ports is now definitely ended. The unofficial strike committee at London decided to call it off. Mr. Shinwell of the Marine Workers' Union said so far as his union is concerned the strike ended over a week ago.

headline: SEVEN YEARS.
text:
Seven years with hard labour was the sentence imposed on a Chinese coolie at the Criminal Sessions this morning by Mr. Justice Gompertz, the crime the man was found guilty of being the theft of keys from a house in Yaumati.

Crown evidence was to the effect that the man worked in conjunction with others, their intention being robbery. The pretext was the hiring of a room by one of them.

headline: FARLIER CABLES.
text:
Interesting comments are made on the results of the Locarno Conference by the newspapers.

... "Petit Parisien" says that the most exacting critics must be satisfied with them.

L'Echo de Paris" says that the complexity of the contradictions in the agreements are disquieting, and that there is a possibility that the Anglo-French defensive accords no longer exist.

“Le Journal Gaulois” says that the entente cordiale is re-born and is again the pivot of European equilibrium.

The “Taeglicherundeschau” says that the German conception triumphed completely and that a peaceful revision of the Treaty of Versailles is not altogether out of the question.

"Germania" says that Locarno proved that Germany is again regarded as a world power.

The "Berliner Tageblatt" says that "the western Pact is the Magna Charta of the future life of European nations, and that never before has Great Britain so bound herself.

“Vorwaerts” says that the idea of a lasting peace has been realised.

The “Diplomatisch Politische Correspondenz,” which is the official mouthpiece, emphasises the importance of article 20 on arbitration treaties which it believes makes almost all the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles subject to arbitration.

Even the Nationalist journals acknowledge that much has been achieved at Locarno though they condemn the various details of the treaties.

M. Krassin, who has arrived with M. Kharkoff to participate at the session of the all Ukrainian Central Executive Committee, in an interview in regard to the results of the Locarno Conference, declared that the Security Pact was a means of drawing Germany into the "sphere" of anti-Soviet policy and preventing her rapprochement with Soviet Russia.

headline: SHIPYARD LOSSES.
text: Newspapers from Berlin say that the contract awarded to the Deutsche Werft to build five motor ships for a British shipping firm, which created a sensation in British shipyards early in the year, has had a sequel in the announcement that the Deutsche Werft is faced with a serious loss in the fulfilment of the order as trade conditions have exercised depression. Most German shipyards declare that the Blohm Voss yards at Hamburg are nearly empty. The Reihersbiog Werft is still closed and unable to complete four vessels under contract for which they accepted an uneconomical figure. The Vulcan yards at Bromen are approaching idleness. The Danziger Werft have paid off 2,000 workers and closed down. The "Boerson Zietung" states that the crisis is so serious that no State help will improve matters.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES

headline: BRITISH TAXIS.
text:
An announcement that the directors have under consideration the purchase of a new fleet of British made taxicabs of an improved design and the sale of the present fleet of vehicles was made at the second annual meeting of the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxi-cub Co., Ltd. held at the registered office of the Company yesterday afternoon.

Mr. H. Birkett presided. Others present were Mr. A. H. Rowe (managing director), Messrs. Fred Ellis, E. M. Raymond (directors), C. A. Fulcher, D. McNeill, A. A. Alves (shareholders).

The Chairman said:—

Gentlemen.—The report and accounts for 1924-25 having been in your hands for some days, I will, with your permission, take them as read.

Before proceeding to deal with the Company's affairs, I desire to refer to the great loss we have sustained in the death, under the tragic circumstances which you will all remember, of the late Hon. Mr. Chau Su-ki, who was a director of the company from its inception and always took the deepest interest in its affairs. Mr. T. N. Chau has been invited by the directors to fill the seat thus vacated, and I am sure he will carry on his father's excellent work.

You will note that the balance sheet shows a loss of $46,680.14, but it has to be borne in mind that $62,303.41 has been written off for depreciation, in addition to the $45,915.04 written off last year, making the total amount written off for depreciation, $108,215.45, which represents about one-third of the paid-up capital of the company and more than half the original cost of our taxicabs, and this has been accomplished in a period of only fourteen months' finding, as the bulk of our taxis did not arrive in the Colony until March, 1924, and further it shows that your directors have pursued a hold policy and made ample provision for depreciation, which I feel sure will meet with the approbation of the shareholders.

A Farming Scheme.

You will also note that the balance sheet before you refers to the period ending April 30, 1925, and since that date the affairs of the company have been conducted on a different plan: the loss of $46,680.14 is to be attributed in a large measure to the fact that our drivers, working as servants of the company, grievously abused the taxicabs, a fact which is borne out by the item in the profit and loss. account of $46,937.85 for workshop and garage charges. Furthermore, by various ways too complicated to describe here, the company was deprived by the drivers of a considerable part of its just receipts. Your directors, therefore, decided to begin the present year with a system of farming out the taxis to a syndicate formed by the drivers themselves. The syndicate pays a fixed rate for the vehicles and they have to meet their own running workshop and garage charges, thus eliminating from our accounts, the items running charges, workshop and garage charges, and trading expenses, which together amount to $210,910.87—an item which will not occur at all in the next statement of accounts to be presented to you. Furthermore, the item "office administration and expenses" has been greatly reduced as the company now employs a much smaller staff. In future, apart from these reduced office expenses, the company has only to meet the cost of depreciation, and is at the same time in receipt of a regular income from the hire of its taxis.

I would also call your attention to the item in the balance sheet of calls in arrear. These shareholders have been served with a notice under registered cover to pay the third call with interest due and informing them that in default of payment within 14 days their shares will be forfeited and sold in accordance with clause 36 (a) of our Articles of Association.

Your directors have under consideration the sale of the present fleet of taxis and the purchase of a new fleet of British made vehicles, for which purpose a visit home to England by your managing director is under contemplation, in order to select the most suitable taxicab, and you may rest assured that the result will be the putting in commission of a greatly improved type of vehicle, especially adapted to hill climbing and generally suited to local conditions, and which will last much

Longer with lower training expenses and smaller repair till than our present fleet of cartoats and for which the directors are of the opinion that there will be no need to make any further calls to meet the cost of the new fleet of taxi-cabs. Although the balance sheet shows a loss, the results of our trading since May 1 under the new system of farming out the taxis has been very profitable and when the books are closed at the end of this month, which will be just six months' trading under the new system, your directors hope to declare an interim dividend.

I have now pleasure in moving the adoption of the report and accounts, and after this has been seconded I shall be glad to answer to the best of my ability any questions which any shareholder may desire to ask.

Shareholder's Questions. Mr. McNeill desired information on a sum of over $60,000 appearing in the balance sheet for office administration and "expenses—a sum which he considered too large.

Mr. Rowe explained that this was due to having to upkeep three branches and pay rent. The expenses over a period of six months had entered the balance sheet figures. Formerly the Company had an office in the Asiatic Building, which cost $2,000 in rent. This had been vacated, and the expenses now amounted to only $2,000 a month.

In querying the expenses for cushion covers and drivers' uniforms, Mr. McNeill said that he had not seen a driver at any time in uniform.

It was explained that each man had been supplied with two suits, but it was difficult to get them to wear the uniforms, and they never kept them clean, so the uniforms had to be withdrawn.

Mr. Rowe also explained that the cost of uniforms was a small one, and that the total included the cost of taximeters, which represented a large sum.

A sum of over $7,000 for furniture was explained by having to fit up the old office at the Asiatic Building.

Mr. McNeill said that he had looked over the Kowloon office; but did not consider the whole place worth more than $50.

The Chairman said that the large expenses was in a large measure due to the showroom at Pedder Street which it was thought necessary with a view to larger sales. The results did not justify the expense, and as soon as the opportunity presented itself the premises were vacated. To another query by Mr. McNeill as regards the hiring of the taxis, it was explained that three men were responsible under the scheme and that the money was collected every day.

Condition: of Vehicles.

Mr. McNeill drew attention to what he termed the bad state and filthy condition of the cars for months and months. There was no inducement to the public to engage them, as he had found for himself after spending hundreds of dollars by riding in them, and he considered that they should be looked after better by the Company. As a small shareholder he would certainly like to see the Company get on. He knew the Chinese were careless when the expenses did not come out of their own pocket, and he thought that the drivers should be pulled up a bit.

The Chairman said that the Company was being constantly pulled up by the Police: They made a thorough inspection periodically of the gears, mechanism and other things, and any cars not in order were not allowed to run.

Mr. Rowe added that prior to the strike they had 30 mechanics on the Hongkong side. They now had only about eight men, and were consequently working under great difficulties. Under the hiring scheme, the farmer has to look after the cars and do everything. He said that all the taxis are now running, and in respect of any vehicle that is not running the farmer has to pay $600 under the contract, which was for three years.

This concluded the questions and the Chairman's proposal that that report and accounts be adopted was seconded by Mr. Raymond and unanimously agreed to.

Election of Officers. The re-election of Messrs. Sam Pak-ming and Chan Lim-pak as directors was proposed by Mr Rowe and seconded by Mr Fulcher Carried unanimously.

It was also unanimously agreed to re-appoint Messrs Lowe, Bingham & Matthews as auditors for the current year on a proposal made by Mr. Filcher and second

headline: WAR IN NORTH / FENGTIEN ADVANCE
text: Sun Chuan-fang's rapid advances have cleared the Fengtian forces out of Kiangsu and have given him control of the railway as far as Pengpu, with a narrow front, but preceded by the movement of forces of the allied provinces the latter are beginning to reach Pukow from Fukien and from Kiangsi while a division has gone to Pengpu from Arhui. With reinforcements Sun has command of 70,000 and Chang Tsung-chang of Fengtian about 80,000. The Fengtian forces are more compact and prepared and apparently intend to strike before the arrival of the allied reinforcements. 15,000 of which are being rushed up to the front. Sun Chuan-fang went to Pengpu from Nanlang this morning and reported that the Fengtian advance had begun.

headline: Ottawa. October 30.
text:
The swing of the elections in favour of Conservatives is probably largely due to the general tendency of the public to favour a change of Government, owing to the dissatisfaction at high taxation and business depression.

Mr. Maighen's main appeal based on a Protective Tariff made the issue significant. The main electoral change occurred in the Province of Ontario which is the most important industrially, although Quebec, which is also a centre of many industries, remained Liberal.

The Maritime Provinces, though said to be opposed to higher tariffs, returned a majority of Conservatives, while the Prairie Provinces returned a majority of Progressives or Liberals.

The Labour Party and Indeper dents cut a small figure.

Only one woman member was elected, namely, Miss Agnes Macphail, a Progressive who was a member of the last Parliament.

headline: EARLIER CABLES:
text:
The latest returns of the elections indicate that the Conservatives have a small clear majority in the new Parliament. Nine members of the Cabinet, including Mr. Mackenzie King, have been defeated.

Later.

The results of the election available early this morning show that Mr. Meighen, the Conservative leader, was returned as the head of the largest group, though whether he will have a clear majority is undecided until the returns from 25 doubtful constituencies are received. According to unofficial figures issued at three o'clock this morning the position is as follows: 118 Conservatives, 89 Liberals, ten Progressives, two independents, two Labour and 25 doubtful.

headline: INTERNATIONAL COMMITTEE'S REPORT
text:
A meeting of the International Cotton Committee at Milan, under the chairmanship of Mr. Fredrick Holroyd, decided to protest against the publication of fortnightly cotton condition reports issued by the Washington Department of Agriculture on the ground that they were extrainely detrimental to the trade and unreliable.

Mr. Holroyd was appointed a delegate to attend the Washington conference on the standardisation of rules.

CONDITIONS GENERALLY QUIET NO STRIKE OR BOYCOTT (An Occasional Correspondent.) Lul Chow, October 15. On returning here I found the district very tranquil. In fact, I understand that the whole of the Ha Sze Fu is now quiet and under the control of the pro-Chan General Tang'Pun-yan.

There is no evidence or a strike or boycott. A very few of the people have expressed surprise at our return but we have been received as usual.

text: There were no actual eye-witnesses of the accident forthcoming when the police appeared on the scene, but it was gathered from some visitors at the Hotel that a crash was heard. One gentleman who came to investigate found the ricsha overturned near the drain and two coolies hastily trying to get it on the road. headline: NOT TRUE. / THAT CORPSE FACTORY STORY.
text:
CHARGES "ABSURD:

Brigadier Charteris, in a statement, emphatically denying the statements attributed to him in regard to the German corpse factory story, during his recent visit to America, said the allegations that he invented the Kadaver story, altered the captions of the photograph, or used faked material for propaganda purposes, were absurd.

He explained the whole circumstances to the Secretary of State who was perfectly satisfied.

A cable message from New York on October 25, said: In connection with the stir arising from the report that General Charteris, Chief of the British Intelligence Staff during the war, told the National Arts Club, at a recent private dinner that the story that the Germans boiled the bodies of dead soldiers for the purpose of obtaining fat was a deliberate invention. General Charteris told a Reuter representative before he left for England that he had been incorrectly reported. His references to propaganda, which were purely incidental, were made with the express purpose of emphasising the principle followed by the British that propaganda, to be effective, must be based on truth. He added that he only mentioned the case of the "corpse factory" for the purpose of emphasising that the report was not utilised for propaganda when it became known that the soldier's diary on which it was founded, was fictitious.

London, November 3.—The results announced early this morning in about eighty of the largest provincial towns in connection with the municipal elections show that Labour had 73 gains and 26 losses, the Conservative, 28 gains and 49 losses, the Liberals 11 gains and 33 losses, and the Independenters 21 gains and 25 losses. — Reuter.

headline: CHAPLIN'S LATEST.
text:
THE MAKING OF THE GOLD RUSH!

QUENN'8 BIO PICTURE

This evening when you go to the Queen's Theatre a pathetically grotesque fellow wearing a smudge moustache, a crestfallen bowler hat, and "bags" not distinctively Oxfordian, will shuffle across a crowded daffce floor with one foot tied up like a brown-paper parcel. He will sit down to a meal of old boots, pulling out a twisted nail for a wish-bone. He will pummel a pillow and subsides in a cloud of feathers. He will kick someone in the very seat of masculine dignity. He will do you a marionette dance at table with two forks stick into rolls. He will rock into a hut on the edge of a precipice. He will sit waiting in a shack, all bedizened for a New Year's party, for a girl who does not turn up. That's all. Such small things, and yet—so big.

That will be Charlie Chaplin, the buffoon of the soul, in "The Gold Rush," a film so long in the making — two years, actually— that it dropped "Charlie's first income-tax re-trip" to that of a ten-cent-store clerk's.

In this, which he regards, as his finest work, Charlie joins the long, long trial of the early goldseekers to white Alaska. There are some 2,500 toughis on the job with him—Southern Pacific Railway "burns," chartered specially for the film and taken up into the High Sierra in the California Rockies for a month's camera-shooting in situ.

To making the HillRoot Pass a pathway, 2,300 feet long was cut through the show, professional ski jumpers being employed to dig steps at the topmost point. Equipment was hauled nine miles from the railroad, and a pioneer's city of shacks built in order that Charlie might phy the fool in it. About $1,000,000 was sunk in the whole enterprise, which included the erection of 200 tons of plaster Sierus at Hollywood, snowed under with 285 tons of salt, 100 barrels of flour, and four cartloads of blizzard confetti! To say nothing of lumber and Burbap, and chicken wire, und

But enough of that, lest some enthusiasm be tempted to measure enough laugh in terms of linear feet. What of the magician himself during these two years of organised buffoonery? Mr. H. d'Abbudie d'Arrast, who has been Mr. Chaplin's assistant director for three years, and is at present in London supervising the presentation of the film, can enlighten us on that.

"He worked fitfully, as the mood took him," sometimes for eighteen hours at a stretch, sometimes for a few minutes, at the end of which he would say, 'It's no good. Come on,' We'll go and have a coffee." He was always going off at new tangents, altering, reconstructing. In the middle of a walk he would strike an idea, get out pencil and paper, and say, 'Yes, we must have it this way.' This film is 8,200 feet. To get that wo shot 400,000. He lived in the film, heart and soul."

As the talk progresses it is�rare, O I'rare, Charlie who emerges. Trudging up the steep of the long snow trial, the railroad "bums," Bolshies among them, get disgruntled. They're not going a-ynd further. They want grub. fed up. Over the meal Charlie gets up and entertains them for an hour on end, harangues them on politics (which they love), and this thing and that, until they are all agog with his galvanic personality. And they trudge on again.

The complete results of the Municipal elections in London and the provinces show Labour's total net gain as 135 seats, of which 88 are in London.

Labour holds the majority in 8 of 28 London boroughs. There was a tie at Greenwich and the remaining 19 are held by the Municipal Reformers.

headline: CABINET CHANGE
text:
SECRETARY OF AGRICULTURE NAMED.

Lt. Colonel, Rt. Hon. Walter Edward Guinness, Unionist M.P. for Bury St. Edmonds since 1907, has been appointed Minister of Agriculture to succeed the Hon. E. L. F. Wood, who is to take the place of Lord Reading as Viceroy of India.

[The new Minister served in the South African war in which he was wounded whilst carrying despatches, for which he received the Queen's medal, four clasps. He also served in the world war as a Brigade-Major. He has had ministerial experience and was Under-Secretary of State for War, 1922-8; Financial Secretary to Treasury, 1928-4. He was also Officer Crown of Roumania. He rowed three years in the Eton eight and was Captain of Boats.]

headline: MARITAL TROUBLE.
text:
FRENCH WOMAN SUES HUSBAND.

SUMMONS AGAIN ADJOURNED.

The case against M. Louis Maurin, a French resident, who is summoned by his wife, Madame Leona Maurin, for alleged desertion and failing to provide for her maintenance, came for hearing again at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell.

At the previous hearing on Thursday an adjournment was made until this morning to enable the parties to settle the dispute outside Court if possible.

Mr. W. B. Hind represented the complaint, and Mr. G. K. Hall Bruton was for the defendant. His Wagship said that he understood an agreement had been reached between counsel for the summing to be put off for one month, and he would therefore adjourn the case until December 4.

headline: "WHOLEHEARTED SUPPORT" ASSURED:
text:
In the same Hall in which thirteen years previously he attended as Acting Colonial Secretary the inauguration of the Hongkong University, Mr. Cecil Clementi, C.M.G., made his inaugural speech as Chancellor of the University and incidentally his first public speech as Governor of the Colony other than the few remarks at the swearing in ceremony at the Council Chambers upon his arrival.

His Excellency the Governor expressed appreciation of the loyal manner in which the students had stuck by their Alma Mater in the recent disturbances and in expressing indignation at the first gesture having come from schoolboy folly said that he found it difficult to conceive of anything more alien to the spirit of Confucianism than the recent happenings in South China and particularly the schoolboy strike.

He assured the University of his sincere sympathy and whole-hearted support in all that tended to advance its welfare. If fortune so far favoured him he might be able to meet some of the needs of the University even perhaps to securing a portion of the Boxer Indemnity.

The occasion on which his inaugural speech was made was the welcome to the new Chancellor and Governor of Hongkong by the University Union. His Excellency was accompanied by Sir Matthew Nathan.

Mr. Ma Char Zur, Chairman of the Union, welcomed the Governor and Sir Matthew Nathan and said that in February last year they had the honour of entertaining three vice-Chancellors, and to day they had the signal honour of entertaining two Governors. (Hear, hear). This was the first time in the history of the University that the undergraduates, voluntarily, out of their enthusiasm and admiration for a great man, had created a special occasion on which to welcome His Excellency the Chancellor. It was a matter of pride to them that they should be among the first to welcome His Excellency. H.E. the Governor was not only a physical giant, but an intellectual giant of world-wide renown. He was a distinguished scholar, author, traveller, explorer and administrator. As a matter of fact, he wrote the University anthem, which was about the only thing they could boast of at present, and which only Dr. Pearce really understood. (Laughter). In welcoming His Excellency, he was sure he was welcoming one who could be relied on to heed the crying needs of the University.

Throughout its infancy, the University had been crying, and until recently the undergraduates and the staff members had been weeping and wailing together. The staff ceased when the superannuation scheme was carried out, extra quarters for staff members promised and 18 months' long leave freely granted. (Laughter.) But the undergraduates were still mewling and puking in their nurses arms. They were not such a band of scoundrels and rascals as some people thought they were.

With the coming of Mr Clementi, they saw an era of prosperity for the University. So far they had been living on dreams for the Boxer Indemnity money, and they hoped that His Excellence would get for them a substantial portion. (Hear, hear). His Excellency was interested in the University, and they hoped they would find in him a practical supporter of the University which as they had never had before.

On behalf of the University Union, he welcomed Mr. Clementi and wished him success in his administration of the Colony. He wished Sir Matthew Nathan every happiness in his retirement. (Applause).

His Excellency the Governor, who was received with loud and prolonged applause on rising to speak, said: Mr. Chairman, Mr. Vice-Chancellor, ladies and gentlemen.—It has been a very real pleasure to me to come among you this afternoon, and I thank you for the welcome you have extended to Sir Matthew Nathan and myself and for the entertainment you have given us. My interest in your University dates from its first beginning, for I was much concerned in the negotiations which led to its foundation and its original endowment, and I was present in this Great Hall at its inauguration. (Applause). I had also, while in British Guiana, the honour of receiving from your former Chancellor, Sir H. King May, an intimation that this University wished to confer upon me its degree of LL.D. and on-quiring whether I could attend to receive the degree in person. I had regretfully to reply that I them saw no hope of being able to revisit Hongkong. As, however, I am now once again in Hongkong and am even your Chancellor, I am glad to have this early opportunity of assuring you of my abiding interest in your University, and I hope that if fortune so far favours me I may be able to dry some of those tears of which your Chairman spoke as being shed by the staff and undergraduate—(Laughter)—and even perhaps to secure for you a portion of the Boxer indemnity to which you aspire. / (Applause).

I also rejoice at having this opportunity so soon after my arrival of expressing to you my great appreciation of the very loyal manner in which you have supported your Alma Mater throughout the troubles in which this Colony is at present involved. (Applause). Schoolboy folly, as I learn with indignation, made the first gesture in the recent strike and deliberately flouted both education and authority but the undergraduates of the Hongkong University knew better than to participate in a movement so stupid and so injurious to everyone who has been misled into joining it. (Hear, hear).

RECENT HAPPENINGS. In each of its various manifestations this strike has done nothing but harm, but its most outrageous absurdity was the strike against education. After all, what is education? I should like to define it as a process which aims at drawing out from every human being the utmost which he or she is capable of giving in the cause of humanity. (Applause). I would lay stress upon this word "humanity," and remind you of a famous phrase in the Chinese classics, "Within the four seas all are brothers." (Applause). Anything more alien to the spirit of Confucianism than the recent happenings in South China, and particularly the schoolboy strike, I find it difficult to conceive. Allow me, therefore, to congratulate you warmly on the attitude taken up and maintained throughout these troubles by the undergraduates of the Hongkong University. It has been a very great encouragement to those who desire to see the cause of higher learning advanced, for it shows that you in incipient manhood have already put boyish folly behind you, that you have the courage of your convictions and that you are able to see through the specious fallacies of Bolshevik propaganda. (Applause). Many centuries ago your own fellow countrymen Confucius and Mencius saw far more deeply into the social and ethical needs of China than any Bolshevik emissary of to-day, and I commend to you a close study of the Chinese classics as a very wholesome antidote to much poisonous doctrine which is being spread abroad at the present time from interested motives by men who have at heart neither the good of China nor of mankind at large. (Applause).

headline: CO-OPERATION.
text:
This is Armistice Day, and it is well for us to remember that in the Great War Britain and China espoused the same cause. (Applause). As for Hongkong, not only during the Great War but for many decades before and in all the years that have followed it, this Colony has been animated by feelings of the most sincere friendship towards China at large and the Cantonese in particular. (Hear, hear). The present situation from which Canton and Hongkong alike suffer is in no way due to any act either of commission or omission by the Government or the people of Hongkong; therefore, I hope that on this auspicious day those now in authority at Canton will reconsider their position and again hold out the hand of friendship to Hongkong. If they do, we shall clasp it warmly and endeavour by cordial co-operation to remedy the harm which has been done by the Boycott.

Gentlemen, I look forward to seeing much of you during the coming months and to acquainting myself with your studies and learning something of your aims and aspirations, and I desire to assure you of my sympathy and wholehearted support in all that tends to advance the welfare of this University. (Loud applause). "who were going to help make the world of the future. It was pleasant, said Sir Matthew Nathan, to see one's successors doing bigger things than one had had the opportunity of doing and in connection with the foundation of the University, the name of Sir Frederick Lugard immediately suggested itself. "I know," said Sir Matthew, "something, at any rate, of the great work of each of his successors, and with perfect confidence I may say I know that better than any of us in helping on this Colony, as well as its University, will be your present Chancellor, my old friend, Mr. Clementi. I may say I am delighted to have been associated with his first visit to the University, and I may add that I am very grateful for the pleasant entertainments you have given to us this afternoon and for the kind references that have been made to myself."

Sir Matthew Nathan also addressed a few words to the undergraduates. He welcomed the opportunity of putting in a few days in Hongkong as he was passing through owing to his affection for the Colony and the interest he had always since felt in it. He had been fortunate in the first day of his short sojourn here to have the opportunity of appreciating what was probably the biggest of all the new things in the Colony—the University of Hongkong. (Applause) He looked upon it as the most important for the undergraduates were the people

VICE-CHANCELLOR'S THANKS. The Vice-Chancellor (Mr. W. W. Hornell) expressed thanks to His Excellency and Sir Matthew Nathan on behalf of both the Union and the University. The real sympathy of a man like his Excellency was going to mean a great deal to them. They ploughed a lonely furrow and were sometimes dazed and often despondent, and yet they knew to misquote Bernard Shaw, that the real joy of life was the being used for a purpose recognised by themselves as a mighty one. They wanted to be a force of good and not feverish, selfish little groups of elements complaining that the world did not devote itself to make them happy.

"The University of Hongkong," continued the "Vice-Chancellor," "like all true Universities, aims at training gentlemen in the truest sense of that much-abused term. Those of us who are in authority here rejoice in the courtesy and goodwill which, in spite of the storms which rage round about us, still animates the students of this University. (Applause). We believe that it is in this spirit of courtesy and goodwill, and in this spirit alone, that Hongkong, nay China, will find the issue from its present afflictions.

headline: WHAT IS A GENTLEMAN?
text:
"We remember that it was as he was setting out his idea of the University that Cardinal Newman wrote that it was almost a definition of a gentleman to say that he was one who never inflicts pain." He seldom, continued the Cardinal,'speaks of himself except when compelled, never defends himself by a mere retort.

he has no ears for slander, or gossip, he is scrupulous in imputing motives to those who interfere with him and interprets everything at its best. He is never mean or little in his disputes, never takes an unfair advantage, never mistakes personalities or sharp sayings for arguments, never insinuates evil which he dare not say out. He has too much good sense to be worried by insults, he is too well employed to remember injuries, and too indolent to bear malice. He is patient, forbearing and resigned. He submits to pain because it is inevitable, to bereavement because it is irreparable, to death because it is his destiny. Your Excellency, the Union is the centre of the social life of the students of this University. We all want that life to be as free and generous as possible. If the members of this University could, as they go out into the world beyond, take with them, as is my confident hope that they can and will take, something of that spirit of life and conversation which inspired Cardinal Newman to write those words which I have just quoted—words which burn themselves into the mind—then assumedly this University for all its many and much advertised defects will be doing something towards the deliverance of humanity from those evils which are now so sorely besetting not merely China but the world. (Applause).

The playing of the Chinese and British National Anthems concluded the proceedings.

headline: LUCKY WINNERS
text: Ten Manils residents, seven of whom are British subjects, two Spaniards and one Filipino, hold ticket No. 2651 which has won the Shanghai Champions Sweep. The men hold equal shares. It is believed this is the first time the prize has been won in Manila. All the men are employees of well known local British houses. They are reported to be Means. E. Holden, N. C. Gude, A. W. Robertson, P. Dunbar, B. J. Eggerau, J. Irvine, E. Little, A. N. D. McFarlane, Catalino and Ortiz. When Carl Laemmle, the greatest producer of films in the world, some time ago returned to America from his European tour, he said in an interview about Continental films: "I saw one picture which was really worth while, and the reason I did not buy it for America was because the high-contracting parties were in America while I was in Germany....The sheer, compelling and overwhelming force of artistry makes this picture the outstanding European production of many years." This film is the "Nibelungs."

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
The Exchange Banks will be closed to the transaction of public business on Monday, October 12.

For cheap living Timor is to be recommended since a man is passing rich on £50 a year there, according to a recently returned traveller.

Admission prices for the 9.15 performance of Harold Lloyd's great comedy "Hot Water" at the Queen's Theatre to-night are $1, $1.50 and $2 (not $2.50 as erroneously stated in one announcement).

The Chinese Government is about to publish a de luxe edition of the Chinese classics. There will be a few copies for sale at $6,000 (Chinese currency) each, and the rest will be donated to libraries in China and abroad.

"We offer a cordial welcome to the claw of the British Eastern squadron,"—so reads the legend on a packet in which picture postcards are being sold at Amanhashidate. It is rather doubtful whether the honoured crew would recognise itself as the "claw"—presumably of the British lion, says the "Japan Chronicle."

A thirsty tourist drank copiously from a roadside spring in Oregon. A sign that read, "The water is contaminated," had been placed beside the spring. An official of the Oregon Highway Department, driving by, saw the drinker and stopped to warn him; only to be met by the question, "What sort of mineral water is this? I never heard of it before." The authorities have now replaced the sign with one reading: "This water is not fit to drink."

Jacob Epstein's eighteen sculptures on the building of the British Medical Association, which opened his career as the stormy petrel of contemporary British art, will not be transferred to the association's new building, now nearing completion. These figures nearly a generation ago caused a furore in staid England and were the reproach of all academicians and were even important enough to bring down the condemnation of the churches. The doctors, apparently, do not wish to mix up with controversies over art. They will not lose on their investment, as they paid $10,000 for the sculptures and already have received offers of $30,000 for them.

The news that one of the new cruisers is to be built at Devonport has been received with great joy, for although the work is unlikely to involve the taking on of any additional men, it guarantees the constant employment for several years of the existing staff, now numbering about 12,000. It is expected that the new cruiser will be up to the Washington limit of 10,000 tons, and that she will be laid down upon the slip at present occupied by the cruiser "Cornwall." The latter vessel in all probability will be ready to leave the slip in February next, in which event the keel of the new one will be laid down in the following month.

The question, What is the queerest address in London? has brought forward an interesting article on the subject in the "Post Annual," the organ of the postalworkers of London. Probably the queerest one given is: "XXplace, Globe-road, E.I." Others nearly as original are:—

Shoulder-of-mutton alley. Frying-pan alley. Farthing fields. Pickle-herring Stairs. Crooked Billet-yard.

The complexity of the postman's problem may be understood when we learn that there are 105 Park-roads, 77 Grove-roads, 56 Victoria-roads, 13 Tennyson-roads, and 12 Shakespeare-roads, in the London district. There are also 112 Church-roads, streets, and crescents.

“The average American film is by no means an accurate portrayal of the American people. For that matter, it is not an accurate portrayal of any nation or race of people. Most of the characters presented in our photoplays are not human beings at all, as they are known, and found upon this earth. It is not the American film producer who is responsible. It is the American public. There is only about one film in every hundred released which dares to transgress, the walls of artificiality and absurdity which the American motion picture public has erected. The American public does not wish to see the truth on the screen. It does not want realism. It wants unadulterated herum. The American producers being caterers, not artists, are giving it to them. From “The Film Mercury,” a Hollywood technical newspaper.

The Australian-Oriental Line, Ltd., Captain Gambrill and owners of the S.s. "Changte" sent out invitations for a reception on board that ship from five to seven p.m. on Friday last at Manila.

Apparently the fame of our popular songs is reaching to as far as the West Coast of Africa. An “educated” native writes to a Midland firm: “I want be happy, make me happy so too. Popula song say well. Do it now. Me, big, black bess man, want plenty size gold ring for beloved. Send so long an valuable present you go.”

If Ken Wood had been in China, the King would not have had to make his moving appeal to the public to avoid littering our parks with paper and other rubbish. The Chinese regard paper as one of the "four precious things," the other three being pens, ink, and ink-slabs. They pick up every loose scrap of paper they see if it bears printing or writing upon it, and the remnants are solemnly burned.—Candide, in "The Sunday Pictorial."

A good story about that man of astonishing memory, “Datas.” Some ten years ago a friend asked him if he liked eggs to which “Datas” readily responded “Yes.” The other who frankly disbelieved in his powers, thinking his marvellous answers were a mere trick, made a careful note of the question. Then, some time ago, he met “Datas” again, and, before anything else was said, hurled at him “How?” Without the least hesitation “Datas” answered “Fried.”

The Liberal Party, which is widely regarded as almost extinct, won a striking success in a debate at the Union Society of Cambridge University recently. The motion before the house was "that this house, rejecting Conservatism, wishes to express its unqualified approval of the Liberal Party and its aims." The motion, of course, was one upon which both Conservatives and Labourites could unite against the Liberals. In spite of this, the Liberals won through by 146 votes to 152. Lord Hugh Cecil, brother of the more famous Lord Robert—now Viscount Chelwood—championed the cause of Conservatism, while the Liberal stalwart was Ramsay Muir, the historian, who edits the "Weekly Westminster."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. and Mrs. A. G. Hewitt are due to leave England for Hongkong on November 8.

The forthcoming weeding is announced of Mr. John Walter Harris, of the Kowloon Docks, to Mrs. Adola Camino, widow, of Jordan Road, Kowloon.

Dr. William Peek, the Managing Director of the London Congress of 700 American doctors, says: "The whole tragedy of modern life is that all the best citizens, the greatest men, are killing themselves before their time." He denounces the mania for overwork, overplay, and the indulgence in night life. The modern hustle is just suicide, and a return to the simple life would do away with the necessity for many doctors.

Bulletin No. 200 of the Canadian Pacific contains the following: — Canadian Pacific—As Others See Us.

A Consulate-General for the Argentine Republic was opened in Kobe on October 1, at 100, Yedo-machi. Mr. Francisco Ortis has been appointed Consul-General.

Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister has now withdrawn his resignation as President of the Board of Trade as a result of pressure from the Premier. Sir Philip tendered his resignation over the Government's subvention to the coal industry, thinking it the proper thing to do, because of his wife's large interests as a coalowner. Mr. Baldwin and his Ministers felt strongly that there was no reason whatever in the circumstances why he should resign, and Sir Philip has now come round to their point of view.

Sir William Joynson-Hicks, British Home Secretary, in an interview with the London “Morning Post” last month, characterised as “premature” the report that a special constabulary was to be recruited to safeguard the public against unrest fostered by the Communists. He admitted, however, that such a plan was under consideration, together with other “safety measures.”

During his stay in Chile, the Prince of Wales received many reminders of his grandfather's association with the Republic. Nominally King Edward acted as arbitrator between Chile and the Argentine, and his name is greatly honoured throughout the 38 degrees of latitude over which the State extends. Conventional boundaries only exist in the south, where by the award of King Edward in 1902, as a result of the examination of the disputed territories by the Commission, led by Sir Thomas Holdie, limits were established to lands where the ownership was not otherwise definable.

The annual dinner of the London Critics' Circle allows the tables to be turned for once and the critics themselves to be criticised by those whom they are in the habit of pillorying. Lord Darling, who presided, said that in proposing the health of the critics he was compelled to do a painful and unpopular thing. He asked anyone who had ever been criticised from the cradle upward to tell him whether he had ever benefited in the slightest degree from it. The court-martial of the officers and soldiers who were implicated in the April military rising at Lisbon ended in an absolvatory sentence, the generals who formed the jury deciding after five hours' deliberation that it had been proved that the revolt had been inspired by patriotic motives. Exceptional interest was attached to the court-martial throughout the country, owing to the high moral and military status of the accused, some of whom rendered distinguished service in the war. The sentence was received with public approval.

Obed Smith, Commissioner of Immigration in London for many years for the Dominion, on a trans-Canada tour, expressed the view that the Government should undertake the work of finding new markets for the grain products of Canada. Colonel Smith made the suggestion that it would be a good thing to distribute millions of loaves of wheat bread in China to accustom the Chinese to eating white bread. Mr. Smith predicted that if proper steps were taken to enlarge the Oriental market, it would within 10 years absorb a large percentage of the wheat grown on the prairies.

The debate on malaria and the suppression of the mosquito at the last meeting of the Board was certainly interesting. The President of the Board was admirably concise and convincing in his account of the work done by his Department, and in view of the fact that the problem is an almost insoluble one—more so when money to cover the cost of continuous "propaganda" is limited—the Sanitary Department deserve some praise for what they have done and are doing. But we find it discouraging to read that people who decide to "live in the country" must do so at their own risk. In other words that they are foolish to think of doing so where no anti-maternal work has been done. This is discouraging to those who desire to see the New Territories peopled, so as to relieve some of the congestion to be found on the island where, if we understand Dr. Koch's right, malaria is to be found on account of this congestion, particularly among the labouring classes, who presumably being of "the lower classes" are riddled with malaria, and are in the fact the reservoirs of it. From this it must be, adjudged that the Niving conditions of the labouring classes are not ideal, and that if there is to be concentration, it must be in the labouring districts. We are forced to the belies that the�illy report may some have some bearing on the

But the day is coming when the enlightened sanitarians of China and those of Hongkong and other places will join hands in a concerted effort to reduce the pest to a minimum. Meanwhile the labouring and poor classes are with us, providing reservoirs, and by the conditions which prevail, making malaria an ever present and disturbing element. The resolution carried at the meeting is not very determined in character. So does the public.....In any event, the discussion will have done good if it only draws attention to the danger of malaria, and to the fact that some are impregnated when a little trouble would have obviated the greater one.
