headline: TOOK FRIGHT.
text:
SAI WAN HO ROBBERY SEQUEL.

FIVE YEARS' SENTENCE.

The evasion of a police searcher at Sai Wan Ho led to the arrest of a man on suspicion of having been concerned in a robbery which took place there earlier in the day.

He was taken to the police station and at an identification parade was picked out by one of the inmates of a house in Tai On Street as the man who came in company with three others when the master of the house was away.

In evidence at the Criminal Sessions this morning the woman said that the prisoner had been armed with a dagger, had taken rings from her and gagged her.

An amah ran to a little iron bridge, outside the room adjacent to the street and called "save life." The prisoner tried to drag her back but was unsuccessful and the robbers then took fright and ran away. When the police called they found that two daggers had been cast away as the men left, also wire and wood to be used for gags.

The prisoner was arrested after evading a police searcher who fired at him and brought him down. Nothing was found on him and when charged with complicity in the robbery he said "I did not know she had been robbed." The jury convicted "and the prisoner was sentenced to five years' hard labour.

headline: CRUEL CONSTABLE.
text:
SERIOUS ASSAULT ON OLD MAN.

JAIL WITHOUT OPTION.

An Indian. Constable was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with misconducting himself and assaulting an old man at No. 112, AppIU Street. on October 15.

The evidence was that at 8.30 p.m. on the day in question an Indian constable visited the first floor of the house to search for opium. An old man objected to this intrusion and was struck across the head with a stick by the constable. Police whistles were blown, and a Chinese constable saw the defendant in the street when he should have been on duty at Cheung Sha Wan.

Defendant. denied the charge and also an allegation that he left another constable with whom he went on duty at 8 p.m.

His Worship said that he had gone carefully into the case and could see no possibility of defendant's innocence on the evidence before him. A fine of $25, or one month's hard labour, was imposed on the first charge. In respect of the second charge. His Worship said that a very serious assault had been committed on an old man, and he could not give defendant the option of a fine. The sentence was two months' hard labour on this charge.

headline: POOR CHILDREN'S EDUCATION.
text:
Another branch of work in which the Society is particularly interested is that of educating the children of the poor, to ensure the efficient management of which, an Education Sub-Committee has been organised by the Council of the Society, their chief duties being to examine and sign the weekly school reports of the students, to look after their moral and intellectual improvement and to provide them with clothes, shoes, books, stationery, etc., when required. It is gratifying to note that this new branch has been working very successfully to the satisfaction of both teachers and parents.

Owing to many of the poor having to live in small premises and congested areas constituting not only a danger to their own health but a grave moral danger for their children, it is gratifying to note that improvements have been effected and flats and cubicles in less overcrowded districts have been secured.

Other works of mercy under-taken by the Society are in connection with temporary relief and passages to Europeans and other destitutes from outside the Colony, the relief of the aged poor of the Colony at the Home in Kowloon Tong, general medical help and supply of clothing and shoes, and finding for the children under their care suitable employment. In this connection most valuable emergency work was done in the strike for which the Society has been especially thanked by the Government.

headline: C.S.C.C. MEETING.
text:
NEW OFFICIALS FOR NEXT YEAR.

Sir Claud Severn (President) presided at yesterday's annual meeting of the Civil Service Cricket Club, held in the club house, Happy Valley.

In proposing the adoption of the report, and accounts Sir Claud referred to the Club winning both divisions of the cricket league last season. The Club was grateful to Messrs. Gipson and Wood for their work on the ground, and to Mr. Squibbs for work on the green.

The balance in hand was $1,436 as against $105 last year.

The following officers were elected. (Cricket) Captain of first XI, Mr. F. J. de Rome; vice-captain, Mr. B. D. Evans. Captain "A" team, Mr. W. H. Edmonds; vice-captain, Mr. F. Squibbs. Cricket representative, Mr. F. H. Holdman; Bowls representative, Mr. R. Smith; Tennis representative, Mr. R. R. Wood; Steward, Mr. Gregory.

Hon. Secretary, Mr. R. S. Vergette; Hon. Treas., Mr. B. Maughan; Greenranger, Mr. H. Rose.

General Committee, Messrs. Deacon, Lamble, Alderman, Brawn, Harrison, Longbotham and Strange.

Proposed by Mr. Maughan and seconded by Mr. Vergette, a motion was passed authorising the committee to draw on fixed deposit account up to $2,000 for repairs and alterations to the club-house. Sir Claud presented Mr. Gregory and Mr. Rose with inscribed silver cigarette cases in recognition of their services in looking after refreshments while the club boys were on strike.

Referring to the impending departure of H.E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs), Sir Claud suggested that a letter be sent to him, as Patron of the Club, thanking him for the great honour he had bestowed and the work he had done while in the Colony. The meeting expressed approval and then Sir Claud mentioned his own departure, speaking of the pleasure it had been for him to be associated with the Club.

Mr. E. W. Hamilton spoke of Sir Claud's services since his arrival here in 1912. They were grateful for all that he had done and trusted that Sir Claud and Lady Severn would be spared to enjoy many years of retirement. Mr. Hamilton said he hoped that among Sir Claud's many recollections of Hongkong not the least pleasant would be his connection with the Civil Service Cricket Club. Replying, Sir Claud said that later, he would take a more formal leave of them.

Proposed by Mr. Alderman, the usual honorarium was voted to the hon. secretary, treasurer and steward, a member having raised the question at an earlier stage of the meeting.

Mr. James and Mr. Williams were re-elected auditors for the year. Votes of thanks were passed to outgoing officers and to Mr. Maughana.

headline: The Bairns of Falkirk.
text:
Not so obvious, however, to the general football public is the reason why Falkirk F.C. are known as the Bairns. But there is usually some local explanation in such a case, and when it is recalled that a familiar slogan in the Stirlingshire town is "Better meddle with the devil than the pairns o' Falkirk," the nickname applied to the Brockville club becomes apparent.

Ayr United are known as the Honest Men, presumably on account of the tribute paid by Burns to the Auld Toon, rather than any suggestion that the Somerset Park players are more truthful and honest than other players throughout the country. It is, however, when we come to consider the nicknames of several famous English clubs that some explanation other than the peculiar colour of their shirts is necessary to account for familiarly shouted exhortations. Hull City are known locally as the Tigers, but there is nothing ferocious about the play of the team in the great Yorkshire seaport. One can rendily understand Aston Villa respondin' to the shouts of the Villans, although the Birmingham club has such a proud record as to discount any suggestion of rascality.

Chelsea players think there is nothing derogatory in the appellation of the Pensioners, while the Toffee Makers, by which nickname Everton are known, is, of course, a reference to the brand of toffee manufactured in the district. There is some reason for New

er, as their jerseys, vivid and white stripes, at once the plumage of that inter-rd, but why Derby County known as the Rams, or the day as the Owls is not understood. Owlerton of the latter club's one answer to the ms, and West that of the Spurs; by am Hotspar

Notte: County, known as the Lambs, would scorn any special consideration being shown them on that account. Of course, with Crystal Palace, who are known as the Glaziers, the reason is pretty apparent owing to the vast amount of glass used in the construction of that huge undertaking.

Barnsley, a famous cup-fighting team, are known as the Colliers, and it is fitting a team belonging to the great East Coast fishing port, Grimsby Town, should answer to the nickname of the Mariners, while the Wolves is a handy and easily uttered substitution for the cumbersome Wolverhampton Wanderers. But why are Coventry City known as the Bantams? Surely the Midland team are not composed of players all approximating to the height and weight of Alan Morton!

Millwall answer to the name of the Dockers, and Northampton, the centre of a great bootmaking industry, to that of the Cobblers, and it is not surprising that Norwich City should be familiarly known all over the country as the Canaries. Down South, when anyone refers to the Railwaymen in a football connection, everybody knows that Swindon Town are the team in question on account of the extensive railway works in the district, while Gillingham players readily answer to the name of the Hoppers.

But perhaps the most interesting nickname of the lot is that applied to Bolton Wanderers; who are known far and wide as the Trotters. How came a famous club like the Wanderers to get a name? The explanation, even although I do not vouch for its accuracy, is interesting:

Bolton is not exactly a town of millionaires, and thousands of busy workers used to consider pigs' feet a bit of delicacy, and they were in the habit of walking through the streets gnawing away contentedly at a cooked pig's trotter. But the nickname Trotters must have been given to the Wanderers by some jealous people who do not claim Bolton as their birthplace.

headline: SOCCER ROWS.
text:
UNRULY SPECTATORS' AT GLASGOW.

CROWD, POLICE, REFEREE.

Two wild demonstrations, involving police and spectators, occurred at the beginning of the season in connection with Scottish League football games at Clydebank and Barrhead respectively.

In the first case the disorder: happened outside the Clydebank F.C.'s ground previous to the match through a number of spectators from Glasgow demanding admission at the boys' gate and being refused.

Several of the crowd received many knocks, and one man's face was covered with blood.

The second unseemly incident occurred just before the conclusion of the Arthurlie. Third Lanark-match at Barrhead, and took place immediately after Green, the Third Lanark centre-forward, had scored from a penalty, giving his side the victory.

The referee was surrounded by an angry crowd of spectators, who were, fortunately, held off by players of both sides and the police.

Several of Third Lanark's players suffered in their efforts to shield the referee.

headline: DF NEED ARISEH
text:
That the members of Hong Kong's mass meeting were not alone in their opinion. that Canton's challenge to British treaty rights called for immediate and prompt action is shown by editorial comment in the leading Home newspapers and journals at the time news reached there of the embargo on British shipping. Instancing the need for direct action, the “Telegraph” refers to the “useful, precedent” which America set a few months ago when the American naval commander threatened to use force if there was any attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America in the light of this and more weighty facts could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese of similar measures should the need for it arise.

Discussing the regulations emanating from Canton, the "Telegraph". states:—

The first is clearly designed to prevent steamers of all nationalities, "other than British and Japanese," from touching at Hongkong, under penalty of being denied an entry to Chinese ports. Does this prohibition also apply to the Chinese vessels, mostly junks, to which goods are generally transhipped from British ships at Hongkong for conveyance to Cantonese river and other southern ports? It is difficult to resist the impression that we are here witnessing a deliberate conspiracy to destroy the economic importance of Hongkong as a great commercial distributing and transhipment centre.

The various inquiries and surveys now in progress will enable a decision to be postponed by London for yet a few days, until the whole situation has been cleared up. But it is now admitted that, once the official review thereof has been completed, prompt action will have to be taken. The feeling is also gaining ground that, in such an emergency as this where the exercise of our specific Treaty rights are directly challenged, and may be denied to us by violence, there is no reason why we should consult the dozen Powers or more, whose rights are unaffected. An exchange of views between London, Tokyo, and Washington should suffice.

As a matter of fact, Washington would be unlikely to raise any substantial objections to such naval measures as we and the Japanese may be constrained to take for the protection of British and Japanese merchantmen and merchandise from physical interference by the Canton: "Reds," to judge from an American precedent a few months old. This was during the struggle for mastery at and around Shanghai between Generals Li and Chi, and the defending commander sought to restrict the freedom of foreign vessels, including American, in the estuary. The retort of the American naval commander was that he would not hesitate to frustrate, by force if necessary, any such attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America, in the light of this and other more weighty facts, could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese naval commanders off Cantonese ports of a similar line of conduct, should the need for it arise. For Chinese labour to refuse to unload British vessels is one thing; for the Chinese central or local authorities to enjoin upon Chinese labour such a course would be a totally different thing — a serious and unfriendly act, contrary to the Treaties. As for any physical molestation of our merchants or seamen, the only suitable retort would be the intervention of the British Navy. The British communities in Hongkong and South China have once more appealed to London that our naval forces in China should be strengthened and allowed greater freedom of action.

The Chinese Government's invitation to the projected Customs Conference claims the right for China to demand complete fiscal autonomy. The demand that made will probably still further prolong the exchanges of views on the subject already is not more than between the numerous Treaty Powers. The view of the British commercial leaders states the Daily Mail is that, whatever policy is adopted by the Foreign Office, it must be one of firmness and the offensive act on such as the Trading of Customs of the Five Months by excluding Chinese shipping. The serious nature of the crisis in Canton and Hongkong is revealed in messages reaching. London headquarters of firms which trade in the Far East. They indicate that the agitation has now resulted in what is virtually a national rising, and show that British trade has nowadays come to a complete standstill.

In almost every cablegram in the last few days, commercial correspondents are appealing for representations to be made to the British Government not to delay definite action further.

Their unanimous recommendation is that the position will be best dealt with by the Foreign Office immediately sending an eminent person to Perking armed with a measure of authority to negotiate an agreement.

The trade representatives declare that the want of evidence of the intention of the British Government to act has become exasperating and is depressing morale in Hongkong. "Every day's delay," states one telegram from Hongkong, "results in increasing financial exhaustion."

Reports from Hongkong and Canton state that the daily financial loss being incurred in both places is about £250,000.

Trade correspondents' messages all allude to the unfortunate absence in Britain, where he is on sick leave, of Sir J. W. R. Macleay, the British Minister to Peking.

A representative of "The Daily Mail" was informed that Sir James Macleay hopes to have recovered sufficiently to enable him to return to Peking in about three weeks.

headline: WAR NOT WANTED.
text:
We do not, of course, want to go to war with China, further states the "Daily Mail," or if we can possibly help it with any one of the domestic or alien tyrannies which usurp authority in that distracted country. With the toiling Chinese millions we have no quarrel, and we do not believe they have any hostile feeling towards ourselves; the majority are scarcely aware of our existence. Our difficulty is with the "students" and other Westernised agitators who are stirring up the mobs and rowdies of the cities at the instigation of the Russian Soviet. These persons care little for the sufferings they may bring upon Chinese peasants, by cutting off their chief source of foreign supplies, provided they can inflict loss upon Great Britain and add to the industrial depression in this country.

That they can do so, if they are allowed to maintain, the boycott they have declared, is obvious. China is one of the great markets for British manufactured commodities. For some of these products it is the greatest foreign market of all. It is Lancashire's largest customer for certain classes of cotton goods, and many mills will have to close down if the Far Eastern trade is arrested. Yorkshire will be no less badly hit. A most substantial portion of the worsteds, woollens, and dyed cloths manufactured in Bradford and the neighbourhood has been prepared for China. The woollens alone came to £8,387,000 in 1924, and the total export of these classes of goods for the year was little short of ten millions sterling.

headline: VALUABLE "LINK." / PATIENCE REWARD:
text:
The Rev. Chapman Andrews, leader of the Third Asiatic Expedition to Mongolia, reports that priceless discoveries have been made of skulls, the discoveries of the dunia dwellers and their culture, also of what might be termed the link between the age of cold blooded reptiles and warm blooded animals through the multituberente lute skull.

The following article is an appreciation of the persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending these repeated expeditions to Mongolia, with such eventual rich reward.

The persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending repeated expeditions to Mongolia appears to have been richly rewarded. Two years ago Mr. Roy C. Andrews and his scientific colleagues found fossil dinosaurs with their eggs, but this summer they have also found many traces, though no remains as yet, of paluolithic man. The reason why Professor H. F. Osborn has for many years past advocated an exploration of the fossil deposits of Mongolia may be stated very simply. That vast country is a lofty and arid plateau, with no mountains and very few rivers. Consequently, there is a good chance of finding the fossilised remains of animals in a comparatively undisturbed condition. This prediction was confirmed two years ago, when Mr. Andrews, working at a place five hundred miles within the Gobi Desert, came upon the complete skeleton of a dinosaur with the nine eggs that she had just laid before a sandstorm came and buried her. This sand, falling gently, killed but did not crush, and the great reptile, with her eggs, remained slowly fossilising through perhaps ten million years.

In Professor Osborn's view, these Mongolian dinosaurs were ancestors of the still larger land reptiles found in Western America, such as the famous diplodocus that we may see at the Natural History Museum. Indeed, he inclines to regard Mongolian as "a centre of dispersal" of animal life—as the region, that is, where the main kinds or orders developed first, and whence tuoy spread to other parts of the earth. To establish such a during hypothesis we need, of course, infinitely more evidence than is yet available, but the American scientists who have repentedly braved the tigers of the Gobi Desert in the search for fossils have, at any rate, made the theory seem plausible. This summer Mr. Andrews has discovered six mammalian skills—and the remains of a giant rhinoceros, orbitally in strata above those containing the dinosaurs.

But special interest attaches to his finding of arrowheads, spear points, drills, and the like relics of man of the Old Stone Age, because very little is known of man's presence in Mongolia in the remote past, long before the Mongols lived there. Mr. Andrews's finds should throw welcome light on the migrations of those remote ancestors of ours in the Glacial Period, who apparently roamed over the whole earth, since their weapons and tools are much the same wherever they are found; whether in England or Egypt or Turkestan. Thus the New World through Mr. Andrews and his generous porters, is helping to elucidate the earliest history of the Old

headline: SHIPPING BOYCOTT. / RELATION TO CHINA'S SINCERITY.
text:
PROOF OF THE PUDDING

The statement of one of the Chinese delegates to the Tariff Conference that it was China's wish to walk and not run; to follow Japan's, not Turkey's example, leads the "North China Daily News" to the belief that China is trying to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any power. "But," states the "N. C. D. News," the past will no, be effaced while the present shipping boycott continues.

Why is the boycott of British shipping allowed to continue? Let us use correct terms. There is no strike. Except, perhaps, for a negligible handful, the Chinese crews would gladly go to their ships. Intimidation keeps them away, the outcome of a boycott which is being actively pushed by certain parties. And we ask, why are they allowed to continue in this nefarious, wholly illegal work?

In other directions the passive warfare of the past four months has to a large extent been stopped. General Shing Shi-lien has done much for the restoration of order by closing labour union headquarters and pro-scribing strike-leaders. But no attempt to touch the Seamen's Union, the most powerful of all.

headline: CHANGE OF SPIRIT.
text:
There is no question but that General Shing Shi-lien's suppression of the agitators had the approval of Peking. In the recent past a change has come over the spirit of the capital. True, it has refused to take part in the judicial inquiry. But it has exchanged letters of a markedly conciliatory tone with the Diplomatic Body. It has sent messages to the provinces recommending the students to go back to school and instructing their betters, if the young men do not heed the advice, at least to see that there are no more demonstrations. And within its own walls Peking has even repressed such demonstrations itself. It has sent out other messages to the provinces, ordering hurried reforms in respect of likin, justice, prisons and opium. It lets it to be known that its attitude towards the Tariff Conference is entirely reasonable: China does not wish to run before she can walk; her model is to be Japan, not Turkey. In a word, everything is being done to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any Power.

But the past will not be effaced, while the shipping boycott continues. There is no parallel that we can recall of a civilised Power permitting such an act—which only open warfare could justify—against a friendly people? It is true that some British ships continue to ply, but under no conditions even approximating the normal. Within the past few days two British vessels have put in to Swatown one from north to south there other from south to north. Swatown has recently been delivered from the Reds by General Cher Chilung-ming and it might be supposed that the boycott would have ceased. But though Swatown is bursting with cargo, not a pound of it might these two vessels take. Here, clearly, was no influence of Canton at work. Whose, then, was it, and why is permitted?

We are willing to admit that what Canton chooses to do, Peking cannot prevent, although that fact does not exactly fit in with the semblance of a civilised and organised China which Peking is so anxious to present for the delusion of the Tariff Conference. But there is no practical doubt that Peking could close the Semmen's Union in Shanghai, could throttle the agitators, could lift the boycott from British shipping, if it wished. Some, at least, of the men who are promoting the boycott may easily be guessed and they are not the men who would dare to disregard such an order from Peking. As for their bullies, a file of Fengtien troops would make short work of them. It may be said that merchants cannot be compelled to ship cargo by any particular line of ships. That is, of course, true enough. But let the boycott be called off and the intimidators put down, and there will be no lack of work for any ship. Repress the minority of ringtoners and British shipping will be quite willing to take its chance with merchants in general, as it is fully entitled to do by treaty, by custom and by every written and unwritten law that governs the mutual dealings of friendly Powers.

We believe that Peking can stop the boycott and allow British ships to trade freely. Will it dare to reply that it cannot? Then here is the alternative before it. Either it can do so, and then we ask, Why does it not? Why does it aid and abut on unlawful, hostile and unparalleled act of aggression against a friendly and innocent Power? How can it have the effrontery, while openly guilty of such conduct, to be asking of that Power all sorts of concessions and privileges? If, on the other hand, Peking speaks the truth, and is unable to stop the boycott, then know can it claim to be a sovereign Government? If it cannot co-peel one section of its people to assist from conduct injurious to the prestige of the whole country, how shall it keep others in subjection on larger issues? What is the use of any Power entering into agreements with such a poor, nerveless imitation of a Government, which all the time is confessing, by unmistakeable acts, that it has no power to perform its part of any bargain?

In shipping boycott strikes at the rezoos of the tariff reform, the�arraterritoriality and every effort of conference imaginative with China. If Peking can stop it, why does it not? If it cannot, where is the sense of entering into negotiation with a thing so helpless?

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text: Comediently with Sofia amminging the signature to the Turco. Bulgarian Treaty of friendship and arbitration, Athens reports a Greece. Bulgarian frontier incident, namely that Bulgarian regulars attacked a Greek outpost at Belles, shooting a sentry and a captain dead. It says that subsequently the Bulgarists hoisted a white flag and explained that the firing was due to a misunderstanding. The Greek Government, however, despite the Bulgarian expressions of regret and the explanations made, is determined to throw full light on the incident and has ordered the Greek forces to advance to occupy certain points, whence it will be possible to ascertain the strength of the Bulgarian force.

headline: TROOPS ORDERED TO BULOARM
text:
According to an Athens telegram, the Government has decided to order Greek troops to advance into Bulgaria and occupy the town of Petritch, the headquarters of the Macedonian-Bulgarian committee, with the object of enforcing the Greek demands for satisfaction for the violation of Greek territory and the punishment of those responsible; also compensation to the relatives of those killed.

AN ULTIMATUM THEATENED. A report from Athens confirms the news that Greek detachments have been ordered to advance into Bulgarian territory to occupy Petritchi. It says that if the Greek demands are not promptly met probably an ultimatum will be addressed to Bulgaria. The Bulgarian Government proposes the formation of mixed commission of Greco-Bulgarian officers to investigate incident on the spot.

headline: TERRIBLE ORDHAL
text:
Varying reports from Damascus indicate that Damascus passed through a terrible ordeal on the 18th and 20th inst.

The city bears the scars of the relentless measures taken to suppress the riots, following the action of the French in parading the corpses of bandits in the streets.

A traveller from Damascus says that on the afternoon of the 18th inst. a band of men headed by Chief Hassan el Karreth, penetrated the Chagour quarter, shouting, "Rise up, your brother druses are here." They attacked the police post and shot dead a French officer.

The inhabitants of the quarter armed themselves and joined the insurgents. All advanced towards the Medam quarter where they were joined by the inhabitants.

A hundred Frenchmen, working with Americans in this quarter, were caught between the insturgents and another body of rebels from the town and died fighting bravely.

Suddenly an aeroplane appeared and bombed the crowds. Thanks and armoured cars and other aeroplanes followed and all joined in spreading death among the rebels who died in all directions from the terrible retribution.

The insurgents continued to fire on public and military buildings and barriers added the streets. They fired certain quarters and finally the artillery opened fire from the clitoral on the rebel quarters. The French made it known that the bombardment would not cease

The bombardment lasted from Sunday night till Tuesday. Shells destroyed the Chagour and Medan quarters, while part of the Elamidieh bazaar and other places were destroyed by fire.

The palace of Azm, one of the finest monuments in the East, was badly damaged.

Hundreds of victims are lying in the streets; probably at least 2,000 are buried beneath the demolished buildings. Apparently, Christians escaped.

The French sent 2,000 soldiers to the Christian quarters, which the insurgents had not attacked directly.

Damascus notables on the afternoon of the 20th inst. presented themselves to the High Commissioner and undertook to fulfil all the French Government's requirements.

Martial law has been declared. Anyone found with the possession of arms will be executed.

Another version says that six organised bands were working around Damascus. A band which entered Damascus on the 18th inst., composed of 40 men only under Karrath, intended to kidnap Marshal Sarrail.

The French bombarded the city to frighten the population whom they accused of connivance with the bands, and having informed the latter of the date of Marshal Sarrail's arrival in Damascus.

The rebels remained in Damascus till the 20th inst., and only -retired because their presence was taken as a pretext to

bombard the city. It is alleged that the rebels did nothing reprehensible. Karith visited the Christian quarters tranquillising them by saying, "You are our brothers."

It is also claimed that large numbers of Moslems took refuge in the Christian quarters during the bombardment and were well received.

Another version says that a band attacked Damascus to avenge themselves on the Armenians in the Medan quarter, who, it is alleged, enrolled in the French army generally.

Bands remain around Damascus, perhaps strengthened by men from Damascus, whose houses have been destroyed and whose families have been killed.

Well-informed people express the opinion that the theatre of operations will be shifted from Jebel Druse to the Damascus region, where bands are being well organised and believed to be composed of thousands seeking revenge.

"The Martin" says that the latest telegrams from Syria are very disquieting. Damascus, where order is far from re-established, has been abandoned by its population, and the Druses who submitted have now broken faith. The situation is not critical but sufficiently serious to demand urgent measures on the part of the Government.

headline: GERMANY'S EXCITING ELECTIONS.
text:
CANTON STRIKERS GROWING UNPOPUARITY EVIDENCED LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

The growing unpopularity in Canton of the strikers has been emphasised in earlier reports, one of its outward manifestations being the driving away of strike pickets attempting to interfere with the landing of passengers from the "Honam". From later reports it would appear that now the military have barred the landing of passengers, but this is not indicative of antagonism between the two factions having been dropped. The Canton authorities have decided to make a determined effort to make their section of the railway pay, now that the anti-Red forces are away from the railway area, and the banning of "Honam" passengers is part of this scheme.

In other directions the Canton Government is expressing its determination to curb the power of the strikers, the merchants having made representations of indignation that they should be called upon to pay so much in taxes while the strikers make a good thing of the strike in the matter of squeeze. A cargo of considerable value which was confiscated by the strikers had to be returned by them on instructions from Dr. C. C. Wu.

The class of strikers who in Canton itself have by far the greater power is curiously enough that of the barbers and cooks. It will be recalled in this connection that on Central Black Wednesday slightly over a year ago the barbers' guild was largely responsible for the conflagration and massacre which followed. When Saikwan was held by the merchants and Dr. Sun's Red forces could not get in, the barbers inside the western suburb are alleged to have let in the Reds and started tires themselves in many places. The power of the barbers and cooks at the present moment is confined, however, to Caiton whilst at Shekki, Kongmoon, Namtau, Taiping, Chinshan and other outlying places power is in the hands of the seamen, trans-Pacific seamen being the more active section and the coastal, seamen more passive.

A publication entitled "the Empire Rebel" was mentioned in the resumed proceedings against twelve Communists at Bow Street. A police sergeant who gave evidence of finding literature at the Communist headquarters, including "a circular" to which the "Empire Rebel" was attached, declared that apparently it circulated amongst factory workers.

The witness produced another circular addressed to Losovsky, Moscow, also to the secretary of the Berlin branch of the Moscow International, complaining of the non-receipt of promised funds. Counsel for the prosecution declared the letter related to money promised to be sent to England, but not sent.

The cause was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: TRAIN'S CRASH.
text:
COACHES FALL INTO RAVINE.

LONELY SPOT DISASTER.

A north-bound passenger train was derailed and rolled down in embankment near Victoria, Mississippi.

Ten people are reported killed, and 20 injured.

The ill-fated train called the Sunnyland Express was crossing a trestle bridge at 50 miles an hour. The engine and luggage van got safely across but the remainder of the coaches crashed into the rayine.

Most of the casualties occurred in three coaches which dived headlong on to a clay bank, the other coaches falling on them, forming a tangled mass of wreckage. The scene is lonely and isolated, and many died before a relief train could be rushed to the place.

headline: HOME RUGGER.
text:
EVIL OF PLACE-KICKING NEGLECT.

NOTES AND COMMENT

(By H. P. Marshall, Oxford Blue & Vice Capt., Harloquins XV.)

London, Oct. 10. Of Services players, I notice that our old friend Luddington is starting the season well for the Devonport Services. Though he may be a little past his best now, he is still a great player, and a thundering hard worker. Moreover, he can kick goals, and, though I have said it before, I may say it again, that it is high time that more attention were paid to the art of place-kicking. There is no reason why the general standard should be so poor. The root of the matter lies in keeping the eye on the ball, as in golf, and in good footwork. That may sound obvious, but I do not mean good work with the kicking foot but placing the other foot so that the kick is delivered with the maximum accuracy and power. Many players charge at the ball savagely, as if they intended to scare it over the bar; the wise man is deliberate about the business, and sees that he stands neither too near nor too far away. Manchester have done well in electing that great player, A. L. Gracie, captain—for this season. There is, I think, more of a touch of genius about his play than about that of any other player who has appeared since the War. He tells me that he has a very young side, whose average age is about twenty-two, but who are full of promise. That is far better than a team of cunning grandfathers, who will all retire from the game about the same time, and leave chaos behind them. Another great outside, Eddie Myers, started the season brilliantly for Bradford. He almost won their match against Manchester off his own bat, scoring one of those amazing tries when he seems to fade through the opposition as if he were a ghost. P. D. B. Spence, the well-known tennis player, is doing very well this year at full-hack for Guy's. The Hospital should have a fairly good season, for they still have in addition to Spence such tried outsides as J. G. Von Schalkwijk, C. L. Steyn, and G. Fellowes Smith, while in the serum W. H. Myburgh, J., Schabort, and E. Hutchinson are turning out for them again. Hutchinson is a most useful forward powerful and hard working, a real follower of the Guy's

Their great rivals, Bart's, are captained this year by R. H. Bettington. He has with him in the serum such excellent forwards as A. W. L. Rowe, E. S. Vergette, and W. S. headline: END OF STRIKE
text:
SIGNIFICANT CANTON MEETING

PEACH NEBLERS NIRST

Considerable significance is attached to a meeting of all four commercial associations (or chambers) in Canton on Monday when the subject discussed by the Chinese merchants was again the end of the strike.

The meeting, which was informal, agreed that something must be done to end the present situation. A proposition was carried that a working committee, composed of two members of each association, sound all classes of opinion in Canton, and report to a mass meeting which will decide the steps to be taken.

News of Strikers

According to a special report to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," the Canton Strike Executive has forbidden (Canton) pressmen to attend their meetings or call at headquarters.

Another message concerns the corps of "special investigators" of strikers formed to supervise the pickets. Apparently discord has set in between the investigators and the pickets.

headline: COTTON TRADE.
text:
To transpires that only an informal exchange of views occurred between Mr. N. U. Wadia, Chairman of the Bombay Mill Owners Association, and the Manchester trade representatives. It is understood that the object of his visit is to secure, if possible, the co-operation of the leaders of the Lancashire cotton industry with the Bombay millowners in legislative action against Japanese competition and the depreciation of Japanese exchange which is said to have created havoo with the sale both of Lancashire and Bombay cotton goods. It is alleged that the Japanese are disregarding the hours and conditions of labour agreed upon in the Washington Convention. The Bombay millowners say that this has compelled them to reduce wages 11½ per cent., which has led to the present strike. It is understood that Mr. Wadia will continue his discussions in Lancashire during the week. In this connection it is noteworthy that a suggestion has been made for the abolition of the 3½ per cent. excise duty on Indian woven cloth which it is said suffers competition with Japanese coarse counts but does not compete with Lancashire's finer counts. Lancashire, however, appears to favour a simultaneous similar reduction of eleven per cent. in the Indian import duty on Lancashire cloth.

Portland, Maine, November 10.—An Army steamer, laden with explosive powder, suspected to be a rum runner by a coastguard patrol boat, found one pound shells being aimed at her before she was able to signal her identity. Not recalling that she was pursued she had veered off and put on steam. The commander of the patrol boat explained later that the circumstances looked most suspicious as the vessel had cases piled up on deck and appeared to be fleeing.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: POSITION IN NORTH. (Reuter's Service.)
text:
Fengtien cavalry have occupied Hsiangho-hsien in addition to Sanhohsien and are advancing on Tungchow.

The Kuominchun (People's Army) is apparently prepared to evacuate Tungchow without fighting.

The Chief Executive, Tuan Chi-jui, is still striving to maintain peace between Fengtien and the Kuomtuchun.

He called a Cabinet meeting yesterday afternoon and urged Mr. Mo Teh-hui, who is an adherent of Chang Tso-lin, to wire to the Marshal, stating that the Kuominchun entertained no hostility towards Fengtien, and asking why the Fengtienites were penetrating the metropolitan area. Mr. Mo Teh-hui accordingly telegraphed to that effect.

Confirmation is to hand of the evacuation of Hsuchowfu by the Fengtien troops.

The town has been occupied by the allied armies, without fighting.

It is notified in Command Orders that Captain G. A. Clements restless, receiving a gratuity, October 7, 1925. Captain Clements is now head of the Shameen police. Also that Captain H. J. Hardiman restles on retired pay, October 8, 1925.

Shanghai, November 10.—The International Commission of Judges investigating the Shanghai affair of May 80, has closed its report which has been forwarded to Peking and the Commissioners will return home at the earliest opportunity.—Reuter.

headline: LAST 15 MINUTES EXCITING LOCAL HOCKEY MATCH
text:
HOW TO GET GOALS

With the score in goal to nil against them 16 minutes from time, the defence of the Hongkong Hockey Club 1st XI suddenly had the inspiration to teach the forwards how to put the ball between the uprights and the Surrey Regiment were defeated by 4-1 when time was called.

This excellent match was played on the U.S.R.O. ground, Kowloon, on Wednesday.

At half-time the Surreys, were a goal up, Lout Dickens playing wing forward, having found the mark.

When only about a quarter of an hour was left Woodward gave a nice pass to Mitchell and the skipper, playing centre-half made the score 1 all.

A few minutes later, Mitchell took the ball on the right and centred accurately. Furqtharson (at buck) covered very well and stepped into Mitchell's place to shoot and give the Club the lead.

Then followed a short period. determined pressure by the Infant-trymen. After Mills (goalie) had rushed out Mitchell saved a possible goal. In the last five minutes the Club forwards showed that they had profited by the example set by their colleagues behind. One or two new men in the forward line did not tend to the best combation and the string hardly got going. But Allan (inside right) put on two goals and the attack thereby made amends in those last five minutes.

The Surrey halves played ex-ordinarily well. Caption Allfree at centre-half. Lieut. Clid-on at left-half and another at right-half all showing up to decided. advantage. Lieut. Dickens and the centre-forward being very speed.

The form of the Club forwards has already been described. Mills played a sound game in goal for the Club, and the backs were safe. The day's honours, however, went to the Club halves, the combined showing of the half-back line being the best displayed by the Club for quite considerable time.

The Club team, as announced, was:—P. W. F. Mills, A. P. T. Farquharson, D. H. Sberman, A. S. Hett, P. J. R. Mitchell Captain), E. W. T. Marlin, J. Prior, R. C. Allen, W. Woodward, G. H. Vallack, and G. P. Laumont

headline: DR. GREENTELL REOBENT CHINA VISIT
text:
CHRISTIANITY AND BOLSHEVIEM Dr. Wilfred Greenfield, the famous missionary and explorer, who recently visited China and spent a short time in Hongkong, writes on his impressions as follows: The Bolshevik element is various menaces. At present it is mainly among students. But the prop成一 at the end of his life it made an impression upon on Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The Reds are, moreover, now sending forty Mongolian students to Moscow, and have actually fully away in outer Mongolia. The resistance to it is another indication of Chinese character. For there is no question that Chinese have much reason to complain of foreigners of sorts, and of imperialism that has been cruel, repressive and reactionary. Grin and bear it, or keep smiling, is, so some think, too much a characteristic of the Chinese. It might well be said of China today that she doesn't yet know what she wants; but, unlike what was claimed for the Irish, she seems to the stranger too content without it, though she has sense to know that Bolshevism is no way out.

The first great fact that strikes any rational human being with a soul all along this crowded cadre of humanity is the extraordinary depth to which already Christian missionaries have dug themselves into the hearts of the Chinese. It is to some extent true that a so-called anti-Christian, really a Bolshevik and anti-foreign movement, is going on—but in any case that could only mean that the power of Christianity really is being felt, and is an excellent proof of a fact which any man cannot help seeing, if he looks, and as the Scotch say, "uses his powers of observation." Still travellers easily miss the ways in which this is coming about, come to wrong conclusions about missions, and carry away wrong impressions altogether of their immense value in the struggle toward world peace. It is scarcely possible, however, to blame round-the-world trippers, who can barely be classed as travellers, as their time and opportunities available are so limited. Even those in business do not take time as a rule to make their own observations, and this has also been one's experience of many even in political life.

Dr. Grenfell is of the opinion that Union Colleges, Union Hospitals, Union Churches and other Christian efforts are giving new strength to the drive for "peace on earth" in all parts of China and thinks that the public school spirit which is taught in Christian educational institutions is a good ground for the gradual absorption of more civilised ideals.

What, however, surprised us perhaps most was that we couldn't get off at a city anywhere, however primeval looking or snelling, without finding a mission hospital, or school, or Christian effort of some sort, sweetening the atmosphere. Don't let anyone at home worry about things they read in the papers re anti-Christian efforts. The men in the field are not a bit disturbed. No one knows better that God is on His Throne. Most of these reports are like those of Mark Twain's death, " greatly exaggerated. Anyhow, no one expects the way of the Cross—which by the bye is the way all real evolution of every kind—to be wheeling a perambulator down the sidewalk any more than it was formerly, or will be in the future. The wagging of the devil's tail is the best sign manual of Christian activity—it won't hurt the real spiritual Church, of which George Adam Smith said, "There is no danger that it will be destroyed by being blown up, but only from being sat upon by endless numbers of indifferent nobodies." Moreover, the Chinese are a wiser race than many take them for—and their hearts are human and can tell the real thing from the false. Or, in other words, they know a good thing when they see it, as their attitude to missions has amply testified in the past. The Boxer outrage was an anti-Imperial political movement, cleverly switched by the reactionary Empress-Dowager into an anti-foreign and only so an anti-Christian one.

headline: BAG OF REDS.
text: Following a police raid on the British Communist Party headquarters in London, three lorry loads of literature were removed and six prominent Communists arrested, including the secretary, Mr. Irkpin, Mr. Harry Pollatt, who is the "Party's principal operator," Mr. Campbell, Editor of the "Worker's Weekly" who became notorious last year dutying the Labour Government's regime when the prosecution abandoned a sedition charge against him.

headline: ARREST AT GLASGOW.
text:
Two more communist leaders, Thomas Bell and William Gallacher were arrested this morning at Glasgow and Paisley respectively. The six arrested last evening were charged at Bow Street with conspiring to incite sedition and mutiny, and remanded for a week. The three in addition to those mentioned are Thomas Winningham, a member of the staff of the "Workers' Weekly," Ernest Cant, of London, an organiser of the Communist party and William Rust, secretary of the young Communist League.

The communists charged at Bow Street have been released on bail of £100 each.

Paris, October 15.—Replying to a member of the Finance Commission M. Painleve stated that the French losses in the campaign in Syria up to July last were 10,042. He promised to supply the figures of losses up to September 30.—Renter.

headline: QUILUTION OF PRIORITY
text:
The Tokyo correspondent of the Observer has the following comments to make on the wireless triangle in China brought about by the action of China in selling identical interests to three countries.

Information has been received from China reporting a wireless triangle which is of international importance, especially with the Conference in sight. According to apparently, authoritative newspaper reports from Peking, the American Minister has demanded confirmation of the American Federal Wireless Company's concession as a condition of the American Government's favourable and sympathetic attitude at the Conference. On the other hand, the "Japanese Minister demands that the Chinese shall demonstrate their good faith by confirming a similar prior concession to the Mitsui Company.

One outstanding fact is clearly that China sold identical concessions separately to two, and possibly three, firms, representing Mitsui, the Federal Wireless, and the British Marconi. Each in turn protested through its respective Government, but China became in different when the transactions were completed. Now the day of reckoning has arrived, and Peking proposes to compromise by a merger of the Japanese and American interests, so that wireless in China would be conducted by the joint management of the three countries, and, for American loan would be secured by the proceeds of the money policy.

Despatches from Peking, announce this proposal as having remained from America, but Japan apparently does not favour it. The situation contains elements of humour, and also of serious danger. Continuous propaganda from China spreads suspicion of the American motive. Some newspapers assert that Britdin and America have combined against Japan's and are seeking to "steal valuable concessions" for which Japan has already found and capitalised heavily.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text:
Englishmen's Foreign Titles.

My reference to the Maltese title which Sir Gerald Strickland has the Royal permission to use, has prompted a correspondent to send me the names of some of the other Englishmen who bear foreign titles which they do not use in England. Among them are Sir Herbert Cook, the art critic, who is Viscount Montserrate in Portugal; Sir Edward Barry, who is Baron de Barry in the same country; and Sir Alexander Nelson Hood, at once time private secretary to Queen Mary, is Duke of Bronte in Sicily. Amongst the peers, the Duke of Wellington is Prince of Waterloo in the Netherlands: Duke of Ciudad Roderigo in Spain, and Duke of Victoria, Marquis of Torres Vedras, and Count of Vimira in Portugal. The Duke of Richmond is Duke of Ambigny in France; and the Earl of Clancarty is Marquis of Heusden in the Netherlands, writes "Gad-about" in the "Daily Chronicle."

The miners' secretary, Mr. A. J. Cook, has a far different temperament from that of the solid, tenacious Mr. Smith. He is mercurial and emotional, and has been described by our Labour Correspondent as the "Peter Pan" of industrial affairs. He has a great gift of fervid rhetoric, but his famous declaration that he is a humble disciple of Lenin need

supervision of the Propelator.

headline: ACTRESS
text:
COMING ATTRACTION

How many foreigners living in the Far East have ever taken the trouble, on have even had the opportunity, to make the acquaintance of the Chinese theatre and Chinese acting?

Amongst those of the more venturesome sort who have penetrated into Chinese localities, the impression has generally been a confused mixture of noise, glare and discomfort.

Now we in Hongkong are to have opportunity to-morrow week of seeing, under comfortable conditions, the one actress in China who, by her personality and wonderful command over her art, can take her place on the same plane as the famous Mei Lan-fang.

Miss Pik Wen-ha is coming to the Theatre Royal in response to numerous requests from those who have paid a visit to the Taiping Theatre and have been impressed by her wonderful acting. Having come under the spell of her charm themselves, they wish others of the foreign community, who do not care to go to West Point and sit through the long hours of a complete Chinese play to have the opportunity of seeing for themselves just so much of the wonderful acting of this charming actress as will give them an insight into a world undreamed of and unexplored by the great majority of foreigners in the Far East.

The usual Chinese play is a matter of hours, and often days. What Miss Pik Wen-ha is going to do is to select scenes from three of her most famous plays, representing tragedy and farce, finishing up with a scene from a comedy which introduces a famous dance composed for the beautiful Yang Kuei-fei, the favourite concubine of the Tang Ming Emperor, of the Tong Dynasty.

These scenes will take about thirty minutes each, and in between, in the 15 minute intervals, the audience will have another surprise. We all have an idea that we know what Chinese music is—a mixture of discordant and ear-splitting noises accompanied by the banging of drums and the beating of cymbals. On this occasion we shall be introduced to a form of Chinese music that, except to those foreigners who are privileged to be admitted to the real Chinese life, is absolutely unknown to us. A really wonderful orchestra of stringed instruments, played by leading Chinese amateurs, will give a selection of old and most interesting Chinese music. This in itself makes the performance one that will stand (Reuter's Service.)

— Malbourne, Nov. 14.

A record poll is assured at to-day's election owing to the compulsory voting.

Mr. S. M. Bruce's final appeal to the electors, particularly the women, declares:

"The paramount issue is the maintenance of the supremacy of constitutional government."

Though bitter class-feeling has been aroused the campaign has generally been very orderly.

The main points of Mr. Bruce's platform are a promise of national insurance legislation, insistence on secret ballots in trade unions before a strike is decided upon; a proposal to subsidize road construction in order to facilitate the transport of farm produce, and a proposal that Parliament vote twenty millions to build cottage homes for city workers.

The Labour Party devoted its energies to denouncing the Red menace as an election bogey, declaring the constitutional Labour Party is more qualified to deal with extremists than the reactionaries.

Both sides especially appeal to the hitherto unpolled non-Party electors, the Ministerialists asking for a mandate to deal with alleged dangerous elements in the community and the Labourites warning the electors not to be influenced by side issues.
